title: 📚 Era 7 Works: Post-War, Postmodern & Contemporary Era
subtitle: Verify publication dates, summaries, characters, storylines & exam traps for 711 works

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first book of English poems, full of mystic joy, colour, and youthful excess.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1918 is correct, but the fiction label and the posthumous badge are wrong. It is a poetry book. The Theosophical Publishing House at Adyar printed it in 1918. He died only in 1990.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is his first book of poems, published when he was nineteen.
The opening poem promises to offer the blue of the sky like wine.
Sri Aurobindo reviewed it and heard a mystic joy in God and Nature.
The verse joins Hindu thought with a Sufi love of colour and image.
James Cousins wrote a foreword.
The book appeared in his lifetime.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A boy of nine raises a young elephant named Kari in the jungle.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1922 is correct. Dutton published this children's animal story. The catalogue calls it poetry. That label is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The boy narrator (A nine year old keeper who cares for Kari); Kari (A young elephant who learns jungle life and saves a drowning boy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dutton published Kari the Elephant in 1922.
The boy narrator is nine when Kari is given to him.
Kari is five months old and lives under a thatched roof.
Kari saves a boy from drowning.
Later the elephant tells a jungle tale his mother taught him.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1922 poetry book whose title he took from lines by the Irish poet George Russell.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1922 is correct. It is a poetry book. Do not confuse it with The Parrot or The Window.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This 1922 book continues his early mystic poetry.
He took the title from lines by George Russell, the Irish poet called AE.
Cambridge allowed him to use this book, with two others, for a thesis.
The planned subject was William Blake and Blake's Eastern links.
It belongs with his poetry, not with the social plays of 1937.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The short catalogue title for the 1927 story of a carrier pigeon.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1927 is correct for the book. This short title and the full title name one Dutton novel. The Newbery Medal came in 1928. The poetry label is a catalogue error.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The boy (The young owner and trainer of the pigeon); Gay-Neck (A prized carrier pigeon, also called Chitragriva); Ghond (A hunter who travels with the boy and the pigeon)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This slug is the short title of the 1927 Dutton book.
The full title is Gay-Neck: The Story of a Pigeon.
Keep this entry separate.
It is not a second story.
A boy trains the pigeon Gay-Neck, also called Chitragriva.
The bird serves as a messenger in France during World War I.
After the war, monks help the bird lose its fear.

items.title: "Gay-Neck: The Story of a Pigeon" (1927) — Dhan Gopal Mukerji

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Gay-Neck: The Story of a Pigeon

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A carrier pigeon from India faces hawks, war, and fear.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1927 is the publication year. The Newbery Medal followed in 1928. This full title and the short catalogue title name the same book. The poetry label is a catalogue error.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gay-Neck (The carrier pigeon whose life the book follows); The boy (The young master, based partly on Mukerji's own boyhood); Ghond (The hunter who goes with Gay-Neck to the war and the monastery)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dutton published the novel in 1927, with pictures by Boris Artzybasheff.
Gay-Neck loses his father in a storm and his mother to a hawk.
Ghond the hunter and the boy take him into the wild.
Fear drives him to a lamasery (a Buddhist monastery), where monks calm him.
In World War I he carries messages in France and is badly frightened.
The American Library Association gave the book the 1928 Newbery Medal.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two friends leave city ambition and return to rebuild a Tamil village.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1927 is correct. Internet Archive and the Triveni essay agree. Svetaranya Ashrama in Madras published it. It is fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ramu (The steady friend who chooses village work. One review also calls him Ramachandran.); Kedari (The lawyer friend who chases quick wealth, then falls); Murugan (The tiller of Ramu's fields, later drawn into crime)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ramu is a steady government clerk.
Kedari is a lawyer who wants fast success.
Murugan, who tills Ramu's land, is pulled into crime.
Kedari falls at the height of his city career.
Ramu leads a plan to build a reservoir on the river Arni.
They found a new village, Meenakshipuram, and Ramu refuses a high government post.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A civil service officer leaves his post and dies in the freedom struggle.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The serial in Swarajya is 1931. The book year is 1932. Wikipedia, the Triveni essay, and Internet Archive agree on the 1932 book. Use 1932 in the exam.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kandan (A former civil service officer who dies at a protest); Rangan (A friend who hopes to reform the government from within); Rajeswari Bai (A patriot who puts the nation above marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Kandan gives up the Indian Civil Service at the start of his career.
His friend Rangan hopes to change the state from inside the government.
Rajeswari Bai puts the nation above marriage.
The plot follows Civil Disobedience, which means peaceful refusal of unjust laws.
Kandan is killed by a stray bullet at a banned public meeting.
The tale ran in the daily Swarajya in 1931 and became a book in 1932.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An Irishman in London tries to live inside his own mind.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1938 is correct for the first edition. Routledge published it in 1938. It was written in English. Beckett's French version came in 1947. The database translation flag does not fit the original book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Murphy (A man who prefers the life inside his mind); Celia Kelly (The woman who tries to pull Murphy back into work and love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Murphy wants peace by withdrawing from the outer world.
Celia, who loves him, wants him to find work.
He takes a job at a mental hospital and plays chess there.
The outer search for Murphy runs beside his inner retreat.
The comedy is dark, and the body never quite lets the mind go.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An ageing woman drifts through Paris, drinking and reliving an unhappy past.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Constable published the novel in 1939. Britannica and the novel page agree on that year. The database year 1939 is correct. A radio version by Selma Vaz Dias was broadcast by the BBC in 1957. That broadcast is not the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sasha Jansen (A middle aged Englishwoman alone in Paris between the world wars)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sasha Jansen returns to Paris with a little borrowed money.
She drinks, takes sleeping pills, and worries about her looks.
Memory brings back a failed marriage and the death of her child.
The city is both a refuge and the scene of old pain.
The bleak mood put many 1939 readers off, and Rhys then fell from public view.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Muslim family in old Delhi watches its world fade under British rule.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1940 is correct. The Hogarth Press published the English novel in 1940. Later reprints include Oxford University Press. The first edition is not 1966.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mir Nihal (The patriarch whose household stands for old Muslim Delhi)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel follows Mir Nihal and his family in old Delhi.
The years run from about 1911 to 1919.
Old courtly habits belong to a fading Muslim world.
British power and family loss move forward together.
Evening light at the close marks a whole way of life dying.

items.title: "The Naked Shingles and Other Stories" (1941) — Manjeri Isvaran

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Naked Shingles and Other Stories

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first English short-story collection, and the book that made his name.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1941 matches notes on his first story collection. Some catalogues title it Naked Shingles, without The and without and Other Stories.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He published this first story collection in 1941.
The Indian English short story was still a young form then.
The pieces are short, carefully written pictures of Indian life.
A later tribute calls this book the craftsman in the making.
Students must date this collection to 1941 and call it fiction.

items.title: "A Dance of the Forests" (1963) — Wole Soyinka

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: At independence, the living call the dead and meet a guilty past, not a golden one.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is only a period label. Soyinka wrote and staged it in 1960 for Nigerian independence. Oxford University Press published it in 1963. The Nobel bibliography confirms the 1963 book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Demoke (A carver whose skill and guilt return in the forest); Rola (A woman linked with an older figure of desire and harm); Dead Man (An unwelcome ancestor invited by the independence feast); Adenebi (A council figure whose past self is a court historian)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the most recognized play of Soyinka.
The play was presented at Nigeria Independence celebration in 1960.
It denigrated the glorious African past and warned Nigerians and all Africans that their energies henceforth should be spent trying to avoid repeating the mistakes that have already been made.
Nigeria's independence celebration wants noble ancestors as guests.
The forest instead sends a Dead Man and other uneasy dead.
Living people repeat old crimes of power, war, and betrayal.
Demoke the carver, Rola, and Adenebi face their earlier selves.
Gods and forest spirits, including Ogun, judge the gathering.
Soyinka warns that a new flag does not clean the past.

items.title: "A Good Man Is Hard to Find" (1955) — Flannery O'Connor

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A Good Man Is Hard to Find

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Georgia family driving to Florida is killed by an escaped convict called the Misfit.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year only opens the postwar period. The story first appeared in the anthology Modern Writing I in 1953. Harcourt, Brace published her collection A Good Man Is Hard to Find in 1955. Use 1955 for the book and 1953 for the story alone.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The grandmother (Bailey's mother, who causes the wrong turn and then faces the Misfit); Bailey (Her son, who drives the family toward Florida); The Misfit (An escaped convict who has the family killed and shoots the grandmother); Red Sammy Butts (The owner of the Tower restaurant, whom the grandmother calls a good man)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bailey drives his family from Georgia toward Florida.
His mother, called only the grandmother, wants to go to Tennessee instead.
She warns them that a convict called the Misfit is loose.
She hides the cat, remembers a false road, and the car crashes.
The Misfit and two men kill Bailey and the children in the woods.
The grandmother calls the Misfit one of her babies, and he shoots her.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Elizabeth, a South African exile in Motabeng, fights a breakdown and two inner figures of power.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year only opens the postwar period. She began the novel in 1971 and finished it in 1972. Davis-Poynter in London published it in October 1973. A New York edition followed in 1974.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elizabeth (A mixed race South African woman living in exile in Motabeng); Sello (A village farmer who appears in her visions as a holy figure); Dan Molomo (A man who appears in her visions as a cruel power); Shorty (Elizabeth's young son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Elizabeth leaves South Africa and lives in the Botswana village of Motabeng with her son Shorty.
By day she teaches and works in a village garden.
At night Sello appears in her mind as a figure like a monk.
Then Dan Molomo appears, a cruel figure of evil power.
The visions drive her into a mental hospital.
She returns to the garden and chooses to go on living.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Blanche DuBois seeks shelter in New Orleans and is destroyed by Stanley Kowalski.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is the period shelf, not the play year. It opened at the Ethel Barrymore Theatre in New York on 3 December 1947. New Directions published the book in 1947. The Pulitzer Prize for Drama came in 1948. The Elia Kazan film is 1951.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Blanche DuBois (A fragile former Southern belle who comes to her sister's flat); Stella Kowalski (Blanche's younger sister, torn between Blanche and her husband); Stanley Kowalski (Stella's rough husband, a war veteran and factory worker); Harold Mitchell (Mitch) (Stanley's friend, who courts Blanche and then turns away)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Blanche arrives in New Orleans to stay with her sister Stella.
She has lost the family house, Belle Reve, and she hides her past.
Stanley, Stella's husband, resents Blanche and checks her story.
Mitch courts Blanche, then rejects her after Stanley spreads the gossip.
Stanley assaults Blanche.
A doctor leads her away at the end.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Nathan Zuckerman tells how a Newark hero loses his daughter to 1960s violence.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Houghton Mifflin published this novel on 12 May 1997. Wikipedia dates the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction to 1998. It is the first book of the American Trilogy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nathan Zuckerman (The narrator, a writer who recreates the Swede's life); Seymour Levov (the Swede) (A Jewish Newark athlete who becomes a glove manufacturer); Meredith Levov (Merry) (The Swede's daughter, who becomes a bomber); Dawn Dwyer (The Swede's wife, once a beauty queen); Jerry Levov (The Swede's brother, who tells Zuckerman the family story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
7. I Married a Communist (1998)
At a 1995 school reunion, Nathan Zuckerman hears about Seymour Levov.
People called Levov the Swede, a blond star athlete and glove maker.
He marries Dawn Dwyer and builds a calm life in Old Rimrock.
Their daughter Merry, angry about the Vietnam War, bombs a post office.
A local doctor dies, and Merry disappears into radical hiding.
The Swede learns that his American Dream was thinner than it looked.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ifemelu leaves Nigeria for America, writes about race, and later returns.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database calls this poetry and sorts it at 1945. Both labels are wrong. It is a novel. Knopf published it in 2013, and her own site dates it 2013.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ifemelu (A Nigerian woman who studies in America and writes a race blog); Obinze (Her first love, who goes to London and later grows rich in Nigeria)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ifemelu and Obinze fall in love as students in Lagos.
Ifemelu goes to the United States and learns what race means there.
She becomes known for a blog about race in America.
Obinze is refused an American visa and lives for a time in London.
Years later both are back in Nigeria and face their old love.
Alfred A. Knopf published the novel in 2013.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A girl's false accusation ruins two lives, and her later novel tries to atone.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database sorts the novel at 1945. That is the period start. Jonathan Cape published it in 2001. It was shortlisted for the Booker that year and did not win.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Briony Tallis (The child writer whose lie sends Robbie to prison); Cecilia Tallis (Briony's sister, who loves Robbie and cuts off her family); Robbie Turner (The housekeeper's son, wrongly accused, later a soldier); Lola Quincey (Briony's cousin, who is attacked in the dark); Paul Marshall (Leon's rich friend, the real attacker, later Lola's husband)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jonathan Cape published the novel in 2001.
In the summer of 1935, Briony Tallis is thirteen and wants to be a writer.
She misreads the love of her sister Cecilia and Robbie Turner.
She tells the police that Robbie attacked her cousin Lola.
The attacker was Paul Marshall, but Robbie goes to prison and then to war.
As an old woman, Briony admits she invented a happy ending for the lovers.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Rosa Burger faces her dead father's life in the fight against apartheid.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database has no year and sorts the book at 1945. That is a period placeholder. Jonathan Cape published it in June 1979.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rosa Burger (The daughter who studies her parents' political life); Rosa's father (A white Communist lawyer and anti-apartheid martyr); Bram Fischer (The real lawyer, defender of Nelson Mandela, behind the father figure)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rosa Burger is the child of white Communist parents in South Africa.
Her father becomes a martyr of the anti-apartheid movement.
Gordimer called the book a coded homage (a hidden tribute) to the lawyer Bram Fischer.
After the Soweto uprising of 1976, Rosa must choose her own path.
Jonathan Cape published the novel in London in June 1979.
South Africa banned it in July 1979, then lifted the ban.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Captain Yossarian tries to stop flying, but a mad army rule keeps him in the war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year only opens the postwar period. Heller began it in 1953. A chapter appeared in 1955 under the title Catch-18. Simon and Schuster published Catch-22 on 10 October 1961. The film is 1970.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Yossarian (A captain and bombardier who tries to survive the missions); Colonel Cathcart (The commander who keeps raising the number of required missions); Doc Daneeka (The squadron doctor who explains the catch); Milo Minderbinder (The mess officer who turns the war into a business)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Yossarian is a bombardier with a US air unit on the island of Pianosa.
Colonel Cathcart keeps raising the number of missions needed to go home.
A doctor can ground a flier who is crazy.
But asking to be grounded proves that the flier is sane.
That trap is Catch-22.
Yossarian watches friends die, then learns that Orr has reached Sweden.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A large gathering of her poems on land, history, love, and loss.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database sorts this title at 1945. That is the period start, not the book year. The first Collected Poems 1942-1970 came out in 1971. Collected Poems 1942-1985 followed in 1994.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of South of My Days (A voice looking at the tableland and its old stories); Old Dan (An old man in that poem who tells tales of droving (moving cattle))

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Angus and Robertson of Sydney published Collected Poems 1942-1970 in 1971.
The book gathers poems from her earlier volumes, starting with The Moving Image.
South of My Days remembers a high, lean country and old storytelling.
Poems such as Bullocky and Bora Ring face settler memory.
A later book, Collected Poems 1942-1985, appeared in 1994.
That 1994 volume won a Human Rights award.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An aging salesman, Willy Loman, breaks under the dream of success.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1945 is the start of a period span. It is not the play's year. It opened at the Morosco Theatre in New York on 10 February 1949. Viking published the book in 1949. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama that year. Wikipedia says he finished the script at Roxbury in 1948.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Willy Loman (A 63-year-old traveling salesman who confuses hope with fact); Linda Loman (Willy's wife, who sees his despair and defends him); Biff Loman (The elder son, whose faith in Willy broke in Boston); Happy Loman (The younger son, who chooses to repeat his father's dream); Charley (The neighbour who lends Willy money and speaks at the funeral)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Willy comes home early, too tired to keep traveling for his firm.
His wife Linda fears he will crash the car on purpose.
His sons Biff and Happy still chase his idea of being well liked.
Howard fires Willy, and Biff fails to borrow money from an old boss.
A memory shows Biff finding Willy with another woman in Boston.
Willy crashes the car so the insurance money might help Biff.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays on how colonial language controls African literature, theatre, and fiction.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That number is a bad life span, not a publication year. Britannica and Wikipedia date the book 1986. The catalog calls it fiction, but it is criticism.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ngugi wa Thiong'o (The essayist, speaking from his own schooling, writing, and politics)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ngugi recalls colonial schools that punished children for speaking African languages.
He says the gun conquered the body, while language conquered the mind.
He challenges African writers who keep European languages as their literary tongue.
He argues that African language literature is the authentic voice for Africans.
He states his plan to write in Kikuyu or Kiswahili from then on.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dream play about a poor charcoal burner who must accept his own name.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1945 is only the period label. The play was first acted in Toronto on 12 August 1967. The book Dream on Monkey Mountain and Other Plays came out in 1970. It won an Obie Award in 1971.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Makak (Felix Hobain) (An old charcoal burner whose dream tests his shame about being black); Moustique (Makak's friend, who wants to make money from the dream); Corporal Lestrade (A mixed race policeman who first mocks Makak and later joins the dream); The Apparition (A silent white goddess who stands for the moon, a muse, and colonial beauty)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Makak, an old charcoal burner, is thrown into jail after a market disturbance.
He says a white woman in a vision told him to go back to Africa.
In the dream his friend Moustique tries to sell Makak's healing power.
The dream turns Makak into an African king who orders the white figure killed.
He wakes, gives his real name Felix Hobain, and goes home to Monkey Mountain.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Susan Barton asks the writer Foe to tell her island story, and Friday cannot speak.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database has no year and sorts the book at 1945. That is a period placeholder. Viking published Foe in 1986.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Susan Barton (A castaway who wants her own account of the island); Friday (The silent man whose tongue has been cut out); Daniel Foe (The writer who reshapes Barton's story); Cruso (The island master who dies before they reach England)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Susan Barton is cast away on the island of Cruso and Friday.
Cruso says slave owners cut out Friday's tongue.
Cruso dies on the voyage to England.
Barton and Friday survive.
She asks the novelist Daniel Foe to write her tale.
Foe wants a different story and invents adventures.
The book asks who owns a story when the silenced cannot answer.

items.title: "Go Tell It on the Mountain" (1953) — James Baldwin

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Go Tell It on the Mountain

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: On his birthday, John Grimes faces his stepfather's church and his family's past.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database sorts the novel at 1945. That is the period start. Baldwin began the book young and Knopf published it in May 1953. An early title was Crying Holy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Grimes (A teenage boy in Harlem who wrestles with faith and his father); Gabriel Grimes (John's stepfather, a severe preacher with a hidden past); Elizabeth (John's mother, who protects him and carries her own grief); Florence (Gabriel's sister, who challenges his pride); Elisha (A young man in the church who stays near John in his vision)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Alfred A. Knopf published the novel in May 1953.
The present action is one long day in a Harlem storefront church (a small church in a shop).
John Grimes fears Gabriel, the harsh preacher he calls father.
Scenes from earlier years give the lives of Florence, Gabriel, and Elizabeth.
At night John prays on the threshing floor (the church place of conversion).

items.title: "Half of a Yellow Sun" (2006) — Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ugwu, Olanna, and Odenigbo are thrown into the Biafran war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database sorts the novel at 1945. That is the period start. Fourth Estate published the British edition in 2006. It won the 2007 Orange Prize, now the Women's Prize for Fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ugwu (The houseboy who grows into a witness of the war); Odenigbo (A radical mathematics professor at Nsukka); Olanna (Odenigbo's partner, a woman from a rich family); Kainene (Olanna's twin, who vanishes while seeking food); Richard (An English writer who loves Kainene and Igbo art)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ugwu, a village boy, becomes houseboy (a young servant) to Professor Odenigbo in Nsukka.
Olanna leaves a rich Lagos life to live with Odenigbo.
Her twin Kainene runs the family business and loves the English writer Richard.
After massacres, the southeast breaks away as Biafra in 1967.
The families flee, go hungry, and live through air raids.
Kainene crosses the lines for food and does not come back.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A troubled professor writes brilliant letters he never sends.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That 1945 is the period, not the book. Wikipedia and the Nobel site date Herzog to 1964. It won the National Book Award for fiction in 1965.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Moses Herzog (A middle aged Jewish professor who thinks through unsent letters); Madeleine (Herzog's second wife, who leaves him); Valentine Gersbach (Herzog's friend, who becomes Madeleine's lover); Ramona (The lively woman who offers Herzog a new bond)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is set in 1964 in the United States and is about the midlife crisis of a Jewish man named Moses E. Herzog.
The novel opens with Herzog in his house in Ludeyville, a town in the Berkshires in western Massachusetts.
Ramona and Maleliene are the chief characters.
Saul Bellow is the novelist who described existential anxiety of Jewish experience.
Moses Herzog, a professor, is near collapse after his second divorce.
His wife Madeleine has left him for his friend Valentine Gersbach.
Herzog writes letters to friends, thinkers, and the dead, and sends none.
He wanders from the Berkshires to New York and then to Chicago.
He thinks of revenge, then sees that his daughter June is safe.
At the end he stops the letters and begins to repair his house and life.

items.title: "Homage to Catalonia" (1938) — George Orwell / Eric Blair

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Orwell's 1938 account of fighting in the Spanish Civil War and then fleeing.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Both are wrong. Victor Gollancz refused it. Secker and Warburg published it on 25 April 1938. It belongs with the 1930s books, before Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty Four.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: George Orwell (The narrator, a British volunteer in the POUM militia); Eileen Blair (Orwell's wife, who is with him in Barcelona)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
6- The Lion and the Unicorn: Socialism and the English Genius 7- Why I write (1946) 8- Politics and the English language 9- Shooting an Elephant (1936) 10- Inside the Whale 11- Such, Such were the Joys (1946, published posthumously)
Orwell arrives in Barcelona and joins the POUM militia.
He serves on the Aragon front and is later shot in the throat.
Street fighting in Barcelona sets left groups against each other.
He and his wife Eileen flee when the POUM is suppressed.
The book attacks the lies told about that war in the press.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poem that cries out against a society crushing its young people and its outsiders.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Ginsberg first read Howl at the Six Gallery on 7 October 1955. City Lights Books published Howl and Other Poems in 1956. Judge Clayton Horn ruled on 3 October 1957 that the book was not obscene.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A voice like a prophet, close to Ginsberg, who sees his generation destroyed.); Carl Solomon (The friend in a mental hospital. The poem is dedicated to him.); Moloch (A nightmare figure for industry, money, and a cruel state.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ginsberg worked on the poem in 1954 and 1955 in San Francisco.
He first read part of it at the Six Gallery on 7 October 1955.
City Lights published Howl and Other Poems in 1956 as Pocket Poets Number 4.
The speaker lists friends hurt by madness and attacks a cruel modern god called Moloch.
Moloch is the poem's name for a society like a machine that devours people.
In 1957 a court tried the publishers for obscenity, and Judge Clayton Horn cleared the book.
Obscenity here means the charge that the book was illegally filthy.

items.title: "In the Castle of My Skin" (1953) — George Lamming

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: In the Castle of My Skin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poetic novel about a boy growing up in a colonial village in Barbados.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is the start of the period label, not the publication year. He reached London in 1950 and finished the novel within about two years. Michael Joseph published it in London in 1953. The American edition has an introduction by Richard Wright. It won the Somerset Maugham Award.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: G (The boy whose childhood and youth the novel follows); The Villagers (The people of Creighton Village, whose shared life is as important as G's own story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Michael Joseph published the novel in London in 1953.
It follows a boy called G from about nine into his teens.
The place is based on Carrington Village, called Creighton Village in the book.
The great labour unrest of 1937 sits behind the village story.
School under colonial rule (rule by Britain) teaches the boy his place.
Friends leave, the old village order cracks, and G moves away.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unnamed Black man tells how America refuses to see him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Random House published the novel on 14 April 1952. Horizon printed the Battle Royal section in 1947. The National Book Award for Fiction followed in 1953.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (An unnamed Black man who calls himself invisible); Dr. Bledsoe (The college president who expels the narrator); Brother Jack (Leader of the Brotherhood, a political group); Ras the Exhorter (A Black nationalist who later calls himself the Destroyer); Tod Clifton (A young Brotherhood leader who is shot by police)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator lives underground in a bright room and tells his life.
As a boy in the South, he is forced into a cruel blind fight.
A Black college expels him after he shows a white trustee too much.
In New York he works at a paint factory and then joins the Brotherhood.
Ras the Exhorter calls that group a trick run by white men.
A riot drives him underground, where he says he may speak for us.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jim Dixon, a junior lecturer, fights pretence and wins a girl and a job.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1945 is the postwar period start, not the publication year. Gollancz published the novel in January 1954. The first printing's title page is dated 1953. It won the Somerset Maugham Award.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jim Dixon (A junior history lecturer who hates academic pretence); Professor Welch (Dixon's absent minded head of department); Margaret Peel (A colleague who holds Dixon with pity and a false story of a suicide attempt); Christine Callaghan (The young woman Dixon loves, at first linked to Bertrand Welch); Bertrand Welch (Professor Welch's affected son, a painter and Christine's boyfriend); Julius Gore-Urquhart (Christine's rich uncle, who gives Dixon a job in London)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(iii)
It is a novel by Amis, published in 1954 by Victor Gollancz.
It is Amis' first published novel and won Somerset Maugham award.
It is set around 1950, Lucky Jim, follows exploits of the eponymous James (Jim Dixon), a reluctant medieval history lecturer at an unnamed provincial English University.
The preliminary pages quote an old song; "Oh Lucky Jim how I envy him… …"
It is dedicated to Philip Larkin.
It is an early example of campus novel. It is a satire on academic life.
The protagonist Jim Dixon who is trying his way out of the working class to become a lecturer in History at a Provincial University.
Jim Dixon teaches medieval history at a provincial English university.
He fears Professor Welch will not renew his job.
He is trapped by Margaret Peel, and he falls for Christine Callaghan.
Drunk, he wrecks his public lecture on Merrie England and loses the post.
Christine's uncle, Julius Gore-Urquhart, offers him a better job in London.
He leaves with Christine, free of Margaret and of Welch.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel about John Self, money, drink, and a fake film deal.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Self (The narrator, a greedy advertising man who is ruined); Fielding Goodney (The producer who invents the film and cheats Self); Selina Street (Self's London girlfriend); Martina Twain (A cultured woman Self wants in New York)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
John Self makes television commercials and wants to direct a film.
Fielding Goodney flies him between London and New York.
Self spends wildly on drink, sex, food, and cars.
The film is a trick, and the contracts are debts.
A character named Martin Amis watches Self fall apart.
Self loses the money and learns that his real father is Fat Vince.

items.title: "Notes of a Native Son" (1955) — James Baldwin

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ten essays on race, protest fiction, Harlem, and life as an American in Europe.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database calls this fiction and sorts it at 1945. It is a book of essays. Beacon Press published it in 1955. The essays themselves had appeared from 1948 onward.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: James Baldwin (The essayist, speaking from his own life and reading); David Baldwin (His stepfather, whose funeral fell on James's nineteenth birthday)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Beacon Press published the book in 1955.
It collects ten essays first printed in magazines from 1948 to 1955.
Everybody's Protest Novel attacks simple protest books, including Native Son.
The title essay recalls his stepfather's death and the 1943 Harlem riot.
Later essays look at Paris and at a Swiss village.
The title points to Wright's Native Son and to Henry James.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A gambling priest and a glassworks heiress bet on moving a glass church into the Australian bush.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database had no year, only the period span. University of Queensland Press published the novel in 1988. It won the Booker Prize in 1988 and the Miles Franklin Award in 1989.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oscar Hopkins (An English clergyman and obsessive gambler); Lucinda Leplastrier (A young heiress who owns a Sydney glassworks)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Won the 1988 Booker Prize, and was shortlisted for 1989 for the Best of the Booker.
It tells the story of Oscar Hopkins, the Cornish son of a Plymouth Brethren Minister who becomes an Anglican priest.
The novel partly takes its inspiration from Father and Son, the autobiography of the English poet Edmund Gosse which describes his relationship with his father Philip Henery Gosse. 4. The Tax Inspector (1991). 5. The Unusual Life of Tristan Smith (1994). 6. Thru History of Kelly Gong (2002): Won 2001 Booker Prize and Commonwealth Writers Prize (2001). The protagonist is Nelly Kelly. 7. My Life as a Fake (2003). 8. Theft: A Love Story (2006). 9. His Illegal Self (2008). 10. Parrot and Oliver in America (2016). 11. The Chemistry of Tears (2012). 12. Amnesia (2014). 13. Jack Maggs (1997):.
It is a novel by Carey.
It is a reworking of the Charles Dickens' novel "Great Expectations".
The story centers around Jack Maggs (equivalent of Magwitch) and his quest to meet his son Henery Phipps (equivalent of Pip,) who has mysteriously disappeared having closed up his house and dismissed his households.
Oscar Hopkins is an Anglican priest from Devon who cannot stop gambling.
Lucinda Leplastrier is an Australian heiress who owns a glass factory in Sydney.
They meet on a ship to Australia and find that both of them bet.
Lucinda bets that Oscar cannot take a glass church to Bellingen.
The glass church becomes the image of their risky love and of colonial settlement.
A 1997 film starred Ralph Fiennes and Cate Blanchett, but the novel is 1988.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Alexander Portnoy confesses his family guilt and sexual shame to an analyst.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Random House published the novel on 12 January 1969. Wikipedia says Roth began the book in 1967. The database genre Fiction is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alexander Portnoy (The narrator, a young Jewish man full of guilt and desire); Doctor Spielvogel (The psychoanalyst who listens and speaks at the end); Sophie Portnoy (Alexander's mother, a powerful figure in his memories)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Alexander Portnoy speaks in one long comic confession.
He talks to his psychoanalyst, Doctor Spielvogel.
A psychoanalyst is a doctor who studies hidden feelings.
He remembers a Jewish childhood in New Jersey.
Desire and duty keep fighting inside him.
The doctor ends the book by saying the treatment may now begin.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A white boy raised by Aboriginal people steps back into a Queensland settler village.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That number is the period label. Chatto and Windus published the novel in 1993. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gemmy Fairley (A white castaway raised by Aboriginal people); Lachlan Beattie (The settler boy who first aims a stick at Gemmy); Janet McIvor (A settler girl who sees Gemmy arrive from the swamp)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In the mid 1840s, the boy Gemmy Fairley is cast ashore in north Queensland.
Aboriginal people raise him, and he stays with them for sixteen years.
He climbs a settler fence and begs the children not to shoot.
A settler family (newcomers on the land) takes him in, but neighbours fear him.
His two lives force the village to face its own terror of the land.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ondaatje returns to Sri Lanka to rebuild the wild story of his parents and grandparents.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Two sources date the first publication to 1982. Toronto: McClelland and Stewart. New York: Norton.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Michael Ondaatje (The narrator, returning to Sri Lanka to research his family); Mervyn Ondaatje (His father, a vivid and troubled man at the centre of the tales); Doris Gratiaen (His mother, from a Burgher family in Ceylon); Lalla (His maternal grandmother, remembered in wild family stories)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
McClelland and Stewart in Toronto and Norton in New York published this memoir in 1982.
Ondaatje had left Ceylon at about eleven and went back in his thirties.
He gathers rumours, poems, photos, and maps of the family.
The brightest figure is his father, Mervyn Ondaatje, charming and often drunk.
His mother Doris Gratiaen and grandmother Lalla fill other chapters.
The book asks how a family story can be true when memory keeps shifting.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about Oskar Schindler, who saved many Jews from Nazi murder by employing them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is the period shelf, not the book year. Hodder and Stoughton published it in 1982. Wikipedia dates the first edition to 18 October 1982. It won the Booker Prize in 1982. The United States title is Schindler's List. Steven Spielberg's film came out in 1993.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oskar Schindler (A German factory owner who protects Jewish workers during the Holocaust); Amon Goeth (The cruel commander of the Plaszow labour camp); Poldek Pfefferberg (A survivor who pushed Keneally to write the book and advised the research)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Oskar Schindler is a German businessman and a member of the Nazi Party.
In Krakow he runs a factory and begins to protect Jewish workers.
The story also shows the ghetto and the camp at Plaszow.
Amon Goeth, the camp commander, stands for the cruelty Schindler works against.
About 1,200 people on his list survive.
Schindler himself is a flawed man.

items.title: "The Adventures of Augie March" (1953) — Saul Bellow

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Chicago youth drifts through jobs, loves, and wars while hunting a fate of his own.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That figure is the period, not the novel. The Nobel site and Wikipedia date publication to 1953. Bellow began it in Paris after a 1948 fellowship. It won the National Book Award in 1954.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Augie March (The narrator, a Chicago adventurer who will not settle); Simon March (Augie's brother, who chases money and status); Thea (The bold woman who takes Augie to Mexico); Stella (The woman Augie later marries)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Augie March grows up poor in Chicago during the Depression.
He has no known father.
His mother is going blind.
He moves from job to job and from one strong friend to another.
He travels to Mexico with Thea, who hunts with an eagle.
In the war his ship sinks, and he survives a lifeboat ordeal.
The book ends with Augie and Stella living an uneasy life in France.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Celie writes letters about abuse in Georgia and finds strength with other women.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database sorts the novel at 1945. That is the period start, not the book year. Harcourt Brace Jovanovich published it in 1982. The Pulitzer Prize for Fiction followed in 1983.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Celie (The letter writer who survives abuse and claims her own life); Nettie (Celie's sister, whose letters Mister hides); Mister (The husband who beats Celie and hides Nettie's letters); Shug Avery (A singer who loves Celie and helps her leave); Sofia (A strong woman who refuses to be beaten down)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Harcourt Brace Jovanovich published the novel in 1982.
Celie, a poor Black girl in Georgia, writes letters to God.
Her stepfather abuses her, then marries her to a farmer called Mister.
Mister hides years of letters from her sister Nettie.
The singer Shug Avery helps Celie see her own worth and leave.
Celie makes a new life and meets Nettie again.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Salem farmer, John Proctor, dies rather than sign a false confession.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1945 is the start of a period span. It is not the play's year. The play opened at the Martin Beck Theatre in New York on 22 January 1953. It won the Tony Award for Best Play in 1953. Miller was questioned by a congressional committee in 1956.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Proctor (A farmer who confesses his affair and then refuses a public lie); Elizabeth Proctor (His wife, spared for a time because she is pregnant); Abigail Williams (The niece of the minister and the leader of the accusing girls); Reverend John Hale (A witchcraft expert who later tries to stop the hangings); Deputy Governor Danforth (The judge who will not undo the trials)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a central work in the canon of American Drama. It is in 4 acts.
John Proctor is the protagonist.
In Salem in 1692, Abigail Williams and other girls accuse neighbours of witchcraft.
John Proctor knows they are lying, but he hides an old affair with Abigail.
His wife Elizabeth is arrested after a poppet (a doll) is used as proof.
In court she lies to protect his name, and the girls turn on him.
He signs a confession, tears it up, and is led out to be hanged.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Tom remembers his mother Amanda and his fragile sister Laura in a Saint Louis flat.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Chicago premiere was 26 December 1944. Broadway opened on 31 March 1945. Random House published the book in 1945. It won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award in 1945. It did not win the Pulitzer Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tom Wingfield (The narrator and son, who works in a shoe warehouse and wants to be a writer); Amanda Wingfield (The mother, a former Southern belle abandoned by her husband); Laura Wingfield (Tom's shy sister, who cares for a collection of glass animals); Jim O'Connor (The gentleman caller, an old school friend who is already engaged)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tom tells the story as a memory of his family.
Amanda, a former Southern belle, wants a husband for Laura.
Laura is shy, limps, and lives among her glass animals.
Tom brings Jim O'Connor home as a gentleman caller.
Jim is already engaged.
Tom later leaves, and he asks Laura to blow out the candles.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Moses and other West Indian men try to live through cold, lonely years in London.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Allan Wingate published the novel in London in 1956. The database calls the book poetry. It is a novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Moses Aloetta (A Trinidadian who has lived in London for years and helps new arrivals); Sir Galahad (A hopeful newcomer from Trinidad whom Moses meets at the station); The boys (West Indian men who meet in Moses's room to share news and jokes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
One winter evening, Moses rides a bus to Waterloo Station.
He meets a new man from Trinidad, later called Sir Galahad.
On Sundays the men gather in Moses's room and swap stories.
They look for work and rooms, and the city often turns them away.
A long summer section runs on with almost no full stops.
Moses grows older in London and feels he has not moved forward.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Larkin's first poetry book, still close to the style of Yeats.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1945 is correct for the first edition. The database calls it posthumous (printed after the writer died). That flag is wrong. Larkin was alive in 1945. Collected Poems, edited by Anthony Thwaite in 1988, is the book after his death. It is not this title.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A lonely voice watching ships, journeys, and failed hope)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(xi)
Fortune Press published the book in 1945.
Most of the poems were written in 1943 and 1944 in Wellington.
The 1945 book has 31 pieces, numbered with Roman numerals.
The last piece, The North Ship, follows a ship going north.
Faber and Faber printed the book again in 1966.

items.title: "The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie" (1961) — Muriel Spark

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Miss Jean Brodie shapes six Edinburgh schoolgirls, and one of them later betrays her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database had no year, only the period span. Macmillan published the book in 1961. The New Yorker also printed it in 1961. The London play opened in 1966, and the film followed in 1969.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jean Brodie (A charismatic teacher who tries to own her chosen girls); Sandy Stranger (The pupil who betrays Brodie and later becomes a nun); Miss Mackay (The headmistress who wants Brodie out of the school); Teddy Lloyd (The married art master whom Brodie loves); Gordon Lowther (The singing master with whom Brodie has an affair)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(v) The Girls of Slender Means (1968) (vi) Loitering with Intent (1961)- It was nominated for Bookers prize (vii)
The first publication of this novel was in the New Yorker magazine and published as a book in 1961.
It is a dystopian novel.
The character of Miss Jean Brodie brought Spark an international fame.
It is a re-writing of a novel of the Victorian novel Jane Eyre by Charlotte Bronte.
In 1930s Edinburgh, Miss Brodie teaches six girls at the Marcia Blaine School.
She calls them the creme de la creme and says she is in her prime.
She fills their lessons with art, her love life, and praise of fascism.
The art master Teddy Lloyd and the singing master Gordon Lowther both love her.
Sandy Stranger later tells the headmistress Miss Mackay how to dismiss Brodie.
Sandy becomes a nun, and the novel ends on Brodie in her prime.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A retired theatre director harms people through jealous love by the sea.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year is only the postwar period label. Chatto and Windus published the novel in 1978. It won the Booker Prize in 1978.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charles Arrowby (A retired London theatre director and the narrator); Mary Hartley Fitch (His first love, now married, whom he still calls Hartley); James Arrowby (His cousin, a former officer drawn to Eastern thought); Titus (Hartley's adopted son, who drowns in the sea)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(ii)
Charles Arrowby leaves the London theatre and moves into a house by the sea.
He starts a memoir and thinks he has left his old life behind.
He meets his first love, Mary Hartley Fitch, now an older married woman.
He calls her Hartley and becomes obsessed with their teenage romance.
He kidnaps her, sure that he is saving her from her husband.
His cousin James, who studies Eastern thought, warns him about his ego.
Titus, Hartley's adopted son, drowns in the sea.
Hartley and her husband leave for Australia, and Charles is left with the wreckage.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Proud ninety year old Hagar Shipley looks back at a life ruled by fear.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year only opens the postwar period. McClelland and Stewart published the novel in 1964. It is the first of the five Manawaka books.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hagar Shipley (The ninety year old narrator, born Hagar Currie); Bram Shipley (The rough husband she chose against her father's will); Marvin Shipley (The older son who cares for her and whom she undervalued); John Shipley (The younger son she favoured, who dies young); Jason Currie (Hagar's stern shopkeeper father)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hagar Shipley is ninety and hates the plan to put her in a home.
She remembers Manawaka, her hard father, and the stone angel on her mother's grave.
She marries Bram Shipley against her father and later leaves Bram.
Pride keeps her cold to Bram and to her loyal son Marvin.
She runs off, weeps at last, tells Marvin the truth, and dies.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A girl in California retells her mother's Chinese tales and the family silences around them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Knopf published the book in 1976. A Vintage paperback is dated 1989. The National Book Critics Circle Award for nonfiction was for this 1976 book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A Chinese American girl whose telling is based on Kingston's own youth); Brave Orchid (The mother, a trained doctor and a powerful teller of talk stories); No Name Woman (The father's sister in China, cast out by the village and then forgotten); Fa Mu Lan (A woman warrior from a Chinese tale whom the girl takes as a model); Moon Orchid (Brave Orchid's sister, who comes to America and loses her hold on life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The mother warns the girl not to repeat the story of a forgotten aunt.
That aunt, called No Name Woman, drowns herself in the family well.
The girl imagines Fa Mu Lan, a woman who goes to war for her father.
Brave Orchid, the mother, studies medicine in China and calls white people ghosts.
Moon Orchid comes from Hong Kong and cannot fit her husband's American life.
The book ends with Ts'ai Yen, a poet who makes a song among strangers.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short novel that tells a Nazi doctor's life backwards in time.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Jonathan Cape published Time's Arrow in 1991. Amis says he first imagined a life told backward about two years earlier.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The inner narrator (A second consciousness that feels the doctor's life in reverse); Odilo Unverdorben (The doctor whose hidden past is a Nazi camp); Uncle Pepi (A camp doctor modelled on Josef Mengele)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A second mind lives inside a doctor and cannot read his thoughts.
Time runs backward, so the doctor grows younger.
In America he hides under a new name after the war.
The story moves back to Auschwitz.
In reverse, killing looks like creation and healing.
The forward story is the life of a Holocaust doctor.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A child in 1930s Alabama watches her father defend a Black man, and learns what innocence costs.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Those figures copy the period, not the book. Lippincott published the novel on 11 July 1960. It won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction in 1961.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Scout Finch (The child narrator, whose full name is Jean Louise Finch); Atticus Finch (Scout's widowed father, the lawyer who defends Tom); Jem Finch (Scout's older brother); Tom Robinson (The Black man falsely accused of raping Mayella Ewell); Boo Radley (The reclusive neighbor who watches the children and later saves them); Dill (The children's summer friend, based on Truman Capote)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Scout Finch tells of about three years in the town of Maycomb, Alabama.
She lives with her brother Jem and their father Atticus, a lawyer.
Scout, Jem, and their friend Dill try to draw out the hidden neighbor Boo Radley.
Atticus defends Tom Robinson, a Black man falsely accused of rape.
An all white jury convicts Tom, and Boo later saves the children from Bob Ewell.

items.title: "True History of the Kelly Gang" (2000) — Peter Carey

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: True History of the Kelly Gang

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ned Kelly tells his outlaw life in a rough voice with almost no commas, and the book is still fiction.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database had no year, only the period span. University of Queensland Press published the novel in 2000. The Booker Prize came in 2001. Do not use 2001 as the first publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ned Kelly (The narrator, an Irish Australian bushranger telling his life); Ellen Kelly (Ned's mother, imprisoned to draw her sons out); Joe Byrne (One of the Kelly Gang); Mary Hearn (A fictional woman for whom Ned says he writes the story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel pretends to be parcels of Ned Kelly's memoir for his child.
Ned's Irish father dies after clashes with the police, and the family slides into poverty.
The bushranger Harry Power trains the young Ned.
A bushranger is an armed outlaw in the bush.
After the Stringybark Creek killings, the gang robs banks and hides among poor settlers.
At Glenrowan the police shoot the armoured gang, and Ned is later hanged.
Mary Hearn, the woman he loves, is Carey's invention, as is the daughter.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about a Kikuyu boy whose school dream breaks during the Mau Mau years.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is not the publication year. The novel was published in May 1964. It was the first English novel by a writer from East Africa. Chinua Achebe had read the manuscript at the 1962 Makerere writers' meeting.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Njoroge (A Kikuyu schoolboy who hopes education will save his family); Ngotho (Njoroge's father, who works for a settler on lost family land); Boro (Njoroge's elder brother, bitter about the settlers and drawn into the fight); Mwihaki (Njoroge's friend, daughter of the wealthy Jacobo); Mr. Howlands (The white settler who owns the farm Ngotho works)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the first novel of Ngũgĩ, published in (1964), under the name James Ngũgĩ.
It was the first English novel to be published by an East African.
It deals with the relationship between Africans and the British Colonist in Africa.
It also deals with the 'Mau Mau Uprising' and the bewildering dispossession of an entire people from their ancestral land.
The Protagonist Njoroge aspiration to attend university is frustrated by both, the violence of the Mau Mau rebels and the violent response of the colonial government.
Some other major characters are Ngotho - Njoroge's father Nyokabi and Njeri - Two wives of Ngotho A Grain of Wheat (1967)
The title is taken from the Gospel of St. Joan.
Mau Mau Rebellion is depicted in this novel (Aftermath situation).
The Novel weaves together several stories set during the state of emergency in Kenya's struggle for independence, focusing on quiet Mugo, whose life is ruled by a dark secret.
The plot revolves around his home village's preparations for Kenya's Independence Day celebration, Uhuru Day. On that day, former resistance Fighter General R and Koinandu plan on Publically executing the traitor who betrayed Kihika.
Characters:- Mugo, Gikonyo, Mumbi, Kihika and Karanja.
Njoroge is the first in his family to go to school, and he trusts education.
His father Ngotho works on land that white settlers took from the family.
Stories of Gikuyu and Mumbi keep the hope that the land will return.
The Emergency and the Mau Mau fight pull the family into violence.
Ngotho is beaten and dies, and Njoroge's faith in school collapses.

items.title: "Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?" (1962) — Edward Albee

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long play about a bitter campus marriage and the games that hold it together.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is the literary period, not the play's year. It opened on Broadway at the Billy Rose Theatre on 13 October 1962. Atheneum published the book in 1962. The Pulitzer jury chose it, but the board gave no drama prize that year. It won the Tony Award for Best Play in 1963.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Martha (Daughter of the college president, loud, wounded, and married to George); George (A history teacher at the college, sharp tongued and tired of Martha's attacks); Nick (A young faculty husband who gets pulled into the older couple's games); Honey (Nick's wife, who drinks too much and is hurt by George's story about her)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After a faculty party, Martha and George invite Nick and Honey home for drinks.
The older couple insult each other while the younger couple stay and watch.
George plays a cruel game that exposes the secrets of Nick and Honey.
Martha breaks their one rule and talks about their son.
George says the son is dead.
The guests learn that the son was never real.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Hazel Motes tries to preach a church without Christ, then blinds himself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year only opens the postwar period. Parts first appeared as stories in 1948 and 1949. Harcourt, Brace published the novel on 15 May 1952. A film by John Huston came in 1979. That is not the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hazel Motes (A veteran who preaches against Christ and later blinds himself); Enoch Emery (A young zookeeper who believes his wise blood tells him what to do); Asa Hawks (A preacher who pretends to be blind); Sabbath Lily Hawks (Asa's daughter, who moves in with Hazel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hazel Motes, a veteran, returns home and finds the house empty.
He goes to the city of Taulkinham and rejects the Christian faith of his youth.
He starts to preach a church without Christ from an old car.
Enoch Emery, Asa Hawks, and Sabbath Lily pull him into their schemes.
A false preacher copies his church and grows rich.
Motes blinds himself with lime and dies after a policeman strikes him.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Thomas Cromwell rises in the court of Henry VIII, from Wolsey's fall to Thomas More's death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That year only opens the postwar period. Fourth Estate published the book on 30 April 2009. It won the Booker Prize in 2009. The stage plays and the BBC series came later. They are not the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Cromwell (A blacksmith's son who becomes Henry VIII's powerful minister); Cardinal Thomas Wolsey (The king's minister, and Cromwell's first master, who then falls); Henry VIII (The king who wants to leave Catherine and marry Anne Boleyn); Anne Boleyn (The woman Henry makes queen, with Cromwell's help); Thomas More (The scholar who resists the king and dies at the end of this book)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Young Thomas Cromwell runs away from his violent father.
By 1527 he is a lawyer and Cardinal Wolsey's trusted man.
His wife and daughters die of the sweating sickness.
Henry VIII drops Wolsey for failing to end the marriage to Catherine of Aragon.
Cromwell stays in favor and helps Anne Boleyn become queen.
The novel follows him through to the death of Thomas More.

items.title: "A Bend in the Ganges" (1964) — Manohar Malgonkar

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A freedom novel that runs from civil disobedience to the Partition riots.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1947 is the period label, not the book year. Hamish Hamilton published the novel in London in 1964. The Hindu and the Sahitya Akademi monograph also date it 1964. The story itself ends with the Partition riots of 1947.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gian Talwar (A young man drawn to Gandhi's nonviolence); Debi Dayal (A revolutionary who rejects nonviolence); Shafi Usman (Debi's comrade in violent resistance, linked with a secular slogan)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel opens with a civil disobedience movement of the early 1930's and ends with partition riots in Punjab.
It encompasses the Swadeshi Movement, the activities of freedom fighters, the outbreak of the second World War, the British retreat from Rangoon, the Bombay dock explosion and division of India in 1947. Main Characters - Gian Talwar and Debi Dayal.
The story opens in the civil disobedience years of the early 1930s.
Gian Talwar follows Gandhi and chooses nonviolence.
Debi Dayal and Shafi Usman choose violent revolt instead.
The plot takes in the war, the fall of Rangoon, and the Bombay dock explosion.
It ends in the Partition riots, when India is divided in 1947.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems of rain, ritual, and suffering, including the famous poem Hunger.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That number is the period label. The University of Georgia Press published A Rain of Rites in 1976. Hunger first appeared in this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (The man who follows the fisherman in Hunger); The Fisherman (A father who offers his daughter because the family is starving); The Daughter (A girl of about fifteen waiting inside the hut)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The University of Georgia Press published the book in 1976.
Rain, dawn, river, and stone return through the poems.
Hunger shows a poor fisherman offering his young daughter.
The speaker follows him and faces both desire and shame.
Inner feeling and social pain in India stay tied together.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sartre's major book on consciousness, nothingness, bad faith, and freedom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: French publication 1943, Gallimard. First full English translation by Hazel E. Barnes, Philosophical Library, 1956. It is not the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jean-Paul Sartre (The philosopher arguing the book); The cafe waiter (His famous example of someone acting a fixed role)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
3- Existentialism is Humanism (1946)
Sartre studies what it is to be a free conscious person.
Things just exist.
He calls that being in itself (existence with no choice).
Consciousness can imagine what is absent.
He calls that nothingness.
Bad faith is lying to yourself, as when a waiter plays at being only a waiter.
The wish to be complete and free at once is, he says, a useless passion.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A writer cannot finish a story about four men who are really one trapped life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database gives no work year, only the period label that starts in 1947. He wrote the play in 1963, while working in Nigeria. It was first published and performed in Bengali in 1965. Girish Karnad's English version was issued by Oxford University Press. Catalogs date that English book to 1974 or 1975. A short page dates the writing to 1962.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Writer (A stuck author who is also inside the story he cannot end); Indrajit (Nirmal) (The rebel who fears his own name and later becomes ordinary); Amal, Vimal, and Kamal (Three middle class men whose jobs and marriages look the same); Manasi (The woman linked to the Writer and to Indrajit)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A Writer has no plot, until he picks four men out of the audience.
Three of them are Amal, Vimal, and Kamal, ordinary men with the same lives.
The fourth hides his name, then says he is Indrajit, though he is also Nirmal.
Manasi is the woman they love, question, and cannot really leave.
Years pass, the office routine returns, and Indrajit accepts the empty path and walks it.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Nine modern poems answer old Bible psalms, with a personal closing note.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1947 is the start of a period span, not this book. Ezekiel wrote the sequence in June 1978. Oxford University Press published it in 1982. The Sahitya Akademi Award followed in 1983.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ezekiel wrote the sequence in a hotel room in Rotterdam in June 1978.
He chose nine psalms, including Psalm 1, Psalm 23, and Psalm 102.
Each poem speaks back to the old Hebrew song in a modern voice.
A tenth poem comments on the whole set.
Oxford University Press published the book in 1982.
It won the Sahitya Akademi Award for English in 1983.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A murder story among Ottoman miniature painters who fear a new Western style.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It is not a book date. The Turkish novel Benim Adim Kirmizi came from Iletisim in 1998. Erdag Goknar's English translation came from Knopf and Faber in 2001. It won the International Dublin Literary Award in 2003.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elegant Effendi (A murdered miniaturist whose corpse narrates the opening chapter); Black (A binder who returns to Istanbul and loves Shekure); Shekure (Enishte's daughter, a widow who also speaks to the reader); Enishte Effendi (Black's uncle, in charge of the Sultan's secret book); Master Osman (Head of the Sultan's workshop, loyal to the old style)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In Istanbul in 1591, artists prepare a secret book for the Sultan.
The book will use Venetian ideas of the portrait and of perspective (depth in a flat picture).
A painter called Elegant is murdered, and his corpse speaks the first chapter.
Black returns after twelve years and loves his widowed cousin Shekure.
They quarrel over personal style in the old art of the miniature (a small manuscript picture).

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A village wife, Rukmani, tells how hunger and a tannery break her family.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1947 is the start of the postcolonial period, not the book year. Putnam in London published the novel in 1954. One catalog dates the New York John Day edition to 1955. Another list gives 1954 for New York as well.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rukmani (The narrator, a village wife who tells the story of her married life); Nathan (Rukmani's husband, a tenant farmer who loses the land); Ira (Their daughter, sent home by her husband and later driven to prostitution); Kenny (An English doctor who treats the family and later builds a hospital); Puli (A street child whom Rukmani brings back to the village)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel is set in India during a period of intense urban development. It is a semi-autobiographical novel by her.
The story is told by Rukmani (the youngest daughter of a village headman) in first person, beginning from her arranged marriage to Nathan at the age of 12 to his death many years later.
The title is taken from 1825 poem Work Without Hope by S.T Coleridge "Work without hope draws nectar in a sieve and hope without an object can not live". 2. The Coffer Dams (1969). Main Characters - Clinton and Helen.
Rukmani, daughter of a village headman, marries the tenant farmer Nathan at age twelve.
They have a daughter, Ira, and then several sons, but food grows scarce.
A tannery comes to the village and takes land, work, and the old way of life.
Flood, drought, and hunger follow.
Ira sells her body to feed a starving child.
The tannery buys their land.
Nathan dies in the city, and Rukmani returns with the child Puli.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A son remembers the rainy night a scorpion stung his mother.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1947 is the start of a period span, not this poem. It was first published in 1965 in the collection The Exact Name.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (The son who remembers the night); The mother (The woman stung by the scorpion); The father (A sceptic (a man who doubts prayer) who still tries every cure); The peasants (Neighbours who pray and explain the sting as fate)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ten hours of rain drive a scorpion under a sack of rice.
It stings the mother and then flees into the rain.
Peasants pray that the pain will burn away sins from an earlier birth.
The father, a rationalist (a man who trusts reason), tries powders, herbs, and even a flame.
After twenty hours the poison fades.
The mother thanks God it was her, not the children.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three dead people locked in one room discover that hell is other people.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First performed at the Theatre du Vieux Colombier, Paris, on 27 May 1944. French book, Gallimard, 1945. British English in 1946 used the title In Camera. The American title No Exit is the 1947 Knopf edition. The database year 1947 matches that American title, not the first night.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Joseph Garcin (A journalist executed for cowardice who wants to be called brave); Inez Serrano (A cruel woman who sees through the others); Estelle Rigault (A society woman who needs a man to confirm her); The Valet (The servant who brings them into the room)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A valet locks three dead people in a plain room.
They are Garcin, Inez, and Estelle.
Each wants love or respect from another, and each is refused.
They expect racks and fire, but the room is only a sitting room.
The door opens, but they stay, because each needs the others' judgment.

items.title: "One Hundred Years of Solitude" (1967) — Gabriel Garcia Marquez

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Seven generations of the Buendia family live and vanish in the town of Macondo.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That number is the start of a period label, not the publication year. Editorial Sudamericana published the Spanish novel in Buenos Aires in May 1967. Harper and Row published Gregory Rabassa's English translation in 1970. Garcia Marquez said he preferred that English text.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
