fields.value: Jose Arcadio Buendia (The founder of Macondo, curious, obsessive, and finally tied to a tree); Ursula Iguaran (His wife and cousin, the long lived head of the house); Colonel Aureliano Buendia (Their son, a soldier who fights many wars and then withdraws); Melquiades (The gypsy who brings inventions and leaves the coded manuscript); Remedios the Beauty (A woman so beautiful that she is said to rise into the sky)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jose Arcadio Buendia and Ursula found the town of Macondo after a killing and a flight.
Gypsies bring marvels such as magnets and ice, and Melquiades befriends the founder.
Colonel Aureliano Buendia fights in the civil wars and later makes little gold fishes.
An American banana company arrives, and the army massacres striking workers.
Rain falls for years, the town decays, and the family repeats old desires.
The last Aureliano reads Melquiades's manuscript as a wind wipes Macondo away.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Townspeople turn into rhinoceroses, and only Berenger refuses to join the herd.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play was written in 1959. It was first staged in German in Dusseldorf in 1959. Catalogues disagree on the exact day, so only the year is given here. The French premiere was at the Odeon in Paris on 20 January 1960. The database year 1947 is a period label, not the play's date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Berenger (A clumsy, kindly man who remains human); Jean (Berenger's confident friend, who transforms into a rhinoceros); Daisy (The woman Berenger loves, who finally joins the herd)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In a small French town, a rhinoceros charges across the square.
More people change, including Berenger's proud friend Jean.
At the office, Mrs Boeuf sees that her husband is a rhinoceros and joins him.
Daisy stays with Berenger for a time, then leaves to join the animals.
Berenger is the last human and shouts that he will not give in.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poem in three parts about leaving English gods and coming home to Tamil.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Some Exile poems were written from 1963. Oxford University Press in Delhi published the book in 1977.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (The poet, looking back on England, love, and his Tamil past); You (The Tamil language and past he addresses on his return)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker looks back as he nears thirty and takes stock of his life.
In Exile he remembers England, fog, and his old love of English culture.
He says he spent his youth chasing English gods.
Trial turns to love, distance, and the feeling of always taking leave.
Homecoming brings him back to Tamil, family, and a tongue still held by English.

items.title: "Rusty, the Boy from the Hills" (2002) — Ruskin Bond

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Rusty, the Boy from the Hills

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A later collection of stories about Rusty, Bond's boy of the hills.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says collected editions vary and sorts the book in 1947. That year is not a publication year. Bond was a child in 1947. Puffin Books in New Delhi published this collection in 2002. Wikipedia lists it as short stories about Rusty.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rusty (A boy based on the young Bond, living in the hills)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rusty is a lonely boy in the hills of north India.
The stories show friendship, school days, and small adventures.
Bond had already used Rusty in his early novels.
Many of these pieces first appeared in magazines or earlier books.
Puffin Books in New Delhi gathered them in 2002.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poet is trapped by snow, love, and a political coup in the town of Kars.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Turkish novel Kar came from Iletisim in 2002. Maureen Freely's English translation, Snow, came from Knopf and Faber in 2004. A Nobel essay's mention of 2005 matches later editions, including the Swedish one.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ka (A Turkish poet home from Germany, the centre of the story); Ipek (A woman in Kars whom Ka loves); Blue (A feared Islamist leader whom Ka both admires and fears); Kadife (Ipek's sister, pressed to remove her headscarf on stage); Sunay Zaim (An actor who turns the theatre show into a real coup)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poet Ka returns to Turkey after twelve years of exile in Germany.
He travels to Kars, and heavy snow blocks the roads out.
He meets Ipek again and is pulled into religious, secular (non-religious), and military camps.
A play at the National Theatre turns into a coup (a sudden grab of power).
Soldiers then fire into the crowd.
Ka leaves, is later killed in Germany, and the only copy of his new poems vanishes.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jaya, a Bombay wife, reviews seventeen years of silence when her husband faces an inquiry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: That is not the publication year. Virago in London published the book in 1988. A Penguin paperback appeared in 1989. The Sahitya Akademi Award came in 1990.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jaya (The narrator, a middle class wife and would be writer); Mohan (Jaya's husband, who faces an inquiry and expects her silence); Rahul (Their son, away with family friends during the crisis); Rati (Their daughter, also away during the stay in Dadar)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mohan faces an inquiry for financial malpractice at work.
He and Jaya leave their Churchgate flat for a small flat in Dadar.
Their children, Rahul and Rati, are away with family friends.
Jaya remembers how she stayed quiet through seventeen years of marriage.
When the outer crisis eases, she will not go back to that silence.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Polite English small talk collapses into nonsense, and the scene begins again.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Ionesco wrote it in 1948 while studying empty phrases in an English primer. Nicolas Bataille directed the premiere on 11 May 1950 at the Theatre des Noctambules in Paris. The database year 1947 is a period label, not this date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mr Smith (A middle-class English husband); Mrs Smith (His wife, who opens the play with polite nonsense); The Fire Chief (A visitor who brings up a bald soprano who never appears); Mary (The Smiths' maid)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mr and Mrs Smith sit at home and trade empty facts about their evening.
The Martins visit and slowly decide that they may already be married.
Mary the maid and the Fire Chief add still more nonsense.
Words break into shouts, and ordinary sense disappears.
The play starts again, with the couples taking each other's lines.

items.title: "The Complete Adventures of Professor Shonku (translation)" (1961) — Satyajit Ray

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Complete Adventures of Professor Shonku (translation)

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Diary tales of Professor Shonku, a Bengali scientist and inventor, later gathered in English.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Byomjatrir Diary page dates the Sandesh serial to 1961, and the first book, Professor Shonku, to 1965. A Times of India report also says 1961. The Satyajit Ray Society page says the Sandesh story is 1965. Puffin published The Final Adventures of Professor Shonku in May 2020.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Professor Trilokeshwar Shonku (The scientist narrator, inventor of strange machines and medicines); Prahlad (Shonku's loyal servant and travel companion); Newton (Shonku's pet cat, named for the scientist Isaac Newton)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Professor Trilokeshwar Shonku keeps a diary of his experiments.
He lives in Giridih with his cat Newton and his servant Prahlad.
The first story, Byomjatrir Diary, sends him to Mars in his own rocket.
That tale was printed in Sandesh in 1961.
Ray gathered it in the 1965 book Professor Shonku.
English volumes came later.
A last Puffin book appeared in 2020.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A social play about the lives of the poor, printed in the 1937 collection Five Plays.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Those labels are wrong. This play is in Five Plays, Pondicherry, 1937. A 1929 book also called Five Plays holds other plays about saints.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Poor workers (Working class people whose hard lives this group of plays puts on stage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Parrot is a social play, not a poem.
It was printed in Five Plays at Pondicherry in 1937.
With The Window, it deals with the lives of poor people.
The 1937 plays protest exploitation and stiff social morals.
They put working class characters on the Indian English stage.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A doctor fights a deadly disease in the closed city of Oran.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The French book La Peste came from Gallimard in 1947. The English translation followed in 1948. The database year 1947 matches the French book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bernard Rieux (A doctor, and the secret narrator of the chronicle); Jean Tarrou (A visitor who helps the sick and hates the death penalty); Father Paneloux (A priest who first calls the plague a punishment); Raymond Rambert (A journalist who plans to escape, then stays to help); Cottard (A criminal who grows rich while the city is closed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rats die in the Algerian city of Oran.
Doctor Bernard Rieux sees that the deaths are plague.
The city is shut, and no one may leave.
Rieux, Tarrou, and others nurse the sick with no hope of glory.
The plague fades, but Rieux warns that the fight is not finished.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unfeeling clerk in Algiers kills a man and will not fake grief.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The French book came out on 19 May 1942. Bookshops had it from June 1942. The first English book came in 1946. Britain called it The Outsider. America kept the title The Stranger. The database year 1947 is wrong for this novel. That year belongs to The Plague.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Meursault (The narrator, a French clerk in Algiers who feels little); Marie Cardona (A former coworker who wants love and marriage); Raymond Sintes (A neighbour who pulls Meursault into a fight); The Arab (The unnamed brother of Raymond's mistress, killed on the beach); The Chaplain (A priest whom Meursault rejects in prison)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Meursault learns that his mother has died.
He shows no grief at the funeral.
He helps his neighbour Raymond, then shoots an Arab man on a beach.
At the trial, the court cares more about his dry eyes than the killing.
He is sentenced to death and accepts a silent universe.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Oskar Matzerath refuses to grow and drums through the Nazi years in Danzig.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1947 is only a period label, not the publication year. The German novel appeared in 1959 from Luchterhand. Britannica and the Nobel press release both give 1959. A film by Volker Schlondorff followed in 1979.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oskar Matzerath (The drummer who narrates and will not grow up.); Alfred Matzerath (Oskar's possible father, a grocer in the Nazi Party.); Jan Bronski (Oskar's other possible father, a Pole in Danzig.); Agnes Matzerath (Oskar's mother.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Oskar tells the story from a mental hospital in the early 1950s.
He is born in Danzig in 1924 and decides at age three to stop growing.
A toy tin drum is his treasure, and his scream can break glass.
He lives with two possible fathers, one Nazi and one Polish.
He sees the war, joins dwarf performers, and later plays jazz.
He lets himself be jailed for a murder he did not commit.
The book is the first part of the Danzig Trilogy.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A social play about poor lives, printed with The Parrot in Five Plays in 1937.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Those labels are wrong. This play is in the 1937 Five Plays. The 1929 Five Plays is a different book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Poor workers (Working class people whose hard lives this group of plays puts on stage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Window is a social play, not a poem.
It was printed with The Parrot in Five Plays in 1937.
The pair deals with the lives of the poor.
The volume protests cruelty, stiff morals, and the suffering of workers.
No Indian English dramatist before him had put so much working class life on stage.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ten stories of ordinary Naga people living through insurgency (an armed revolt) and army rule.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Scroll and Wikipedia date the Penguin and Zubaan book to 2005. Some library catalogues print 2006. Use 2005 for the first publication. The stories look back to the Naga conflict from the 1950s onward.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The preface speaker (Ao, asking readers to remember pain that history books skip); Khatila (Punaba's wife in The Jungle Major, who disguises him and faces the soldiers); Punaba (A short village man who joins the underground (a hidden armed group) and rises to captain); Sashi (An old man who tells his grandson, Moalmba, about years in the jungle)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A preface, Lest We Forget, says these tales are not a record of facts.
The fight over Naga independence sits behind daily village life.
In The Jungle Major, Khatila hides the fighter Punaba from the army.
In An Old Man Remembers, Sashi tells his grandson about a stolen youth.
Curfew, raids, and sudden loss enter homes, schools, and paths.
Ao counts victims and scarred minds, not a winning side.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The hunter Vilie seeks a stone of power from a river that sleeps in the Naga hills.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database calls this work poetry and sorts it under 1947. That year is the Indian period label, and the genre label is wrong. Zubaan published the novel in 2014. It won The Hindu Prize for Fiction in 2015. The publisher spells the hunter Vilie.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Vilie (A lone hunter who quests for the stone in the sleeping river)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Vilie, a lone hunter, dreams of a river that falls asleep.
He sets out to take a stone from its sleeping waters.
People say the stone will give great power.
On the way he meets spirits, a weretiger (a person who becomes a tiger), and armed men.
The quest tests what he will do if he wins that power.
The forest spirits are as real in this book as the villagers.

items.title: "All About H. Hatterr" (1948) — G. V. Desani

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mixed race comic hero rushes through India in search of wisdom, in wild English.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1948 is correct. Aldor in London issued it in 1948 as All About Mr. Hatterr. A revised edition soon used All About H. Hatterr. The database keeps that later title.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: H. Hatterr (The mixed race hero who seeks wisdom and speaks in a wild mix of Englishes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
H. Hatterr stands for 'Hindustanwallah Hatterr'.
The novel is about the adventure of the protagonist H. Hatterr who searches for wisdom and Enlightment.
The boy H. Hatterr was adopted by English missionary society.
The novel is written in Picaresque mode.
This novel also acted as an influence on Salman Rushdie in forging a new narrative style in English.
The name Hatterr is pinpointing his 'Hat' that is very large for him which suggests his Anglo-Indian environment.
'Hatterr' can be a mark of both Masculine and Feminine Values.
H. Hatterr is part European and part Malay, a man of mixed birth.
He travels in search of wisdom and enlightenment.
Desani called him a portrait of the common vulgar species, East and West.
The prose leaps between high talk, bazaar talk, and jokes.
T. S. Eliot praised the book and said he had met nothing quite like it.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1949 Spanish story collection whose title tale shows a point that holds all space.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The title story was printed in Sur in September 1945. Four stories were added in 1952. The English volume The Aleph and Other Stories, 1933-1969, published in 1970, is not the same book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Borges the narrator (A fictional version of the author, mourning Beatriz Viterbo); Beatriz Viterbo (The dead woman whose memory opens the story); Carlos Argentino Daneri (Beatriz's cousin, a vain poet who uses the Aleph for his epic)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title story first appeared in the magazine Sur in September 1945.
Losada of Buenos Aires gathered the stories as El Aleph in 1949.
The narrator mourns Beatriz Viterbo and visits her cousin Carlos Argentino Daneri.
In a dark cellar he sees the Aleph, a tiny sphere that contains all places.
He pretends he saw nothing, so that Daneri will doubt himself.
A 1952 edition adds four more stories.
A 1970 English book is a different selection.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A white farmer's wife in Rhodesia breaks down and is killed by her black servant.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1950 is correct. Michael Joseph published the British book in 1950. Thomas Y. Crowell published the American book in the same year. The title comes from The Waste Land.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mary Turner (A white town worker who becomes a frightened farmer's wife); Dick Turner (Mary's husband, a struggling white farmer); Moses (The black servant who kills Mary)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A news note says Mary Turner, a white woman, was killed by her servant Moses.
The story then goes back to Mary's lonely life and her hasty marriage.
She marries Dick Turner, a poor farmer, after hearing friends laugh at her.
The farm fails, and Mary treats the black workers with cold contempt.
She once strikes Moses with a whip, and Dick later makes Moses the house servant.
Fear, poverty, and that tense bond end in Mary's murder.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dying man in bed tells stories while his possessions fail him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1951 is the French year. Editions de Minuit published Malone meurt in 1951. Beckett's English text, Malone Dies, appeared in 1956. He finished the French book in the summer of 1948, after Molloy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Malone (A dying narrator who writes until he cannot); Sapo (A boy in Malone's story); Macmann (The later name and figure in Malone's tale)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Malone lies in a room and waits to die.
He plans an inventory of his goods and a few stories.
One story follows a boy, Sapo, who later resembles Macmann.
The stories break off as the pencil and the life run out.
The book is the middle novel of the three French books.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Molloy struggles toward his mother, then Moran is sent to find him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1951 is the French year. Editions de Minuit published Molloy in 1951. The English text, by Patrick Bowles with Beckett, appeared in 1955. It is the first of the three novels. Malone Dies follows it.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Molloy (The first narrator, a decayed son looking for his mother); Moran (An agent sent to search for Molloy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel is set in Ireland.
It is the first novel among the trilogy being other two are Malone Dies and The Unnamable.
Molloy is the Protagonist of the novel while Moran is a private detective. 3. Murphy.
It is an avant-garde novel. It was written in English.
The novel opens with the protagonist Murphy having tied himself naked to a rocking chair in his apartment, rocking back and forth in the dark.
The book has two parts and two failing quests.
Molloy wanders, often with a bicycle, toward his mother's room.
His body breaks down as the journey goes on.
Moran is ordered to find Molloy and write a report.
Moran's own body and mission collapse until he resembles his prey.

items.title: "The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian" (1951) — Nirad C. Chaudhuri

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Autobiography of an Unknown Indian

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Chaudhuri tells his Bengali youth as a history of India under British rule.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1951 is correct. He dated the start of writing to 5 May 1947. Macmillan published the book in 1951.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nirad C. Chaudhuri (The narrator, telling his own early life and the life of Bengal)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He began the book on 5 May 1947, and it came out in 1951.
He describes Kishoreganj, his ancestral village, his mother's village, and Calcutta.
He records the Bengali Renaissance (a cultural revival) and the start of nationalism.
He says the book is more ethnology (the study of a people) than a private life.
The dedication offers the book to the memory of the British Empire in India.
Many Indian readers attacked that dedication, while he said it also condemned unequal rule.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first book asks how a poet should live, love, and return home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1952 is correct. The Fortune Press in London published A Time to Change in 1952, while Ezekiel was returning from England.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ezekiel wrote much of the book while living poorly in London.
The title poem asks how those who leave home in April can return.
The poems weigh desire, God, the city, and the wish for an exact style.
He pays the Fortune Press to print the book in 1952.
In India the book marks a turn toward modern, personal poetry in English.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A future novel where machines run work and one man rebels.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1952 is correct. Scribner's published this first novel. A 1954 reprint used the title Utopia 14. The database labels the work as drama, but it is a novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Paul Proteus (An engineer who turns against a society run by machines)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In a future America, machines do most jobs.
Paul Proteus is an engineer inside that system.
People still have goods, but their work and purpose are gone.
He is sent among the poor and joins a revolt against the machines.
The revolt fails, and the warning about blind progress remains.
Vonnegut drew on his job at General Electric.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two men wait by a tree for Godot, who never arrives.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He wrote En attendant Godot from October 1948 to January 1949. It opened in Paris on 5 January 1953. Grove Press printed the English text in 1954. London first saw it on 3 August 1955.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Vladimir (One waiter, also called Didi); Estragon (The other waiter, also called Gogo); Pozzo (A master who drives Lucky with a rope); Lucky (Pozzo's servant, who speaks one wild long speech); The boy (A messenger who says Godot will come tomorrow)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Vladimir and Estragon meet by a bare tree and wait.
Pozzo enters with his servant Lucky on a rope.
A boy says Godot will not come tonight, but tomorrow.
Act two repeats the wait.
The tree has a few leaves.
Pozzo is now blind.
Godot still does not come.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A nameless voice talks on because it cannot stop.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1953 is the French year. Editions de Minuit published L'Innommable in 1953. Grove Press published The Unnamable in English in 1958. Beckett finished the French text in 1950.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The unnamable voice (A speaker who may be mouth, or thought, and has no fixed body)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
7. Mercier and Camier (written 1946, published 1970); English translation (1974)
The speaker has no stable name or body.
Earlier figures such as Molloy and Malone seem to be masks.
The voice says it must speak, yet it has nothing sure to tell.
Words circle, cancel, and begin again.
The book ends by going on even while it cannot go on.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Boys stranded on an island try to govern themselves and slide into killing.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1954 is correct. Faber and Faber published Lord of the Flies on 17 September 1954. An early title was Strangers from Within.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ralph (The elected leader who wants shelter, rules, and a signal fire); Jack Merridew (The choir leader who turns the boys toward hunting and fear); Piggy (A fat, clever boy whose glasses light the fire); Simon (A quiet boy who understands that the beast is human); Roger (A cruel boy who kills Piggy)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a 1954 dystopian novel about a group of British boys struck on an inhabited island who try to govern themselves with disastrous result. Title of the novel Lord of the Flies refers to Beelzebub, another name for the devil.
This book was rejected by 56 publishers but finally accepted by Faber and Faber.
The novel is a reaction to the youth novel The Coral Island by R.M.Ballantyne, which is not a dystopian novel. (Character Ralph and Jack Martin are there in The Coral Island as well).
This was the first novel of Golding and gained a worldly success after publication.
In the novel Ralph represents rationality, piggy- pragmatism, Jack -savagery and Simon -innocence.
A plane crash leaves British boys alone on an empty island.
Ralph is chosen chief.
The conch shell gives a boy the right to speak.
Jack leads the hunters.
Fear of a beast splits the group.
Simon learns the beast is inside the boys, and the others kill him.
Roger kills Piggy and smashes the conch.
The boys hunt Ralph.
A naval officer arrives, and the children weep.
His own ship is also at war.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Gentle early humans meet a cleverer people, and the new people destroy them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1955 is correct. Faber published The Inheritors in 1955, one year after Lord of the Flies.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lok (One of the early people, simple, loyal, and lost); Fa (A woman of Lok's group who sees the danger more clearly); The new people (The cleverer humans who bring weapons and deceit)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is fantasy fiction by Golding.
It is the second novel of Golding and it concerns with the extinction of one of the last remaining tribes of Neanderthals at the hand of more sophisticated Homo-sapiens.
The novel explains that innocence and happiness existed before homo-sapiens developed and with him an all destroying urge to evil.
Loc and Fa are the chief characters.
Lok and his small group are early humans, often read as Neanderthals (an earlier kind of human).
They think in pictures and do not understand lies.
A new people arrive, with bows, boats, and more cunning.
The new people kill and capture members of Lok's group.
Fa, who understands more than Lok, is taken.
The last chapter switches to the new people, who see the old ones as devils.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The 1955 book that made Larkin's mature voice public.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1955 is correct. The Marvell Press dated copies October and issued them in November 1955. The posthumous flag in the database does not fit this book. Larkin died in 1985.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The church visitor (The speaker of Church Going, unsure why the church still matters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(xiii) Party Politics (Last Published Poem) (xiv)
The Marvell Press at Hessle published it in 1955.
Many of the poems were written while he worked in Belfast.
Church Going describes a visitor in an empty church.
Toads and Deceptions cut through easy ideas of work and love.
The Times listed the book among its books of the year.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A farmer and his wife build a life in the bush as the city grows around them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1955 is correct for first publication. Viking published it in the United States in August 1955. Eyre and Spottiswoode published the London edition in 1956. An early title was A Life Sentence on Earth.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Stan Parker (The farmer whose whole life the novel follows); Amy Parker (Stan's wife, who shares the long work of the farm)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Stan Parker and his wife Amy clear land and start a farm.
They raise children, face flood and fire, and grow old on the same ground.
The bush settlement slowly becomes part of the spreading suburbs.
White treats this ordinary marriage as an epic of endurance.
The book was his first large success outside Australia.

items.title: "To Whom She Will" (1955) — Ruth Prawer Jhabvala

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Delhi comedy in which family plans defeat a love match across communities.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1955 is correct for the London novel. It was published in the United States in 1956 as Amrita. That is a new title, not a new book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amrita (A wealthy young Delhi woman who wants to choose her own husband); Hari (A poor young man from a Punjabi refugee family); Krishna (The messenger who later marries Amrita)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Amrita is a young woman in Delhi who works as a radio announcer.
She loves Hari, a poor Punjabi refugee who also works in radio.
Both families scheme to stop a marriage they think is unfit.
Hari marries a girl chosen from his own community.
Amrita marries Krishna, who had carried messages between the lovers.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young husband rages at his wife, her class, and a Britain with no great cause.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1956 is correct. The English Stage Company first staged it on 8 May 1956 at the Royal Court Theatre, London.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jimmy Porter (The angry young husband who feels trapped between classes); Alison Porter (Jimmy's upper middle class wife); Cliff Lewis (The Welsh lodger who tries to calm the house); Helena Charles (Alison's friend, who later stays with Jimmy); Colonel Redfern (Alison's father, a former army officer)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(iv)
(ii)
It concerns a love triangle involving an intellectual and educated but dis-affected young man of working class origin Jimmy Porter, his upper middle class impassive wife Alison and her haughty best friend Helena Charles.
It is written in 17 days in a deck chair. It is an autobiographical piece based on Osborne's unhappy marriage to actress Pamela Lane.
It begins in a flat of Jimmy Porter and Alison Porter.
The setting in mid 1950's small town England.
Jimmy and Alison share their apartment with Cliff Lewis, a young working class man and best friend of Jimmy while Alison is from a prominent family.
Cliff and Jimmy both are from a working class background and they do business together running a sweet stall.
The first act opens with Jimmy and Cliff reading Sunday papers while Alison is ironing.
Jimmy attempts to provoke his wife by making fun of her family and her well heeled life before marriage and also provoked Cliff for his working class background and low intelligence.
Alison confides to Cliff that she is pregnant with Jimmy's child though she has not told Jimmy about it.
Alison informs Jimmy about her friend Helena Charles who visits them but Jimmy don't like this and in rage he wishes Alison to suffer and curses her that she could have a child only to watch it die.
When Jimmy asked Alison to make decision either to accompany him to see the dying Mrs. Tanner or to go with Helena, and thus Jimmy is heartbroken by his wife's decision.
Alison packs her luggage and her favorite toy squirrel to go with her father Colonel Red Fern and leaving Jimmy alone.
Alison leaves a letter for Jimmy explaining why she left him and handed the letter to Cliff.
Cliff blames Helena for this situation, Helena tells jimmy that Alison is pregnant but he ignored saying he don't care.
In act III, Alison again returns back, she has lost her baby.
Helena confesses her presence as a reason for the situation and she prepares to leave.
When Helena laves, Jimmy again becomes angry on Alison but she tells him that she has now gone through the emotional and physical suffering that he always wanted her to feel.
Jimmy realizes this and becomes softer and tender towards her.
The play ends with Jimmy and Alison embracing, once again playing their game of bear and squirrel.
In this play Jimmy Porter displays a sense of restlessness and rebelliousness.
Jimmy Porter, an educated working class man, runs a sweet stall and lives in a small attic.
He attacks his wife Alison, while their lodger Cliff tries to keep the peace.
Alison is pregnant but does not tell Jimmy.
Her friend Helena sends for Alison's father.
Alison leaves.
Helena stays, and she and Jimmy begin an affair.
Alison returns after losing the baby.
Helena leaves, and the couple make a sad peace.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first full book of poems, chosen by Auden for the Yale Younger Poets series.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1956 is correct. Auden chose the manuscript for the Yale series. Do not move this book to 1975.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Yale University Press published the book in 1956.
W. H. Auden selected it for the Yale Younger Poets series.
Early poems show the touch of Auden and Wallace Stevens.
French surrealist art also leaves a mark.
Surrealist art joins dream pictures with ordinary things.
The voice is clearer here than in The Tennis Court Oath.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Todd Andrews spends one day deciding whether his life is worth keeping.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1956 is the first publication. He finished the novel in 1955. Anchor issued a revised text in 1967 and restored an earlier ending. Keep 1956 as the first year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Todd Andrews (A Maryland lawyer who narrates one day of suicidal thought)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Todd Andrews, a Maryland lawyer, thinks about suicide.
A floating showboat gives the book its title and its day.
He asks whether life has any firm value.
He decides that relative values are still real enough for living.
The first edition of 1956 softened the ending.
A 1967 revision restored an earlier one.

items.title: "The Room on the Roof" (1956) — Ruskin Bond

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lonely boy in Dehradun leaves a strict guardian and finds friends in the town.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1956 is correct for publication. He began it in London at seventeen, about 1951. The Rhys Prize is 1957. A journal list gives London: Deutsch, 1956.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rusty (An orphaned boy of British and Indian descent, based on Bond); John Harrison (Rusty's stern guardian in the European part of Dehradun)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rusty lives in Dehradun with his strict guardian, John Harrison.
He makes Indian friends in the market and hides those visits.
He runs away from the guardian's house.
He shares a small room on a roof and learns the life of the town.
Bond wrote this partly from his own youth, when he was seventeen.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: During the 1947 Partition, a border village must choose between revenge and a single act of mercy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chatto and Windus published Train to Pakistan in London in 1956. Grove Press issued the same novel in 1956 as Mano Majra. The database year 1956 is correct for both titles.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Juggut Singh (A rough Sikh villager who loves the Muslim girl Nooran); Nooran (Daughter of the village imam (Muslim prayer leader), and Juggut's lover); Iqbal (An educated outsider who is jailed and is slow to act); Hukum Chand (The magistrate (local official) who knows the attack plan and feels guilty)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mano Majra is a mixed Sikh and Muslim village beside the railway.
A moneylender is murdered, and Juggut Singh is jailed though he is innocent.
Iqbal, an educated outsider, is jailed with him by mistake.
Trains full of dead bodies arrive, and Sikhs plan to attack a Muslim refugee train.
Juggut cuts the killing rope and dies so that the train can pass.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first book of poems, published in London while he was still at Oxford.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1957 is correct for the book. Parton Press published it in 1957. The Hawthornden Prize followed in 1958. Some catalogues print 1958 because of the prize.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
David Archer's Parton Press in London published the book in 1957.
Moraes was still a student of English at Jesus College, Oxford.
The poems use rhyme, myth, and figures such as kings, knights, and dragons.
In 1958 the book won the Hawthornden Prize for imaginative writing.
He was the youngest winner, and the first Indian to win that prize.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A map of literature by modes, symbols, myths, and genres.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Four public lectures at Princeton in March 1954 were expanded into the book. Princeton University Press published Anatomy of Criticism in 1957. The database year 1957 is the publication year.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Frye asks criticism to study literature as a system, not only to praise or blame books.
Essay one sorts heroes into five modes, from gods down to ironic victims.
Essay two reads symbols from the plain sense up to the archetype.
Essay three sets four mythoi on the seasons: comedy, romance, tragedy, and irony.
Essay four names four genres: epos, prose fiction, drama, and lyric.
Epos means the teller speaks directly to a listening audience.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Hamm, blind and still, waits for an end with Clov and his parents.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1957 matches the French book and the first night. It opened in French at the Royal Court Theatre, London, on 3 April 1957. The original language is French. Beckett's works list also dates the English title Endgame to 1957.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hamm (A blind master who cannot stand); Clov (Hamm's servant, who cannot sit); Nagg (Hamm's father, kept in an ashbin); Nell (Hamm's mother, kept in an ashbin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a one act play by Beckett with four characters, written in style of the theatre of the Absurd.
It was originally written in French entitled Fin de Partie.
Chief characters.
Hamm - unable to stand and blind.
Clov - servent of Hamm.
Nagg - Hamm's father.
Nell - Hamm's mother.
Hamm sits blind and cannot stand.
Clov cannot sit.
Nagg and Nell live in two ashbins and rarely emerge.
Outside the bare room, the world seems already finished.
Hamm tells a story and orders Clov about.
Clov prepares to leave, and the end still hangs.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two strangers break a lodger during a fake birthday party.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1957 is the writing year, not the first night. Pinter wrote it in 1957. It opened at the Arts Theatre, Cambridge, on 28 April 1958. Wikipedia dates an Encore edition to 1959. The Nobel list gives the Methuen collection in 1960.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Stanley Webber (A former piano player hiding in the boarding house); Meg Boles (The landlady who treats Stanley like a child); Petey Boles (Meg's husband, a deck chair attendant who fails to save Stanley); Goldberg (The smooth leader of the two intruders); McCann (Goldberg's tense partner); Lulu (A young neighbor who comes to the party)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Stanley Webber lodges with Meg and Petey at a seaside house.
Goldberg and McCann arrive and will not let Stanley leave.
They hold a party, though Stanley says it is not his birthday.
A toy drum, a game, and questions break Stanley down.
They take him away.
Petey calls after him, but he cannot stop them.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A failing music hall comic stands for a Britain that has lost its old confidence.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1957 is correct for the first production. Laurence Olivier played Archie Rice at the Royal Court. The database genre label Poetry is wrong. This is a play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Archie Rice (A failing music hall comedian and the play's hero); Billy Rice (Archie's father, from an older music hall age); Phoebe Rice (Archie's weary wife); Jean Rice (Archie's daughter, who sees through the act)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(v) Epitaph for George Dillon (1957): It is written in collaboration with Anthony Creighton. (vi) Tom Jones (1964): It is an adaption of Fielding's novel into a film. (vii)
(iii)
It is a three act play.
Osborne wrote it on Lawrence Oliver's request about an angry middle aged man.
The protagonist of the play is Archie Rice, a falling music hall performer.
Archie Rice is a tired comic in a music hall that is dying.
His family is bitter, short of money, and split by private pain.
The play is tied to the Suez crisis and Britain's loss of power.
Songs and comic turns sit beside the family's bad news.
Osborne uses the old hall as a picture of national decline.

items.title: "The Hawk in the Rain" (1957) — Ted Hughes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first book of poems, full of hawks, foxes, storms, and war memories.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1957 is correct. Faber published the book in 1957. The database calls it posthumous. That flag is wrong. Hughes died in 1998.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Thought Fox speaker (A writer who feels a poem arrive like a fox in the dark); The hawk (A fierce bird that stands for power in nature)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the first book of Hughes poetry.
The book received immediate acclaim in both England and America where it won Galbraith prize.
Many of the book's poem imagine the real and symbolize lives of animals including a fox, a jaguar and the eponymous hawk.
This book is dedicated to Hughes first wife Sylvia Plath.
It is a collection of 40 poems.
Faber and Faber published this first collection in 1957.
Sylvia Plath sent the manuscript to a New York contest judged by Auden, Spender, and Marianne Moore.
The book won first prize, and Harper published it in America.
Many poems watch animals, including a hawk, a jaguar, and a fox.
Other poems remember the First World War, which his father survived.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ganesh, a failed writer, becomes a healer and then a colonial politician.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1957 is correct for publication. He wrote it in autumn 1955. It won the John Llewellyn Rhys Prize in 1958.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ganesh Ramsumair (The hero who rises from healer to politician as G. Ramsay Muir); Leela (Ganesh's wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a comic novel by Naipaul. It is set in Colonial Trinidad but published in London.
The novel is about a frustrated writer of Indian descent who rises from an impoverished background to become a successful politician on the back of his dubious talent as a 'mystic' masseur, a masseur who can cure illness.
Naipaul wrote the novel quickly in autumn 1955.
Andre Deutsch published it in June 1957.
Ganesh Ramsumair is a Trinidad Indian who wants to be a writer.
He gains fame as a mystic masseur (a healer who rubs the body).
People call him Pundit Ganesh.
He ends as a successful politician under the name G. Ramsay Muir.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A German explorer tries to cross Australia while a woman in Sydney shares his inner journey.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1957 is correct. Eyre and Spottiswoode in London published Voss in 1957.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Johann Ulrich Voss (A proud German explorer who leads the expedition); Laura Trevelyan (A young woman in Sydney who is spiritually tied to Voss); Mr Bonner (Laura's uncle and the patron who pays for the journey); Judd (A member of the party who survives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Johann Ulrich Voss plans an expedition across the continent.
In Sydney he meets Laura Trevelyan, niece of his patron Mr Bonner.
Their strange bond continues after Voss leaves for the desert.
The party splits, and almost all of the explorers die.
Years later Laura attends the unveiling of a statue of Voss.
The story uses the lost explorer Ludwig Leichhardt, but Voss is fictional.

items.title: "A Time to Be Happy" (1958) — Nayantara Sahgal

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A rich young man seeks an Indian self as the country nears freedom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Her bibliography dates this first novel to 1958. Kirkus reviewed a Knopf text in its 15 June 1957 issue. Use 1958 unless a question names that review.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sanad Shivpal (A young English educated man of a rich family, caught between two cultures); Kusum (Sanad's wife, from a family that follows nationalist values)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story follows the rich Shivpal family in Saharanpur, a town in north India.
Sanad is young, English educated, and works for a British firm.
He feels that he belongs fully neither to Britain nor to India.
He marries Kusum, whose family stands with the nationalist movement.
He learns Hindi and turns toward Gandhi and ordinary Indian life.

items.title: "The End of the Road" (1958) — John Barth

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jacob Horner, unable to choose, is pulled into a marriage and a fatal affair.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1958 is the first book year. A revised edition appeared in 1967. A loose film came in 1970. Keep 1958 for the novel. The database calls it drama. It is fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jacob Horner (The narrator, paralysed by too many possible choices); Joe Morgan (A history teacher who trusts strict reason); Rennie Morgan (Joe's wife, caught between the two men)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jacob Horner freezes because every choice seems possible.
A doctor sends him to teach at a college in Maryland.
He enters the marriage of Joe and Rennie Morgan.
The affair ends when Rennie dies after a botched abortion.
Doubleday published the novel in 1958. A revised edition came in 1967.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tragedy of an Igbo warrior whose village collapses under the arrival of British colonial rule.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The novel was first published in London by Heinemann on 17 June 1958.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Okonkwo (A proud and hot-tempered Igbo leader who fears failure and weakness above all else.); Ikemefuna (A young hostage from a neighboring clan who is raised in Okonkwo's household.); Nwoye (Okonkwo's gentle oldest son who later abandons his father to join the Christian church.); Obierika (Okonkwo's loyal and thoughtful best friend who questions some tribal customs.); Mr. Brown (The first British missionary who wins converts through patience and peaceful dialogue.); Reverend James Smith (A strict and intolerant British missionary who replaces Mr. Brown and inflames conflict.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Okonkwo is a respected wrestler and wealthy leader in the Igbo village of Umuofia.
He is terrified of weakness because his late father was lazy and unsuccessful.
Okonkwo takes in a captive boy named Ikemefuna and grows very fond of him.
An elder warns him not to help kill the boy, but Okonkwo strikes Ikemefuna to hide fear.
Okonkwo accidentally shoots a boy at a funeral and suffers seven years of exile.
When he returns, Christian missionaries and British officials have divided and changed the clan.
Okonkwo kills a colonial messenger to spark rebellion, but his people refuse to fight.
Realizing that his world has fallen apart, Okonkwo hangs himself in despair.

items.title: "I Shall Not Hear the Nightingale" (1959) — Khushwant Singh

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: I Shall Not Hear the Nightingale

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In wartime Punjab, a magistrate's son joins a violent group that wants the British to leave.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Grove Press in New York published the novel in 1959. The London edition from Calder came in 1961. The database year 1959 is the first publication. The story is set before Train to Pakistan.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Buta Singh (A Sikh magistrate loyal to the British); Sabhrai (His religious wife, who becomes the moral centre of the family); Sher Singh (Their son, torn between safety and violent revolt); Champak (Sher Singh's wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Buta Singh serves the British and hopes for an honour.
His son Sher Singh leads young men who want an armed revolt.
Sher is arrested after a village informer is killed.
Buta disowns him, but Sabhrai tells Sher not to betray his friends.
Sher had dreamed that nightingales would sing after freedom.
The title doubts that hope.

items.title: "The Lion and the Jewel" (1963) — Wole Soyinka

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The old chief Baroka, the Lion, wins the village beauty Sidi from the modern teacher.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was first acted in Ibadan in 1959. That is the catalog year. Oxford University Press published the book in 1963, as the Nobel bibliography records. One web page says the book came in 1962. Use 1959 for the stage and 1963 for the usual book date. London's Royal Court staged it in 1966.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Baroka (The sixty two year old Bale, called the Lion); Sidi (The village beauty, called the Jewel); Lakunle (A Westernised teacher who mocks bride price and still wants Sidi); Sadiku (Baroka's senior wife and his messenger)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This play chronicles Baroka, the Lion who fights with modern Lakunle over the right to marry Sidi, the titular jewel.
Baraka is a 62 years protagonist referred as a lion in the title while Sidi is referred as Jewel.
In this Play Soyinka, emphasises the theme of the corruption, African culture and how the youth should embrace the original African culture.
Lakunle, a young teacher, woos Sidi but will not pay her bride price.
A magazine makes Sidi famous and makes Baroka look small.
Baroka, the Bale of Ilujinle, asks for Sidi as a wife.
He pretends that he has lost his manhood.
Sidi visits him to mock him and is seduced.
She chooses the old Lion, and Lakunle is left behind.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An army novel about loyalty among Indian officers before and after Independence.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1960 is correct. The Hindu and the Sahitya Akademi monograph both call Distant Drum his first novel and date it 1960. He was 47 then. A 1959 life of Kanhoji Angre is history, not this novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kiran Garud (The officer hero, shaped by duty and the army code); Abdulla Jamal (Kiran's friend, who shares danger with him across the communal line)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Kiran Garud, an Indian officer, is the centre of the story.
He and his friend Abdulla Jamal each save the other's life.
The novel recalls the code of the old British Indian Army.
Religious tension fades when the two men keep faith with each other.
It also looks at Indian and Pakistani soldiers after the armies divide.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His second book, with famous animal poems such as Hawk Roosting and Pike.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1960 is correct. Faber published the book in 1960. It is not posthumous. The database flag that says so is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The hawk in Hawk Roosting (A bird that speaks as if nature itself is thinking); The pike (A river hunter remembered from the poet's childhood)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber and Faber published Lupercal in 1960.
The title names an old Roman fertility rite (a festival for new life).
The style is simpler and harder than in the first book.
Hawk Roosting speaks in the voice of a hawk that claims the whole wood.
Pike and other poems keep his focus on hunters, farms, and Yorkshire places.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The story of an educated Nigerian civil servant who falls into financial debt and bribery.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published by Heinemann in 1960. It forms the second installment of Achebe's African trilogy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Obi Okonkwo (An educated young Nigerian civil servant and grandson of Okonkwo who succumbs to bribery.); Clara Okeke (A nurse and Obi's fiancee who belongs to the osu outcast group.); Isaac Okonkwo (Nwoye) (Obi's father and former Christian convert who refuses to let Obi marry an osu.); William Green (Obi's British colonial supervisor who holds rigid prejudices about Nigerian civil servants.); Joseph (Obi's practical friend in Lagos who advises him to follow clan traditions.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the second novel of the African Trilogy.
The Protagonist is Obi Okonkwo, grandson of Okonkwo (protagonist of Things Fall Apart).
Obi leaves his village for British education and gets a job in the Nigerian Colonial Civil Service.
The Struggles in the novel to adapt a western lifestyle and ends up taking a bribe.
The title of the novel is taken from the closing lines of T. S. Eliot's The Journey of the Magi.
The novel opens with the trial of Obi Okonkwo for accepting a bribe in Lagos.
The narrative flashes back to Obi receiving a community scholarship to study in Britain.
Obi returns to Lagos with idealistic hopes to serve the civil service without taking bribes.
He falls in love with Clara, but discovers she is an osu (hereditary outcast).
His Christian parents and village elders strictly forbid him from marrying an osu.
Crushed by high living costs, family debts, and Clara's abortion fees, Obi takes a bribe.
Police arrest him in a sting operation, marking his complete moral downfall.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tramp and two brothers fight over a room and a job.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1960 is right for the book and the premiere. Methuen published it in 1960. It opened at the Arts Theatre, London, on 27 April 1960. Pinter wrote it in 1959.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Davies (A tramp who also calls himself Bernard Jenkins); Aston (A quiet man who offers Davies a bed); Mick (Aston's brother, quick in speech and keen to dominate)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mick and his brother Aston live together in a West London house until one night Aston brings home Mac Davis.
The actual name of Mac Davis was Bernard Jenkins.
Aston brings the homeless Davies into his junk filled room.
Aston's brother Mick also claims power in the house.
Davies gives a false name and talks of papers left in Sidcup.
Both brothers float the idea that Davies could be caretaker.
The offer never becomes safe, and Davies is shut out again.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Plath's first poetry book, full of careful images of death, family, and myth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1960 is the British book. Heinemann published it in England on 31 October 1960. Knopf published the United States edition on 14 May 1962. It is the only poetry book issued in her lifetime.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of The Colossus (A daughter figure trying to piece a giant father together)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is a book of separate poems, not one story.
The title poem speaks to a huge broken father figure.
The speaker tries to repair him and cannot.
Other poems watch gardens, the sea, dead people, and animals.
The voice is controlled, exact, and already uneasy.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ten poems from 1959 about failed journeys, the city, and an unfinished self.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1960 is correct. The poems were written in 1959. Writers Workshop, Calcutta, published the book in 1960.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book holds ten poems written in 1959.
A verse from Yeats stands at the front as an epigraph (a short opening quotation).
Enterprise tells of a pilgrimage that ends in fatigue and small deeds.
Urban shows a city man whose mind never reaches the hills or the sky.
Writers Workshop in Calcutta published the book in 1960.

items.title: "A House for Mr Biswas" (1961) — V. S. Naipaul

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Mohun Biswas spends his life trying to own one house of his own.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1961 is correct. Naipaul said the writing took about three years and that he passed the proofs in May 1961.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mohun Biswas (A Trinidad Indian whose one aim is a house of his own); The Tulsis (The powerful in-laws who house him and mock him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel makes Naipaul to achieve acclaim worldwide. It is dedicated to first wife of Naipaul Patricia.
It is an apocalyptic Novel.
It is the story of Mohun Biswas, an Indo Trinidadian who continually strives for success and mostly fails. He married to Tulsi family but was dominated by them and then plan of owing his own house.
It is devided into 2 part with a prologue and epilogue. Characters of A House for Mr. Biswas.
Mohun Biswas - Protagonist.
Shama - The wife of Mr. Biswas.
Bipti - Mother of the Mr. Biswas.
Raghu - Father of Mr. Biswas Apocalyptic Novel/ Apocalyptic Fiction.
Apocalyptic literature is mainly science fiction or horror fiction with a revealing event typically being Climatic.
The story may involve attempts to prevent an apocalypse or alien invasion.
The time frame may be immediately after the catastrophe focusing on the survivors.
For example V S Naipaul's - A House for Mr. Biswas Dorris Lessing's - The four gated city H. P. Hartley's - Facial Justice.
Dehuti - Sister of the Mr. Biswas.
Pratap and Prasad - Elder brothers of Mr. Biswas.
Tara - Sister of Bipti.
Ajodha - Tara's husband.
Mrs. Tulsi - Shama's mother.
Owad and Shekhar - Sons of Mrs. Tulsi.
Savi - Oldest child of Shama.
Anand - Only son of Mr. Biswas.
Myna and Kamla - Younger daughters of Mr. Biswas Plot.
Mohun Biswas is born in rural Trinidad to the parents of Indian origin. He is the last among three brothers.
His birth is considered inauspicious as he is born (Astrologically inauspicious hour of mid night) "in the wrong way" and with extra finger on each hand.
A Pandit prophesizes that the child will be a lecher and a spendthrift possibly a liar as well and will eat up his mother and father.
The Pandit advises that the boy be kept away, from trees and water.
Mohun once goes in the water but hides in fear of punishment and his father is drowned in order to save him, partially fulfilling the prophesy of Pandit. After his father's death he is sent to live with the relatives (Aunt Tara).
Mahun is withdrawn from the school and apprenticed to a Pandit but is cast out on bad terms.
Ajodha, aunt of Mohun, puts him in the hand of her brother Bhandat, which also ends badly.
Finally the young Mr. Biswas decides to make his own fortune.
He goes to Hanuman house to paint signs for the Tulsi.
While attempting to romance with Tulsi's daughter Shama, he is misinterpreted as a wedding proposal and after marrying her becomes a member of the Tulsi household(Also called Hanuman House). Here he found himself trapped.
Mr. Biswas becomes very unhappy with his wife Shama (16 year old) and her overbearing family.
Mr. Biswas is offered a place in the Tulsi's but Mr. Biswas wants more, by his instinct he is a modern man.
He wants to be author of his own life and thus he becomes a journalist. He had four children with Shama and attempts several times to build a house which will symbolize his independence.
He moves to 'The Chase', after fighting with one of his son-in-law and runs a small food shop owned by Tulsis.
After boredom of 6 year he moves to a squalid barrack in Green Vale as a sub overseer on the Tulsi land still feeling trapped.
He dreams of building his own house with wife Shama, daughter Savi and son Anand.
The novel is an imagined life of Naipaul's father, Seepersad.
Mohun Biswas is pushed into the large Tulsi family.
He tries many jobs, from sign painter to reporter.
The Tulsis feed him and also trap him.
Near the end he borrows money and buys a house.
He dies at 46. Naipaul passed the proofs in May 1961.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Winnie, buried in a mound, talks through her daily routine.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1961 matches the first performance. It opened at the Cherry Lane Theatre, New York, on 17 September 1961. Alan Schneider directed. The play was written in English. The French text, Oh les beaux jours, was published in 1963.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Winnie (A woman buried in a mound who talks to fill the day); Willie (Her husband, mostly silent and out of sight)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Winnie wakes to a bell, buried to her waist in a mound.
She speaks to Willie, who is mostly hidden and silent.
She sorts a bag, prays, and calls the day happy.
In the second act she is buried to her neck.
She still talks, and she still tries to call the day happy.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A voice crawls through mud and tells life in three parts.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1961 is the French year. Editions de Minuit published Comment c'est in 1961. Grove Press published How It Is in 1964. An early piece, L'Image, appeared in 1959. Part of the English text was printed in the journal Arna in 1962.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A voice crawling in the mud and quoting what he hears); Pim (The figure he finds, hurts, and then loses)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The French title is Comment c'est.
A narrator crawls naked through mud in the dark.
The three parts are before Pim, with Pim, and after Pim.
He meets Pim, torments him, and then is left alone.
Short blocks of words replace ordinary sentences.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four outsiders in a suburb share a vision of the chariot from scripture.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1961 is correct. Eyre and Spottiswoode in London published Riders in the Chariot in 1961.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mary Hare (An eccentric woman who lives in a decaying house); Mordecai Himmelfarb (A Jewish refugee and scholar who works in a factory); Ruth Godbold (A kind washerwoman who cares for the suffering); Alf Dubbo (An Aboriginal painter who tries to paint the vision)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel is set in the made up suburb of Sarsaparilla.
Four people each see the same chariot from the prophet Ezekiel.
They are Mary Hare, Mordecai Himmelfarb, Ruth Godbold, and Alf Dubbo.
Himmelfarb, a Jewish refugee, is mocked and attacked at a factory.
The attack is staged like a crucifixion (a killing like that of Jesus).
The book asks who can see a holy vision in dull suburb life.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The sequel, in which Rusty and Kishen wander and learn the limits of freedom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1961 is not supported. Bond wrote the sequel in 1956. India Book House published it in 1981 as The Young Vagrants. Penguin India reissued it in 1993 as Vagrants in the Valley, in one volume with The Room on the Roof.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rusty (The boy from The Room on the Roof, now on the road); Kishen (Another runaway who travels with Rusty)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story starts after Rusty has left his guardian.
Kishen, another runaway, joins him on the road.
They find new friends and new scrapes in the valley.
The adventure also shows that even free boys meet limits.
Bond wrote the sequel in 1956, the year of the first novel.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A violent youth is cured of choice by a state treatment, then faces the result.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1962 is correct. Heinemann in London published it on 17 March 1962. That edition has 21 chapters. The 1963 American edition omitted chapter 21 until 1986.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alex (The narrator and gang leader, who loves Beethoven and violence); Dim, Georgie, and Pete (Alex's droogs, the gang mates who later turn on him); F. Alexander (A writer whose home the gang attacks, and who later uses Alex); The prison chaplain (The man who asks if the state may steal free will)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(viii) The Wanting Seed (1962): It's a dystopian novel. (ix)
It's a dystopian novel.
The protagonist is Alex, a 15 year old anti-hero living in near future, dystopian England. He is the leader among his droogs. He refers himself as "your humble narrator", as he is the narrator of the novel. He raped two 10 year old girls in his bedroom.
Alex refers to himself as "Alexander the large".
F. Alexander is an author in the novel who was in the process of writing his magnum opus A CLOCKWORK ORANGE. Alex and his droogs broke into his house; beat him, tore up his work and then brutally gang raped his wife that caused her subsequent death.
Alex, aged 15, leads a gang in a near future city full of youth violence.
They speak Nadsat, a slang that mixes English with Russian.
After a murder, prison offers him the Ludovico Technique (a cure that makes violence feel sickening).
The cure also spoils his love of Beethoven, and he can no longer choose to be good.
The British last chapter shows an older Alex growing bored with violence and wanting a family.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His breakthrough book of early poems on Caribbean beauty and colonial history.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1962 is correct for the book. The subtitle dates the poems from 1948 to 1960. Nobel, Britannica, and the Poetry Foundation all give 1962 as the breakthrough book.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems were written from 1948 to 1960 and collected in 1962.
They praise the green landscape of the islands.
They also face the scars of empire, slavery, and divided language.
This book first brought Walcott a wide international audience.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Writer Anna Wulf tries to join the broken pieces of her life in one gold notebook.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1962 is correct. Michael Joseph published the novel in Britain in 1962.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anna Wulf (The writer who keeps the notebooks); Molly Jacobs (Anna's actress friend in the Free Women sections); Saul Green (An American writer who shares Anna's breakdown); Mother Sugar (The psychoanalyst (a doctor of the mind) who treats Anna and Molly)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(iv)
This novel is written in 1962. This novel is called Lessing's "Inner Space Fiction" by Margaret Drabble.
The book also contained a powerful anti-war and anti- Stalinist message.
Anna Wulf, a writer in London, keeps four notebooks of different colours.
The black notebook holds her years in Africa and the novel those years produced.
The red notebook holds her years in the Communist Party.
The yellow notebook is a story based on her own love affair.
The blue notebook is her private diary of dreams and feelings.
Sections called Free Women show Anna with her friend Molly.
A fifth, golden notebook is her attempt to make one life out of the pieces.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A daring 1962 book of broken sentences, written while he lived in France.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1962 is correct. Wikipedia and the Flow Chart Foundation both give 1962. It is a poetry book.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
He wrote the book in France.
Wesleyan University Press published it in 1962.
Phrases collide, and a clear story often never arrives.
Critics called the method radical, which means it breaks the usual rules.
It sits between the clearer Some Trees and the later Self-Portrait.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A satire in which the crystal ice nine freezes the world's water.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1963 is correct. Holt, Rinehart and Winston published it. One list says March 1963, and another says April 1963. The year is not in doubt. It was nominated for the Hugo Award.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jonah (The narrator, a writer who tells the end of the wet world); Felix Hoenikker (A cold scientist who invented ice nine); Bokonon (Founder of the island's banned religion)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator, called Jonah, wants to write about the day of Hiroshima.
He studies the family of Felix Hoenikker, a bomb scientist.
Hoenikker invented ice nine, a crystal that freezes any water it touches.
On the poor island of San Lorenzo, people follow a banned comic faith.
That faith is Bokononism, a made up religion of comforting lies.
The crystal reaches the sea, and the world's water turns solid.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Maya, a fearful young wife, is destroyed by a prophecy and by loneliness in marriage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1963 is correct. Peter Owen in London published this first novel in 1963.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Maya (The young wife whose fear and loneliness drive the story); Gautama (Maya's older husband, a practical lawyer)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Maya is the heroine of the novel married to Gautam.
The novel opens on a body lying in the April heat, and Maya is terrified.
Maya is a sensitive, superstitious woman married to the lawyer Gautama.
An astrologer's old prediction fills her with dread about death.
Gautama stays calm and practical, so he cannot share her fear.
The cry of peacocks in the heat makes her panic grow.
She kills Gautama, and her mind gives way.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Esther Greenwood's bright summer cracks, and a bell jar of illness closes over her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Heinemann published it in London on 14 January 1963. Britain reissued it under Plath's name in 1966. The first United States edition is 1971.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Esther Greenwood (The narrator, a student whose breakdown follows Plath's own 1953 crisis); Buddy Willard (Esther's boyfriend, whom she comes to distrust); Doreen (A bold fellow intern in New York); Doctor Gordon (A psychiatrist whose treatment frightens Esther)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Esther Greenwood wins a summer magazine job in New York.
The story opens in the summer the Rosenbergs are put to death.
Fashion, parties, and success leave her numb.
She returns home, is rejected by a writing course, and stops sleeping.
A harsh hospital treatment makes her more afraid.
She enters a mental hospital and slowly begins to recover.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lonely clerk kidnaps an art student and locks her in a cellar.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He drafted it from late 1960 into 1962, and Jonathan Cape published it in 1963. The database year 1963 is correct. The database marks this novel as a translation. That flag is wrong. Fowles wrote it in English.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Frederick Clegg (A lonely clerk and butterfly collector who kidnaps Miranda); Miranda Grey (An art student held in his cellar, who tells her side in a diary); G. P. (An older artist Miranda admired, and who appears in her memories)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Frederick Clegg collects butterflies and suddenly wins a large pools prize.
He buys a lonely house and kidnaps Miranda Grey, a student at the Slade.
He hopes captivity will make her love him, and he promises to respect her.
Miranda's diary shows her fear, her pity, and her failed plans to escape.
She falls ill and dies.
Clegg buries her and thinks of taking another girl.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Prince Abhayraj inherits a princely state just as that world ends.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1963 is correct. The Hindu lists The Princes among his English novels of 1963. The Sahitya Akademi monograph does the same. This is a novel about a princely state, not a history book. The database label of non fiction prose is a catalog error. His history of the Puars of Dewas is a different book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prince Abhayraj (The heir of Begwad, who grows up as princely India disappears); Maharaja Hiroji (Abhayraj's father, the old ruler of Begwad); Kanakchand (A new political climber who profits from the changing order)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel is set in the fictional state of Begwad from about 1938 to 1949.
Maharaja Hiroji has ruled with unchecked power.
His son Abhayraj is the heir, and he is king for only 49 days.
Abhayraj learns, through hard experience, to value human bonds.
New politicians such as Kanakchand rise as the princely order collapses.
