items.title: "An Area of Darkness" (1964) — V. S. Naipaul

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first India book records a year in the land of his ancestors.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1964 is correct. The visit began in 1962. The catalog mark that calls it a translation is wrong. Naipaul wrote it in English.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: V.S. Naipaul (The traveller and narrator of his first return to India)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
II.
Naipaul reached India in early 1962 for a long first visit.
The book came out in 1964.
The title names his struggle to understand India, not a place on a map.
He writes as a Trinidad Indian who feels faceless in the ancestral land.
The book is travel prose in English.
Nissim Ezekiel later answered it in the essay Naipaul's India and Mine.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A traditional Igbo chief priest confronts British indirect rule and suffers a tragic collapse of authority.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The novel was published by Heinemann in 1964.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ezeulu (The unyielding chief priest of Ulu who views himself as an arrow of his god.); Captain T. K. Winterbottom (The British district officer who seeks to govern Umuaro through indirect rule.); Nwaka (A wealthy village rival and orator who openly challenges Ezeulu's religious authority.); Obika (Ezeulu's handsome and impulsive son who dies while running a masked funeral ritual.); Oduche (Ezeulu's son sent to learn European ways, who locks a sacred royal python in a box.); John Goodcountry (An aggressive indigenous Christian catechist who urges converts to eat sacred yams.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
4. A Man of the People (1966) , Protagonist - Nanga (Boss of Odile) 5. Anthills of the Savannah (1987): It takes place at the imaginary place of 'Kangan'.
It is the third novel of African Trilogy.
The novel centers on Ezeulu, the chief priest of several Igbo villages of colonial Nigeria, who confronts colonial powers and Christian missionaries in the 1920's.
The phase "Arrow of god" is drawn from and Igbo proverb in which a person or sometimes an event is said to represent the will of god.
Ezule declared himself "Half spirit and half man".
Ezeulu is the proud chief priest of Ulu, the protector deity of six allied Igbo villages.
He tells the truth during a border land dispute, which impresses the British colonial captain Winterbottom.
Winterbottom tries to appoint Ezeulu as a colonial warrant chief under indirect rule (local puppet leadership).
Ezeulu firmly refuses to serve the British and is imprisoned for two months.
To punish his ungrateful villagers upon release, Ezeulu delays announcing the sacred New Yam Feast.
Without the feast, the village yams rot in the soil and widespread starvation begins.
Villagers abandon Ulu to harvest yams under the protection of the Christian mission.
Ezeulu's favorite son dies suddenly, and the broken priest descends into madness.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first book, a collection of strange and comic short stories.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1964 is correct. Little, Brown published the finished collection in 1964. A database flag calls the book unfinished. That flag is wrong. Me and Miss Mandible was written in October 1960.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (A man of 35 whom the school records call a child, in Me and Miss Mandible); Miss Mandible (The teacher who wants him, but thinks the records make him a child)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Little, Brown published the collection in Boston in 1964.
It gathers early stories, including Me and Miss Mandible.
In that story the school lists a man of 35 as a child of eleven.
He sits in a small desk while the teacher hesitates over him.
Other stories drop famous figures into absurd situations (situations that make no ordinary sense).

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1964 Faber book about trains, weddings, rooms, and time.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1964 is correct. Faber published the British edition on 28 February 1964. An American edition followed later that year. This book is not posthumous.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The train passenger (The speaker who watches wedding parties join his journey); Mr Bleaney (The former lodger whose dull room the speaker inherits)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It records the poet's impression while travelling a long journey to London by train.
It establishes a "We" voice of collective outlook.
In this poem Larkin describes a stopping train journey from Paragon station on a Whitsun Saturday afternoon to London.
It is a collection of 32 poems by Larkin, published by Faber and Faber.
It contains some of his famous poems like:.
The Whitsun Wedding.
Days.
Mr. Bleaney.
MCMXIV.
An Arundel Tomb.
It describes the autobiographical element. In the poem, he describes the sights and sounds that he saw in his journey from Hull to London.
Faber and Faber published it in Britain on 28 February 1964.
The title poem follows a train ride at Whitsun, a late spring holiday.
Wedding parties keep boarding the train.
Mr Bleaney is a poem about a mean rented room.
An Arundel Tomb ends on love and a stone couple.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq's grand plans for Delhi end in cruelty and chaos.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1964 is the Kannada play. A student production in Urdu was staged at the National School of Drama in 1966. The famous open air show at Purana Qila in Delhi came in 1972. Oxford University Press published an English book in 1972. The database marks the work as a translation, which fits the English text students usually read.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (The Sultan of Delhi, brilliant, idealistic, and later cruel); Aziz (A cunning man who cheats the Sultan by changing his disguise); Aazam (Aziz's friend and partner in the tricks); Barani (A historian who stays close to the Sultan); Najib (A sharp adviser who is later murdered); The Stepmother (The Sultan's stepmother, who fears his wild decisions)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
8. Taledanda (Death by Beheading) 9. Agni Mattu Male (Agni aur Versha) (The Fire and the Rain) 1995.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq rules Delhi and plans to move the capital to Daulatabad.
He wants Hindu and Muslim subjects to feel they share one kingdom.
Aziz pretends to be a Hindu Brahmin and cheats the court for money.
The Sultan sends a critic out in royal dress, and enemies kill that man by mistake.
Copper coins, a ban on prayer, and the march to Daulatabad ruin the people.
Aziz fools the Sultan once more, and the play ends with Tughlaq near madness.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A boy's schooling is broken by the Mau Mau war and stolen family land.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Heinemann published it in 1964. It is often called the first English novel by an East African writer. He wrote it in English at Makerere. The catalog translation flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Njoroge (A schoolboy who hopes education will save his family); Ngotho (Njoroge's father, a worker on Mr Howlands's farm); Boro (Njoroge's elder brother, a bitter Mau Mau fighter); Mwihaki (Jacobo's daughter and Njoroge's friend); Mr Howlands (A white settler who holds the family's ancestral land)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Njoroge is the first child in his family to go to school.
His father Ngotho works land that once belonged to the family.
A workers' strike turns violent, and Ngotho attacks the chief Jacobo.
Jomo Kenyatta's trial kills the family's hope of a quick rescue.
Arrests and a death in the family end Njoroge's school dream.
He tries to hang himself, and his mothers stop him.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Plath's fierce last poems, published after her death in an order set by Ted Hughes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Faber and Faber published it in 1965. The first American edition is 1966. Frieda Hughes restored the manuscript order in 2004. The 1982 Pulitzer is for The Collected Poems, not this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of Lady Lazarus (A voice that compares repeated suffering to a public performance); The speaker of Daddy (A daughter addressing a dead father in violent images)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Plath wrote many of these poems in a late burst of work.
She chose the title Ariel, also the name of a horse she rode.
Poems such as Daddy and Lady Lazarus face father, pain, and rebirth.
She left a planned order for the book.
Ted Hughes published a different order in 1965 and cut some poems.
Their daughter Frieda Hughes restored Plath's order in 2004.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His third book of poems, about a man homesick in both India and England.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1965 is correct. Eyre and Spottiswoode of London published John Nobody in 1965.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Nobody (The named speaker of the title poem, a traveller at home in no single country)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Eyre and Spottiswoode published the book in London in 1965.
It was his third collection of poems.
The title poem moves between the Valley of Jezreel and Trafalgar Square.
In one place he dreams of London.
In the other he dreams of India.
Mythic figures remain, but the voice is more personal than in the first book.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first English poetry book, direct about love, heat, and the self.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Everest Press in New Delhi published Summer in Calcutta in 1965. An Introduction appears in this book. The database year 1965 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of An Introduction (A woman who defends her English, her body, and her right to say I)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This 1965 book is her first collection of English poems.
The poems use a personal voice about love and betrayal.
An Introduction is the famous poem in the book.
In it she claims the right to write in English.
She calls herself Indian, brown, and born in Malabar.
The book pushed Indian English poetry toward a frank personal voice.

items.title: "The Adventures of Feluda (English translations)" (1965) — Satyajit Ray

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Bengali detective stories about Feluda, Topshe, and Jatayu, later translated into English.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wikipedia dates the first Sandesh story, Feludar Goyendagiri, to 1965. Penguin India dates an English omnibus, The Complete Adventures of Feluda, to May 2021. Do not use 1921 as the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Feluda (Pradosh Chandra Mitter) (A tall Calcutta detective who solves cases by observation); Topshe (Tapesh Ranjan Mitter) (Feluda's young cousin, assistant, and narrator); Jatayu (Lalmohan Ganguly) (A comic writer of wild thrillers who joins the later cases)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Pradosh Chandra Mitter, called Feluda, is a private detective in Calcutta.
His young cousin Topshe tells the stories and helps on the cases.
The first case, Feludar Goyendagiri, appeared in Sandesh in 1965.
From Sonar Kella onward, the writer Lalmohan Ganguly, called Jatayu, joins them.
They travel, observe small clues, and unmask the culprit in a final meeting.
English translations, including a Penguin omnibus, came many years later.

items.title: "The Continent of Circe" (1965) — Nirad C. Chaudhuri

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An essay that treats India as Circe's island and argues that violence sits inside Hindu history.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1965 is correct. Chatto and Windus in London published it in 1965. The Duff Cooper Prize followed in 1966. The database genre label Poetry is wrong. This is non-fiction.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Circe is the witch in Homer who turned men into animals.
Chaudhuri uses her island as a picture of India.
He studies Hindu society from early history to modern times.
He rejects the idea that India has always been only a land of peace.
He points to war in the epics and in Hindu kingdoms.
The book won the Duff Cooper Memorial Prize (a British non-fiction prize) for 1966.

items.title: "The Dilemma of a Ghost" (1965) — Ama Ata Aidoo

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Ghanaian graduate brings his African American wife home, and both families clash.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1965 is the Longman printing. Wikipedia dates the first run to March 1964 at the University of Ghana, Legon. The Guardian obituary says the Ghana Drama Studio in 1964. Both agree on 1964 for performance and 1965 for print.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ato Yawson (A Ghanaian graduate torn between his US life and his home); Eulalie Rush (Ato's African American wife, new to Ghanaian family rules)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ato Yawson returns to Ghana after study abroad.
He brings his African American wife, Eulalie Rush, without warning the family.
Eulalie expects a warm Mother Africa.
Daily custom is harder.
Childbearing and food become the sharpest fights.
The title recalls a ghost who cannot choose a road.
The clash is private, but it also shows the new nation.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems of 1960 to 1964 seek the exact word, the patient watcher, and the real name.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1965 is correct. The subtitle is Poems 1960-1964. Writers Workshop, Calcutta, published it in 1965.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book gathers twenty poems written between 1960 and 1964.
Night of the Scorpion is the best known poem in the book.
Poet, Lover, Birdwatcher says the best poets wait for words.
Philosophy ends by refusing to explain what cannot be explained.
Writers Workshop published the book in Calcutta in 1965.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A professor brings his wife home, and the family keeps her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1965 matches the Methuen book and the London opening. Pinter wrote the play in 1964. Tryouts opened in Cardiff on 26 March 1965. The Royal Shakespeare Company opened it at the Aldwych Theatre, London, on 3 June 1965. Broadway followed in 1967 and won a Tony Award.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Max (The old father, a retired butcher); Lenny (Max's son, sharp tongued and menacing); Sam (Max's brother, a chauffeur); Joey (Max's son, who works in demolition and boxes); Teddy (Max's son, a professor who has lived in America); Ruth (Teddy's wife, who chooses to remain with the family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a two act play written in 1964 but published in 1965.
It won the Tony Award for best play in 1967.
It is set in North London.
The play has five male characters: Max, Sam, Teddy, Lenny and Joey; and one female character: Ruth.
Ruth is Teddy's wife and the play concerns Teddy's and Ruth's homecoming which has distinctly different symbolic and thematic implications.
Teddy, a philosophy professor in America, visits his old house.
He brings his wife Ruth to meet the men of the family.
Max, the father, insults his sons and then turns on Ruth.
Lenny, Joey, and Sam circle Ruth with sex and power.
Ruth stays.
Teddy goes back to America alone.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first poetry book, shared with Geoffrey Lehmann and published in 1965.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1965 is correct, and the note with Geoffrey Lehmann is correct. Australian National University Press in Canberra published it. It is not a book by Murray alone.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Murray and Lehmann published the book together in Canberra.
It was issued by Australian National University Press.
The poems begin Murray's attention to rural Australia.
The book is linked to the Grace Leven Prize for 1965.
One poem in the book is Driving through Sawmill Towns.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young teacher on a Greek island is trapped in a rich man's godgame.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Jonathan Cape published the first edition in 1965. Fowles published a revised edition in 1977. The database years 1965 and 1977 are correct, and the revision flag is right. The translation flag is wrong, because he wrote the novel in English.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nicholas Urfe (A young Oxford graduate teaching English on a Greek island); Maurice Conchis (The rich man who runs the psychological game); Alison Kelly (Nicholas's Australian girlfriend, whom he leaves behind); Lily (A young woman in the masks, also called Julie, with whom Nicholas falls in love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nicholas Urfe leaves Alison Kelly in London and teaches English on Phraxos.
Bored and hopeless, he meets Maurice Conchis, a rich recluse.
Conchis draws him into masks, playlets, and scenes from the Nazi occupation.
Nicholas cannot tell truth from theatre, and the tricks are called the godgame.
The ending stays uncertain, and Fowles refused to close it for his readers.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first full book digs up childhood, farm work, and a boy's first deaths.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1966 is correct. Faber and Faber published it. A small pamphlet, Eleven Poems, had appeared in 1965.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet as a boy (The speaker who watches farm work and then chooses the pen)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber published this first major collection in 1966.
The opening poem, Digging, sets the pen beside his father's spade.
Poems recall turf cutting, frogs, blackberries, and school.
Mid-Term Break remembers his four-year-old brother, killed in 1953.
The title poem turns wonder at frogspawn into disgust and fear.
The book won the Geoffrey Faber Prize and made his name.

items.title: "Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead" (24 August 1966) — Tom Stoppard

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two minor men from Hamlet wait, joke, and die without understanding the plot.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A short 1964 version grew into this play. Edinburgh Festival Fringe, Oxford Theatre Group, 24 August 1966. National Theatre at the Old Vic, 11 April 1967. The database line premiered 1966, London 1967 matches those two stage dates. The separate book month was not confirmed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rosencrantz (One of Hamlet's old friends, often confused with Guildenstern); Guildenstern (The more anxious of the pair, who questions fate and art); The Player (Leader of a travelling acting troupe); Hamlet (The prince, seen only in short crossings from Shakespeare's play)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rosencrantz and Guildenstern flip coins that keep landing heads.
They are minor courtiers inside Shakespeare's Hamlet.
They wait in the wings while the famous scenes happen nearby.
A Player and his actors show them plays about death.
They carry a letter that orders Hamlet's death.
Hamlet switches the letter, and the two men are killed instead.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Oedipa Maas hunts a secret postal network that may be real or a joke.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1966 is correct. Lippincott published it on 27 April 1966. Pynchon later called it a short story with gland trouble.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Oedipa Maas (A California woman who may be uncovering a plot, or imagining one); Pierce Inverarity (Her rich former lover, whose estate starts the search); Metzger (A lawyer who helps her and becomes her lover)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lippincott published the novel on 27 April 1966.
Oedipa Maas is asked to settle the estate of Pierce Inverarity.
She finds a muted post horn and the name Tristero, or Trystero.
Clues point to a hidden mail system opposed to the old firm Thurn and Taxis.
The book ends at an auction, as she waits to see who bids for lot 49.

items.title: "The Origin of the Brunists" (1966) — Robert Coover

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: After a mine blast, one survivor is turned into a prophet and a cult grows around him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1966 is correct. Putnam published the novel in 1966. It won the William Faulkner Foundation Award for a notable first novel. Reports split the award year between 1966 and 1967, so that year is not fixed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Giovanni Bruno (The only miner pulled alive from the blast, then treated as a prophet); Justin Miller (Editor of the local paper, who covers the cult and cannot stay outside it); Marcella Bruno (Giovanni's sister, caught between Miller and the cult)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A coal mine explosion in the town of West Condon kills almost every miner.
Giovanni Bruno is the only survivor, and his few words sound like prophecy.
Townspeople form the Brunists and wait for the end of the world.
Newspaper editor Justin Miller reports on the cult and is pulled into it.
The final gathering turns violent, and the promised end does not come as they hoped.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first English poetry book, named for water bugs that seem to walk on water.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1966 is correct. Oxford University Press published it in London. The database marks it as a translation. That flag is wrong. These are his own English poems.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of The Striders (A watcher who compares a water bug to a prophet on the water)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Oxford University Press in London published The Striders in 1966.
The title poem watches thin water bugs on the skin of a stream.
The speaker says that not only prophets walk on water.
Other early poems look at family, the body, and South Indian scenes.
A River, set in Madurai, is one of the famous poems from this early work.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Antoinette Cosway's Caribbean life before she becomes the attic woman of Jane Eyre.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Andre Deutsch published the novel in October 1966. Britannica also dates it 1966. The database year 1966 is correct. It won the WH Smith Literary Award in 1967. It is not one of the 1930s novels.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Antoinette Cosway (A Creole heiress whom the husband renames Bertha, the madwoman of Jane Eyre); The English husband (The man readers link with Mr Rochester, who rejects her Creole past); Annette (Antoinette's mother, a Martinican widow who breaks down after the fire); Christophine (Antoinette's old nurse, who distrusts the husband and knows obeah, Caribbean folk magic); Grace Poole (The servant set to watch Antoinette in the English attic)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After slavery ends, the Cosway family declines on the Jamaican estate Coulibri.
A fire, local hatred, and her mother's collapse shape Antoinette's childhood.
She marries an Englishman and honeymoons at Granbois in Dominica.
He renames her Bertha, believes she is mad, and takes her to England.
Locked in the attic of Thornfield, she dreams of fire and walks out with a candle.

items.title: "A Grain of Wheat" (1967) — NgIgI wa Thiong’o

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: On the eve of Uhuru, a village hero confesses that he betrayed a freedom fighter.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Heinemann published it in 1967, while he was linked with Leeds. The catalog year 1967 is correct. He wrote it in English. The catalog translation flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mugo (A lonely man honoured as a hero, who betrayed Kihika); Kihika (A Mau Mau fighter who is captured and hanged); Gikonyo (A carpenter who confessed the oath to leave detention); Mumbi (Gikonyo's wife and Kihika's sister); Karanja (A collaborator who served the colonial chief's office)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Thabai village prepares for Uhuru, Kenya's independence day.
People want Mugo, a quiet detainee, to speak as a hero.
Mugo's secret is that he betrayed the fighter Kihika.
Gikonyo returns from detention and cannot forgive Mumbi.
The crowd expects Karanja, the collaborator, to be the traitor.
Mugo confesses in public, and the celebration turns uneasy.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A theory book that says writing is not a mere copy of speech.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Editions de Minuit published the French book in 1967. Johns Hopkins University Press published Spivak's English translation in 1976. A corrected English edition came in 1997.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jacques Derrida (The philosopher who argues for a new study of writing); Ferdinand de Saussure (The linguist whose view of speech and writing Derrida unsettles); Jean Jacques Rousseau (The writer whose essay on language fills the second half)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
3. Writing and Difference 4. Dissemination (1972)
The French title is De la grammatologie.
Derrida reads Saussure, who treated writing as a stand in for speech.
He says that belief is phonocentrism (trust in the spoken voice as full presence).
The second half reads Rousseau on the origin of language.
A supplement (something added) is already inside the thing it seems to complete.

items.title: "Silence! The Court Is in Session" (1978) — Vijay Tendulkar

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Silence! The Court Is in Session

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A village mock trial turns on Miss Benare and exposes the group's cruelty.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Marathi play was first staged in 1967. That is the catalog year. An Oxford English book is recorded at Calcutta in 1978, and some lists say 1979. The catalog marks a translation and an edition trap. Both notes are right. It is a play, not a novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Leela Benare (A schoolteacher who becomes the accused in the mock trial); Mr Kashikar (The amateur judge, with his wife Mrs Kashikar beside him); Sukhatme (The lawyer who turns the rehearsal into an attack); Samant (A local man who joins the game and supplies a plot)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A theatre group reaches a village to stage a play about a trial.
The play is late, so they hold a mock trial for practice.
Miss Benare, an unmarried teacher, is pushed into the dock.
The game uses a real pregnancy and a real lover's name.
The amateur judge and lawyers enjoy the power.
Benare's long speech cannot stop their verdict.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short novel that retells the fairy tale in broken, joking pieces.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1967 is correct for the book. Atheneum published it in 1967, after parts ran in The New Yorker. A database flag calls it unfinished. That flag is wrong. It is a completed novel, not a children's book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Snow White (The heroine, now a modern woman waiting for a prince who may never act); Jane (A jealous rival who takes the old stepmother role and prepares a poison); Paul (The prince figure, passive, and later the victim of the poison); Hogo (A rough suitor whom Snow White does not welcome)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Atheneum published the novel in New York in 1967.
Parts of it had already appeared in The New Yorker that same year.
Snow White lives with seven men and waits for a prince.
Jane, Paul, and Hogo play twisted forms of the old tale.
A questionnaire stops the story and asks the reader what he thinks.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her 1967 English poems, even franker about women, love, and the body.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Writer's Workshop in Calcutta published The Descendants in 1967. The Looking Glass is in this book. The database year 1967 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of The Looking Glass (A woman advising another woman about love and the body)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is her second book of English poems.
Writer's Workshop in Calcutta published it in 1967.
The Looking Glass is the famous poem in the book.
The speaker tells a woman what she might give a lover.
The voice is more open about the body than before.
Critics compared this directness with Sylvia Plath.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A wild satire about a believer crushed by a rotten state.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Doubleday of Garden City, New York, published the first edition in 1967. A British edition followed in 1968. The database year 1967 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bukka Doopeyduk (The narrator, a believer who tries to succeed in HARRY SAM); Harry Sam (The crude ruler who sits above the city and holds power)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bukka Doopeyduk lives in a land called HARRY SAM.
The ruler Harry Sam sits on a toilet and keeps hold of power.
Bukka trusts the public creed and tries to rise.
Leaders, teachers, and the media all look corrupt.
He finally sees the ruler's evil and tries to seize power.
He fails, and the state destroys him.
The book mocks white power and some Black leaders too.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English translations of classical Tamil love poems from the anthology Kuruntokai.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1967 is correct for the first book. Some later lists give 1970 for another edition. This one is a translation. The database flag is right here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lovers and their friends (Speakers in classical Tamil poems of secret love and separation)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The full title adds Love Poems from a Classical Tamil Anthology.
The first publication was in 1967.
The poems come from the old Tamil book Kuruntokai.
They are akam poems, meaning poems of inner life and love.
Landscapes such as hill, forest, field, seashore, and desert stand for phases of love.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1967 collection of essays, including the lecture that shook structuralism.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Editions du Seuil published the French book in 1967. Alan Bass published the English translation in 1978. Structure, Sign, and Play was delivered in 1966, before the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jacques Derrida (The essayist who reads other thinkers against their own claims); Michel Foucault (The historian criticized in Cogito and the History of Madness); Emmanuel Levinas (The philosopher of the other person, read in Violence and Metaphysics)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The French title is L'ecriture et la difference.
Cogito and the History of Madness criticizes Michel Foucault and caused a rift.
Violence and Metaphysics reads Emmanuel Levinas on ethics and the other person.
Structure, Sign, and Play was a 1966 lecture at Johns Hopkins University.
That lecture says a structure has no fixed center that can stop all play.

items.title: "“The Death of the Author”" (1967) — Roland Barthes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An essay that moves meaning from the author to the reader.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: English came first, in Aspen, numbers 5 and 6, in 1967. The French text appeared in Manteia, number 5, in 1968. A later English text is in Image Music Text (1977).

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Roland Barthes (The essayist arguing against author centred criticism); The reader (The place where the many writings of a text meet)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Barthes attacks criticism that explains a book by the writer's life.
He says giving a text one author puts a limit on that text.
Writing, for him, destroys the idea of one single voice.
A text is a tissue of quotations from many cultures.
He ends by tying the birth of the reader to the death of the Author.

items.title: "Dance of the Happy Shades" (1968) — Alice Munro

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first story book, set in small Ontario towns, about girls and women.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1968 is correct. Ryerson Press in Toronto published Dance of the Happy Shades in 1968. It won the Governor General's Award that year. The database file calls this book poetry. That label is wrong. It is short fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator of Boys and Girls (A child on a fox farm who helps her father and resists being called only a girl); Her father (A fox farmer whose last words in the story dismiss his daughter)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The stories show ordinary lives in rural southwestern Ontario.
In Boys and Girls, a child on a fox farm learns what the word girl costs.
Her father later dismisses her with the words that she is only a girl.
The Office is about a woman who wants a room of her own in which to write.
The book won the 1968 Governor General's Award for English-language fiction.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Stories that keep showing the reader how a story is being built.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1968 is correct. It was nominated for a National Book Award. Barth won that award later, in 1973, for Chimera, which is a different book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ambrose (A boy who appears in three family stories, including the title story); The speaking story (A tale that knows it is a tale and complains about its author)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Doubleday published the collection in 1968.
Ambrose, a boy, is lost in a seaside funhouse of mirrors.
Other pieces include a sperm's night journey and a story that tells itself.
The opening piece is meant to be cut into a paper loop with no end.
The book follows his 1967 essay on used up realistic plots.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A rootless young man learns that real detachment means right action.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The novel was published in 1968. The database year 1968 is correct. Critics often set it beside Camus's The Stranger, which is a different book from 1942.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sindi Oberoi (The narrator, a rootless man of Indian and English parentage); June Blyth (An American woman whom Sindi will not fully love); Babu Rao Khemka (An Indian friend whose family business Sindi later holds together); Muthu (An office worker who teaches Sindi that detachment can mean joining in)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sindi Oberoi tells his story after a death in Delhi.
An Indian father and an English mother died when he was young.
He studied in Kenya, London, and America and tried to want nothing.
June Blyth and Babu Rao Khemka are hurt by his refusal to commit.
In Delhi he stays to run a firm and learns that detachment can mean action.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unhappy accountant runs a dice baseball league until the game becomes his world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1968 is correct. Random House published it in 1968. The full title is The Universal Baseball Association, Inc., J. Henry Waugh, Prop.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: J. Henry Waugh (An accountant who invents the league and starts to play God inside it); Damon Rutherford (A young pitcher whose dice death breaks Waugh's distance from the game); Jock Casey (The pitcher whose throw kills Damon, and whom Waugh then dooms)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
J. Henry Waugh, a lonely accountant, lives for a dice baseball game.
Charts and dice decide every play and the lives of eight teams.
Rookie Damon Rutherford pitches a perfect game, and in a later game the dice kill him.
Waugh tries to punish the pitcher Jock Casey and finally fakes a roll so Casey dies.
Years later the league treats those deaths as a holy story, almost a religion.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A story collection that retells familiar tales and lets one evening happen in many ways.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1969 is correct. The printed title uses an ampersand: Pricksongs and Descants. It is a story collection. A film of The Babysitter came later, in 1995, and is not the book date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The babysitter (A girl whose one night is told in many conflicting versions)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is a set of short pieces, not one continuous plot.
Several stories take fairy tales and Bible scenes and twist them.
The Babysitter tells many possible versions of a single evening.
Each short block can contradict the block before it.
The reader must notice that the story is being made, and remade, on the page.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Billy Pilgrim survives Dresden and lives his life out of time order.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1969 is correct. Delacorte Press published it in March 1969. The full subtitle is The Children's Crusade: A Duty Dance with Death. Vonnegut lived through the Dresden bombing as a prisoner.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Billy Pilgrim (An American soldier and later an optometrist who comes unstuck in time); Kurt Vonnegut (The narrator, who also survived Dresden and says he is the author); Kilgore Trout (A failed science fiction writer whom Billy reads)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The opening says the war parts are mostly true.
Billy Pilgrim, a chaplain's helper, is captured in the Battle of the Bulge.
He survives the 1945 firebombing of Dresden in a slaughterhouse cellar.
After the war he becomes an optometrist in Ilium, New York.
He believes aliens from Tralfamadore keep him in a zoo and see all time at once.
Whenever death appears, the book says, So it goes.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A method book on statements, discourse, and the archive of a field.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Gallimard published the French book in 1969. Tavistock and Pantheon published the English book in 1972.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Michel Foucault (The writer setting out his method)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The French title is L'Archeologie du savoir.
Archaeology here means uncovering rules of statements, not digging up ruins.
A statement is what can be said inside a discourse (a regulated way of speaking).
The archive is the system that decides which statements can appear.
The book explains the method used in The Order of Things.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young woman stops eating after she agrees to marry.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1969 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published this first novel in 1969. Atwood later called it protofeminist in a 1979 foreword, meaning it stands just before a full feminist novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Marian MacAlpin (The young woman whose appetite collapses after her engagement); Peter (Marian's fiance, tidy and sure of his future); Duncan (A graduate student who offers Marian a messy alternative)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Marian MacAlpin works at a consumer survey firm in the city.
She becomes engaged to Peter, a neat and controlling man.
Food starts to seem human, and she cannot eat.
Her body and her social self pull apart.
She bakes a cake shaped like a woman and offers it to Peter.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Victorian love story whose modern narrator offers three different endings.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Fowles dated the first image of the woman to autumn 1966 and a full draft note to 27 October 1967. Jonathan Cape published the novel in 1969. The database year 1969 is correct. It is an original English novel, so the translation flag is wrong. The 1981 film is a later adaptation.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sarah Woodruff (The title woman, a disgraced former governess who stares out to sea); Charles Smithson (A gentleman and amateur naturalist engaged to Ernestina); Ernestina Freeman (The woman Charles plans to marry, daughter of a rich London tradesman); Sam Farrow (Charles's servant, who fails to deliver a crucial letter); The narrator (A twentieth century voice that comments on the story and flips a coin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In Lyme Regis, Sarah Woodruff is shunned as the French lieutenant's discarded woman.
Charles Smithson, engaged to Ernestina Freeman, becomes obsessed with Sarah.
A modern narrator interrupts the Victorian tale and even enters it.
One ending marries Charles to Ernestina and leaves Sarah unknown.
Two later endings meet Sarah in London, one hopeful and one bitter.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1969 poetry book about loneliness between Europe and the Caribbean.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1969 is correct. The full title is The Gulf and Other Poems. The database calls it drama, but it is a poetry book.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems continue Walcott's lush and chanting early style.
The speaker feels alone between European learning and Caribbean folk life.
Race, language, and place stay in tension.
The book sits between The Castaway and the long poem Another Life.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lecture on the author function, the job a writer's name does in discourse.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The French bulletin printed the lecture in 1969. The standard English text is in the 1977 essay book edited by Donald Bouchard. An abridged English text appeared in Partisan Review in 1975. The catalog calls the essay poetry. It is theory.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Foucault gave the lecture to the French Society of Philosophy in 1969.
He asks what role the author's name plays in grouping texts.
The author function (that grouping role) is not the same as a living person.
He says some writers, such as Freud and Marx, founded whole discourses.
He closes by asking what difference it makes who is speaking.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young woman marries against her parents and is destroyed by her husband's slave wealth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1970 matches the Longman first edition. A Guardian obituary dates Anowa 1969, which may mean composition. Do not replace 1970 with 1969 in a publication answer. A London production at the Gate Theatre came in 1991. That is not the first printing.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anowa (The heroine, who chooses her own husband and rejects slave labour); Kofi Ako (Her husband, who becomes a rich slave trader); Abena Badua (Anowa's mother, who wants a traditional marriage); Osam (Anowa's father, who leaves the choice to his daughter); The Old Man and the Old Woman (A pair called the Mouth That Eats Salt and Pepper, who comment on events)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The play is set in the 1870s on the Gold Coast.
Anowa rejects the husbands her parents would choose.
She marries Kofi Ako and leaves the town of Yebi.
Kofi grows rich by trading in slaves.
Anowa hates that wealth.
An old man and an old woman comment like a chorus (speakers who judge the action).
Kofi shoots himself after the truth about their childlessness.
Anowa drowns.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1970 story collection about city life, lists, and failed quests.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1970 is correct. Farrar, Straus and Giroux published the finished collection in 1970. A database flag calls it unfinished. That flag is wrong. The Glass Mountain was later reprinted in Sixty Stories (1981).

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Climber (The narrator of The Glass Mountain, who climbs with plumber tools while the crowd mocks him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Farrar, Straus and Giroux published the book in 1970.
It is a collection of short stories, not one continuous novel.
The Glass Mountain is a list of one hundred numbered sentences.
A man tries to climb a glass mountain on a New York street corner.
The old goal, a golden castle and an enchanted symbol, is treated as a joke.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dark sequence of poems about Crow, a trickster bird in a broken creation.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1970 is correct for publication. Most poems were written from 1966 to 1969. The book is not posthumous. Hughes was alive in 1970.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Crow (A black trickster bird who survives a ruined world)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The full title is Crow: From the Life and Songs of the Crow.
Faber and Faber published the book in 1970.
Hughes wrote most of the poems between 1966 and 1969.
Drawings by Leonard Baskin helped start the Crow poems.
Crow cheats, suffers, and grins through a harsh version of creation.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A history teacher tells how one snowball tied his life to a saint, a tycoon, and a magician.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1970 is correct. Macmillan of Canada published the novel in October 1970. The Danish looking opening quotation was invented by Davies.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dunstan Ramsay (The narrator, a teacher and scholar of saints, who calls himself fifth business); Boy Staunton (Ramsay's rich friend, once Percy Boyd, who threw the snowball and will not own it); Mary Dempster (The preacher's wife, hurt by the snowball, whom Ramsay treats as a kind of saint); Paul Dempster (Mary's son, born too soon, later the magician Magnus Eisengrim)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dunstan Ramsay writes a long letter to the headmaster of his old school.
As a boy, Percy Boyd Staunton throws a snowball with a stone inside it.
The snowball hits pregnant Mary Dempster, and her son Paul is born too soon.
Ramsay fights in the First World War, loses a leg, and studies saints.
Paul becomes the magician Magnus Eisengrim, and Boy Staunton dies with a stone in his mouth.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Henry Lawrence rises in Punjab after Ranjit Singh's death, then falls through pride.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1970 matches the book. Wikipedia says Oxford University Press published it in 1970. The same page dates a Bombay staging to 1969. The Sultan Padamsee Prize came in 1968. A Times of India review of 24 November 1968 already calls the play prize winning.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Henry Lawrence (The British hero, called Larins Sahib, whose pride brings him down.); Rani Jindan (Ranjit Singh's widow and a queen of Punjab.); Sher Singh (A Sikh figure close to Lawrence who later leaves him.); Ranjit Singh (The dead Lion of Punjab, whose memory drives Lawrence.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The play is set in the 1840s, after Maharaja Ranjit Singh has died.
The British have entered a confused Punjab.
Henry Lawrence, called Larins Sahib, tries to stand with the Sikhs.
He grows obsessed with Ranjit Singh and with power.
Rani Jindan, the late king's widow, turns against him.
Caught between the British and the Sikhs, he is transferred in disgrace.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Pecola Breedlove wants blue eyes because her world calls her ugly.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1970 is correct. Holt, Rinehart and Winston published this first novel in 1970. Morrison was 39. It began as a story about a Black girl who wanted blue eyes.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pecola Breedlove (A young Black girl who longs for blue eyes); Claudia MacTeer (A neighbour girl who narrates much of the book); Cholly Breedlove (Pecola's father, whose violence destroys her); Pauline Breedlove (Pecola's mother, who also feels marked as ugly); Soaphead Church (A false spiritual healer who tricks Pecola)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is set in Lorain, Ohio, around 1940 and 1941.
Claudia MacTeer helps tell the life of Pecola Breedlove.
Pecola is a poor Black girl whom people call ugly.
She prays for blue eyes, the look she links with white beauty.
Her father, Cholly, attacks her, and the town turns away.
A false healer tricks her, and her mind breaks.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first poetry book, issued by Writers Workshop in India in 1970.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1970 is correct. Writers Workshop, India, published this first collection.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The patrol speaker (A police voice watching a city under curfew)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The opening poem shows a town under curfew after a riot.
A police voice moves through fog, blood, and fear.
Other poems look at disease, death, and a hard public life.
The book made his name in Indian English poetry.

items.title: "Close the Sky, Ten by Ten" (1971) — Jayanta Mahapatra

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Close the Sky, Ten by Ten

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An early book of short poems about private feeling, the sky, and a closed inner space.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Dialogue Publications in Calcutta issued the book in 1971. The database year 1971 is correct. Svayamvara and Other Poems also appeared in 1971.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A voice that withdraws into a small private space)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dialogue Publications in Calcutta brought the book out in 1971.
The title comes from the poem Sanctuary.
In that poem the speaker shuts the sky into a small square.
The lyrics use odd word order and sharp pictures.
Meaning is hinted at, not told as a straight story.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A horse headed man and a love triangle ask what makes a person whole.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1971 is the Kannada play. Karnad himself translated it into English. Oxford University Press published the English book in 1975. The database marks the work as a translation, which fits that English text.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bhagavata (The narrator who speaks to the audience and guides the play); Hayavadana (A man with a horse's head who wants a complete body); Devadatta (A learned Brahmin, Padmini's husband); Kapila (Devadatta's strong friend, a man of the body); Padmini (The woman who wants both mind and body); Goddess Kali (The goddess who restores the dead friends)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The play opens with a prayer to Ganesha and a narrator called Bhagavata.
Hayavadana has a horse's head and a man's body, and he wants to be complete.
Devadatta has learning, and Kapila has strength.
Both are tied to Padmini.
The two friends behead themselves at the temple of Kali.
Padmini fixes the heads on the wrong bodies, so mind and body are swapped.
A wise voice says the head is the husband, but the new mix still fails.
The friends kill each other.
Padmini chooses death.
Hayavadana becomes a full horse.

items.title: "In a Free State" (1971) — V. S. Naipaul

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three stories and a travel frame show the cost of a doubtful freedom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1971 is correct. Andre Deutsch published it, and it won that year's Booker Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bobby (A white official driving back from the capital in the title story); Linda (The colleague's wife who travels with Bobby)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Naipaul got Bookers Prize for this novel.
The plot consists of a framing narrative and three short stories while the theme is not correctly spelled out.
The narrator is initially on a ferry to Egypt and concludes many years later as a tourist in Egypt again.
The first tale concerns an Indian servant from Bombay, who having no real alternative at home, accompanies his master on a diplomatic mission to Washington D.C.
The second tale is about a rural West Indian family, a set of cousins, one of whom manages to humiliate the narrator.
The third and main tale is set in an African Great Lakes state that has recently got independence.
Andre Deutsch published the book in 1971.
A prologue and an epilogue frame three stories.
One out of Many follows an Indian servant in Washington.
Tell Me Who to Kill follows a West Indian brother in England.
The title story follows Bobby and Linda on a drive through a new African state.
The book won the Booker Prize in 1971.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His second English poetry book, best known for the family poem Obituary.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1971 is correct. Oxford University Press published it in London and New York. The database marks it as a translation. That flag is wrong. Relations is his own English poetry.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The son in Obituary (A speaker who remembers his father through leftovers, rites, and debts)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Oxford University Press published Relations in 1971.
The poems return to parents, marriage, and the family house.
Obituary lists what a father left behind, including debts and daughters.
The tone is dry and ironic, not a grand public elegy.
Small scale family scenes carry the larger idea of relation.

items.title: "The Book of Daniel" (1971) — E. L. Doctorow

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A son investigates the trial and execution of his parents, who stand in for the Rosenbergs.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1971 is correct. Random House published the novel in 1971. A film titled Daniel followed in 1983.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Daniel Isaacson (The narrator, a graduate student and the older son); Susan Isaacson (Daniel's sister, who dies after a suicide attempt); Paul and Rochelle Isaacson (The parents, executed after a spy trial); Selig Mindish (The family friend whose evidence helps convict the parents)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Daniel Isaacson is a graduate student writing about older American radicals (the Old Left).
His parents, Paul and Rochelle Isaacson, were tried and executed for spying.
They stand in for Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, but the names and some facts differ.
The story jumps between 1967 and the late 1940s and early 1950s.
His sister Susan dies after trying to kill herself, and student protests close the library.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Nicholas Payne roams a loud, greedy America and refuses to settle into a normal life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Simon and Schuster published it in New York in 1971. Yardley's New York Times review is dated 14 March 1971. The novel won the Rosenthal Award. The database year 1971 is correct. It is fiction, and it is not always taught as postmodern.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nicholas Payne (A restless young traveler, sardonic and romantic at once); The woman he loves (A respectable family's daughter, who stands for the safer life Payne will not join)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nicholas Payne leaves a comfortable background and stays on the move.
He loves a young woman whose family does not accept him.
His journey runs through a crude, money-mad America.
The comedy is loose, like a string of adventures, not a tight mystery.
Payne keeps trying to remain his own man inside that noise.

items.title: "The Strange Case of Billy Biswas" (1971) — Arun Joshi

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Strange Case of Billy Biswas

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An American trained Indian anthropologist leaves Delhi to live with a tribe.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The novel came out in 1971. The database year 1971 is correct. It is his second novel, after The Foreigner and before The Last Labyrinth.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Billy Biswas (An anthropologist who leaves elite Delhi for a tribal life); Romesh Sahai (The friend who narrates Billy's disappearance and death); The Bhils (The tribal people of the Satpura hills among whom Billy lives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Billy Biswas returns from the United States and teaches in Delhi.
City parties and a settled marriage feel false to him.
He disappears into the Satpura hills and lives among the Bhils.
A friend, the narrator, finds him and hears why he left.
When the family tries to bring him back, he is hunted and killed.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical book on themes and methods in the Indian novel in English.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Heinemann Educational Books, New Delhi, published it in 1971. The catalog year 1971 is correct. The catalog genre Fiction is wrong. This is criticism, not a novel.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book studies Indian novels written in English.
It treats English as a second birth for many Indian writers.
It groups novels by theme, not only by the writer's name.
It looks at village life, the city, and the meeting of India and the West.
It argues that this novel has its own history.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Adah, a Nigerian mother, struggles with her children on a poor London housing estate.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Columns in the New Statesman were collected as a book. Barrie and Jenkins published it in 1972. Allison and Busby issued a revised text in 1979. Database year 1972 is the first book date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Adah (A Nigerian single mother trying to survive on a London estate); Adah's children (Five children she must house and feed alone)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Adah is left in London to raise five children.
She lives on a rough estate that people call the Ditch.
She works and also uses welfare (state support) to feed them.
Officials, neighbours, and cramped rooms test her every week.
The book grew from her 1971 columns in the New Statesman.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Marco Polo describes 55 invented cities to the emperor Kublai Khan.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Giulio Einaudi published the Italian book in 1972. William Weaver's English translation appeared in 1974. Use 1972 as the first publication. The database English year is the translation date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Marco Polo (The Venetian traveller who describes the cities); Kublai Khan (The Mongol emperor who listens and questions Polo)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is a conversation between Kublai Khan and Marco Polo.
Polo describes 55 cities, and each city has a woman's name.
The cities fall into 11 groups, such as memory, desire, and signs.
Short talks between the two men frame the city sketches.
Polo says that each city also says something about Venice.
The hidden pattern is a game, in the spirit of Oulipo.
Calvino said the book has conclusions along every edge.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1920s mystery about a dancing spirit that official culture tries to kill.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Doubleday published Mumbo Jumbo in 1972. It was nominated for the National Book Award in 1973. The database year 1972 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: PaPa LaBas (A Harlem Hoodoo detective who searches for the lost text); Black Herman (LaBas's ally, based on a real stage magician); Abdul Sufi Hamid (A militant linked to the missing sacred text)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jes Grew (a spirit of jazz, dance, and freedom) spreads in the 1920s.
It moves through Black America and frightens the guardians of order.
PaPa LaBas, a Hoodoo detective, hunts the sacred text Jes Grew needs.
Hoodoo here means African spirit practice used as healing and as art.
The Wallflower Order and the Atonists try to stop the dance.
Real Harlem history mixes with a wild conspiracy plot.
Pictures, letters, and notes break the usual shape of a novel.
Jes Grew is held back, but LaBas says it can return.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A bookbinder who rejects marriage takes in cast off women, and the house ends in murder.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The catalog says 1972, and adds that English translation and production dates vary. Wikipedia dates the Marathi play to 1972. Britannica dates it to 1971. Hind Pocket Books issued an English text in Delhi in 1973. Use the catalog's warning. Do not pick one year and hide the others.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sakharam Binder (A bookbinder who keeps women without marrying them); Lakshmi (A deserted wife who tries to make his house a home); Champa (A fiercer woman who refuses to be grateful); Dawood (Sakharam's friend and witness in the house)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sakharam Binder says he will not marry.
He takes in women whose husbands have thrown them out.
He offers food and a roof, and he uses them sexually.
A quiet woman and a bold woman answer him in different ways.
The bold woman's violent husband returns.
The house ends in a killing, and Sakharam's freedom speech fails.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A woman returns to the Quebec bush to search for her father.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1972 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published the novel in 1972. It is her second novel. A film version appeared in 1981.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (An unnamed woman who returns to her father's island); Joe (Her boyfriend, who wants a child and a firmer bond); David and Anna (The couple whose marriage shows cruelty and performance)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator goes back to her childhood lake in northern Quebec.
She is searching for her missing father.
Friends from the city come with her and scar the place.
She sheds language, clothes, and the city self.
The search becomes a test of what it means to be human and Canadian.

items.title: "The Infernal Desire Machines of Doctor Hoffman" (1972) — Angela Carter

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Infernal Desire Machines of Doctor Hoffman

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young clerk hunts a scientist whose machines replace reality with desire.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The British edition appeared in 1972. The United States title is The War of Dreams. The database year 1972 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Desiderio (The narrator, a young official sent to kill Hoffman); Doctor Hoffman (A scientist who attacks reason with desire machines); Albertina (Hoffman's daughter and Desiderio's dreamed lover); The Minister of Determination (The ruler who wants logic and stable reality restored)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Doctor Hoffman's machines fill a city with living mirages.
Desiderio is sent to find Hoffman and stop the machines.
On the journey he meets Albertina, Hoffman's daughter, in many disguises.
Hoffman wants their desire to power a new world.
Desiderio kills Hoffman and Albertina, and the mirages end.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Boy Staunton's son tells his life to a Jungian analyst in Zurich after his father's death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1972 is correct. Macmillan of Canada published the novel in 1972. It won that year's Governor General's Literary Award for English fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: David Staunton (Boy Staunton's son, a barrister who narrates his analysis); Johanna von Haller (The Zurich analyst who leads David through Jungian talks); Boy Staunton (David's dead father, the rich man whose death starts the book); Dunstan Ramsay (The narrator of Fifth Business, whom David both trusts and suspects)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
David Staunton, a rich lawyer, breaks down in a Toronto theatre.
He goes to Zurich and talks with the analyst Johanna von Haller.
The talks uncover his drinking, his pride, and his mixed love of his father.
A dream beast, the manticore, stands for the hidden parts of his mind.
He later meets Dunstan Ramsay, Liesl, and Magnus Eisengrim in the mountains.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long autobiographical poem about growing up as an artist in Saint Lucia.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1973 is correct. This is a long autobiographical poem, not a play. The database genre label Drama is a catalog error.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet speaker (Walcott remembering his youth as a painter and writer in Saint Lucia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker looks back on childhood in Castries.
Painting and poetry compete as his early vocations.
Friends, teachers, and the island's light shape his memory.
The poem asks how a Caribbean artist uses English literary tradition.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel in which a car dealer takes a science fiction book as truth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1973 is correct. Delacorte Press published it. The other title is Goodbye Blue Monday. It is a novel, and a film came later, in 1999.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dwayne Hoover (A Midland City car dealer who loses his grip on what is real); Kilgore Trout (A science fiction writer whose book Hoover reads as fact)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is set mainly in the made up city of Midland City.
Dwayne Hoover is a rich car dealer there.
Kilgore Trout is a little known science fiction writer.
Hoover reads Trout's novel as a message from the Creator and turns violent.
Vonnegut also steps into the book as a character, and he adds his own drawings.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A huge war novel about V2 rockets, Tyrone Slothrop, and systems of power.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database publication year 1973 is correct. Viking published it on 14 March 1973. It shared the National Book Award in 1974 with Isaac Bashevis Singer. The Pulitzer board gave no fiction prize that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tyrone Slothrop (An American lieutenant whose map of affairs matches rocket strikes); Pirate Prentice (A British special operations man in the opening London scenes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viking Press published the novel on 14 March 1973.
Most of the story is set in Europe at the end of the Second World War.
Tyrone Slothrop's love affairs seem to match the spots where V2 rockets fall.
Many characters hunt a secret device meant for rocket 00000.
The book is in four parts and has hundreds of characters.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In hot Key West, Thomas Skelton tries to become a fishing guide and collides with a rival.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Farrar, Straus and Giroux published it in 1973. It was nominated for a National Book Award. The New Yorker reviewed it in June 1973. The database year 1973 is correct. The 1975 film is an adaptation, not the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas Skelton (A young man who drops marine studies and bets his life on guiding); Nichol Dance (A skilled, dangerous guide who treats Skelton's new business as a threat)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Thomas Skelton comes home to Key West determined to guide fishing parties.
Nichol Dance, an older guide who has already killed a man, warns him off.
Skelton's grandfather still chases schemes, and his father has given up.
The title names the Florida heat, about ninety-two degrees.
Pride and territory push the two guides into threats and revenge.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: English translations of Kannada vacanas, short poems by Virasaiva saints.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1973 is correct. Penguin first published it in 1973. This book is a translation, so the database flag is right. It is not his own English lyric book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Basavanna (A Kannada saint whose vacana says the body can be Siva's temple); Virasaiva saints (Medieval devotees of Siva whose poems Ramanujan translates)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Penguin published Speaking of Siva in 1973.
The poems are vacanas, free verse speeches of devotion.
They come from the Virasaiva movement, devotees of Siva in Karnataka.
Basavanna asks what a poor man can offer when the rich build temples.
The body itself becomes the temple in his answer.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A trilogy of poems on African migration, slavery, and a return to the Caribbean.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Rights of Passage, Masks, and Islands appeared in 1967, 1968, and 1969. They were gathered as The Arrivants in 1973. The database year 1973 is the collected book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Migrant Speaker (A Caribbean voice moving among Africa, the islands, and cold cities); Tom (An old man in Rights of Passage who has watched the journeys)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rights of Passage follows people leaving the islands for cold cities.
Masks turns to Ghana, drums, and the hope of an African return.
Islands comes home to Caribbean history, faith, and daily speech.
The three books were gathered as The Arrivants in 1973.
Drum rhythm and Caribbean speech hold the long work together.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two linked novellas show violence in Vietnam and in old South Africa.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1974 is correct. The first South African printing appeared on 18 April 1974. He began the book in Buffalo in 1970.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Eugene Dawn (An American myth writer who collapses during the Vietnam War); Jacobus Coetzee (An 18th century hunter who attacks the Nama)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
2. In the Heart of the Country (1977): Early novel is a notable for being of Coetzee's more experimental novels and is narrated through 266 numbered paragraphs rather than chapters. 3. Waiting for the Barbarians (1980): It won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and Geoffry Faber Memorial Prize for fiction. Coetzee took the title from the poem "Writing for the Barbarians" by Greek poet Constantine P. Lavafy. 4. Life and Times of Michael K (1983): It won the Booker prize for Literature in 1983. It is the story of the man named Michael K. who makes an arduous journey from Cape Town to his mother's rural birth place, during an imaginary civil war during the apartheid era 1970-1980's. 5. Foe (1986): It is woven around the existing plot of Robinson Crusoe. Foe is written from the perspective of Susan Barton, a castaway who landed on the same island inhabited on 'Crusoe' and 'Friday' as their adventures were already underway.
The novel was the subject of criticism in South Africa where it was regarded as politically irrelevant on its release. 6. Age of Iron (1990): It depicts the inward journey of Mrs. Lurren, and Old classics professor dying slowly of cancer. 7. The Master of Petersbury (1994): It features the Russian writer "Fyodor Dostoyevsky" as its protagonist. The antagonist is Sergey Nechayev, real life leader of the Nechaevisto, a clandestine group of Nihilist terrorists. 8. Disgrace (1999): He got the Booker Prize for this work; it is set in a violent Post-apartheid South Africa. David Lurie, a Cape Town academic reaches a similar conclusion when his daughter Lucy is gang raped by three black men at her isolated homestead in the Easter Cape. 9. Elizabeth Costello (2003): Elizabeth Costello is a celebrated aging Australian writer, travels around the world and gives lectures on topics including the lives of animals and literary censorship.
In her youth Costello wrote "The House" on Eccles Street, a novel that retells James Joyce's Ulysses from the perspective of the protagonist's wife Molly Bloom.
Elizabeth Costello is also a character in Coetzee's academic novel The Lives of Animals (1999). This character also appears in Coetzee's 2005 novel Slowman. 10. Slowman (2005): It was the first novel of Coetzee after he got Nobel Prize. 11. Diary of a Bad Year (2007). 12. The Childhood of Jesus (2013).
Ravan Press published this first book in South Africa in 1974.
The Vietnam Project follows Eugene Dawn, a propaganda writer.
His work breaks him.
He stabs his son Martin.
The Narrative of Jacobus Coetzee is set in the 18th century.
Jacobus leads a hunting trip, falls ill among the Nama, and returns with a killing party.
Both stories show the mind of the coloniser.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Larkin's last book of new poems, published in 1974.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1974 is correct. Faber published the book in June 1974. Larkin wrote little poetry after it. He died in 1985, so this book is not posthumous.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A blunt voice on parents, sex, age, and empty sky)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(iii)
It is a collection of poems by Larkin published in 1974.
It includes the famous poems like :.
High Windows.
Dublinesque.
This be the Verse.
It contains 24 poems.
It is ironic tribute to the sexual freedom and permissiveness of 1960's.
He had admiration for D. H. Lawrence's Lady Chatterly's Lover.
Opening stanza of the poem: "When I see a couple of kids, and guess he's fucking her, and She is taking pills or Wearing a diaphragm, I know this is the paradise everyone old has dreamed of all their lives".
Faber and Faber published High Windows in 1974.
It was the last book of new poems before his death in 1985.
This Be The Verse speaks bluntly about parents and misery.
The title poem looks out from high windows.
The Building and The Old Fools face illness and age.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In a broken future city, a woman cares for a girl named Emily and a wall that opens.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
