fields.value: Database year 1974 is correct for the first publication. Octagon Press published the British book in 1974. Alfred A. Knopf published the American book in 1975. The printed title is often The Memoirs of a Survivor. The database drops the word The.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Narrator (A middle aged woman who tells the story from her flat); Emily Cartwright (The teenage girl placed in the narrator's care); Hugo (Emily's cat, who stays with her when others leave); Gerald (A young man who gathers homeless children)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
(vii)
After a disaster called the Crisis, city life in Britain slowly falls apart.
A quiet woman is given charge of a teenager, Emily Cartwright, and Emily's cat Hugo.
Gangs of young people pass through, and Emily joins their rough new life.
Emily loves Gerald, who tries to lead homeless children, including wild children from the sewers.
The narrator sometimes passes through a wall into rooms that show Emily's sad childhood.
At the end the wall opens, and the small group walks into another world.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Adah leaves Nigeria for London, writes a novel, and escapes a husband who burns it.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Allison and Busby published it in London in 1974. George Braziller published the US edition in 1975. It shows Adah's life before In the Ditch, though it was published later. Database year 1974 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Adah (A young Nigerian woman who becomes a writer in London); Francis (Adah's husband, who burns the manuscript she calls her brainchild)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Adah fights to stay in school in Nigeria after her father dies.
She sends her husband Francis to study in Britain, then follows him.
In London she meets cold rooms, racist signs, and his violence.
After their fourth child, she writes a story in exercise books.
Francis burns the manuscript, and Adah leaves with the children.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A rich white farmer cannot keep a dead man, or apartheid, buried on his land.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1974 is correct. Jonathan Cape published it in London. It shared that year's Booker Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mehring (A rich white industrialist and the owner of the farm); Jacobus (The black foreman who finds the dead body); Antonia (Mehring's lover, a political activist who must leave Africa)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mehring is a rich white businessman who buys a farm outside the city.
Black workers run the farm.
Mehring knows little about it.
The foreman Jacobus finds an unnamed dead black man on the land.
The police bury the body quickly.
A flood later brings it back.
The workers then give the stranger a proper burial.
The novel shared the 1974 Booker Prize with Stanley Middleton's Holiday.

items.title: "The Last Days of Louisiana Red" (1974) — Ishmael Reed

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Last Days of Louisiana Red

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: PaPa LaBas hunts the killers of a man who was fighting heroin.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Random House published this novel in 1974. It continues PaPa LaBas from Mumbo Jumbo (1972). The database year 1974 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: PaPa LaBas (The Hoodoo detective who investigates the murder); Ed Yellings (Owner of the Solid Gumbo Works, killed at the start); Minnie Yellings (Ed's youngest daughter, leader of the Moochers); Wolf Yellings (Ed's son, who inherits the business)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ed Yellings runs the Solid Gumbo Works in Berkeley, California.
He is murdered while he seeks a cure for heroin addiction.
PaPa LaBas, from Mumbo Jumbo, investigates the crime.
Louisiana Red is a name for destructive rage and violence.
Minnie Yellings leads the Moochers, a band of opportunists.
The novel satirizes militant politics of the 1960s.
Hoodoo practice stays at the centre of the detective plot.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Old Henry Carr misremembers Joyce, Lenin, and Tzara in Zurich in 1917.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1974 is the premiere. Royal Shakespeare Company, Aldwych Theatre, London, 10 June 1974. The Tony Award for Best Play came in 1976. Do not use 1976 as the first date. The first book month was not confirmed on the pages used here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Henry Carr (A British consular official whose memory shapes the play); James Joyce (The novelist, shown staging Wilde and writing Ulysses); Tristan Tzara (The Dada poet, who argues about what art is); Vladimir Lenin (The revolutionary waiting in Zurich before 1917)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Henry Carr, now old, recalls Zurich during the First World War.
James Joyce, Lenin, and Tristan Tzara were all in the city in 1917.
Carr acts in The Importance of Being Earnest, which Joyce helps stage.
He quarrels with Joyce about a pair of trousers.
His memory slips, so the past turns into a Wilde style comedy.
He boasts that he knew everyone, then forgets his own third lesson.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1975 novel about a Sialkot family forced to leave home during Partition.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first edition appeared in 1975. A paperback from Orient Paperbacks followed in 1979. The Sahitya Akademi Award came in 1977. The catalog year 1975 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lala Kanshi Ram (A grain merchant of Sialkot whose family is forced to leave); Prabha Rani (His wife); Arun (Their son, who comes of age during the flight from Sialkot); Madhu (Their daughter); Nur (A Muslim girl Arun has known since childhood)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
On 3 June 1947, Lala Kanshi Ram hears that Partition is coming.
He lives in Sialkot with his wife Prabha Rani, daughter Madhu, and son Arun.
Communal violence, meaning violence between religious groups, drives them into a refugee camp.
They travel toward India and lose the home and work they knew.
The story ends in Delhi on 30 January 1948, when Gandhi is killed.

items.title: "Death and the King’s Horseman" (1975) — Wole Soyinka

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The king's horseman fails a ritual death, his son dies in his place, and the world is thrown off balance.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Eyre Methuen published the play in 1975. The catalog year 1975 matches the book. The catalog genre Poetry is wrong. This is a play. The Nobel life note says it was performed in 1976. A later page gives a 1975 premiere at the University of Ife. Use 1975 for the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elesin (The king's horseman, who delays the ritual death); Olunde (Elesin's son, a medical student who dies in his place); Iyaloja (Mother of the market, who judges Elesin's failure); Simon Pilkings (The district officer who arrests Elesin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This play is based on a real incident that took place in Nigeria during British colonial rule. The horseman of an important chief was prevented from committing ritual suicide by the colonial authorities.
Soyinka says that the play should not be considered as "Clash of Cultures".
The play builds upon the true story of the character 'Elesin' the King's Horseman of the title. According to Yoruba tradition, the death of a chief must be followed by the ritual suicide of Chief's horseman because the horseman's spirit is essential to helping the chief's spirit ascend to the afterlife, otherwise chief's spirit will wander the earth and bring harm to Yoruba people.
The first of the play, documents the processes of the suicide ritual, with the potent life loving figure 'Elesin', living out his final day in celebration before the ritual process begins.
At the last minute, the British colonial ruler, Simon Pilkings ; intervenes, the suicide being viewed as barbaric and illegal by the British authorities.
When Yoruba people accuses Elesin's son Olunde to commits ritual suicide in his father's place as to restore the honour of his family. Consequently Elesin kills himself.
A Yoruba king has died, and his horseman Elesin must die after him.
Elesin spends his last day in music, praise, and a new marriage.
The colonial officer Simon Pilkings stops the ritual death.
Soyinka calls that stop a catalytic incident, not the whole play.
Elesin's son Olunde, home from medical study, dies in his father's place.
Elesin then kills himself, too late to restore his honour.

items.title: "Dread Beat an’ Blood" (1975) — Linton Kwesi Johnson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems in Jamaican Creole about police pressure and Black youth in Britain.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1975 is the Bogle-L'Ouverture book. Virgin issued the album in 1978 under the name Poet and the Roots. A documentary film used the same title in 1978.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The young speaker (A Black youth facing street violence and the police in Britain)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is his second book, after Voices of the Living and the Dead (1974).
Bogle-L'Ouverture published it in London in 1975.
The poems use Jamaican Creole and a reggae beat.
They speak of street fights, dread (Rastafarian seriousness), and police pressure.
In 1978 the same title became his first album and a documentary film.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An immortal young man searches for death on a strange mountain island.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1975 is correct. Grimus is Rushdie's first novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Flapping Eagle (A young Indian man who cannot die); Grimus (The powerful figure Flapping Eagle seeks on Calf Island)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Flapping Eagle drinks an elixir (a magic drink) that will not let him die.
He wanders for centuries, tired of a life that will not end.
He sails to Calf Island to find a way to become mortal again.
There he meets Grimus, a figure of strange power.
The book mixes myth, science fantasy, and quest story.
Readers mostly ignored this first novel.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A later woman in India uncovers the scandal of Olivia and a Nawab in the 1920s.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1975 is correct. John Murray published it on 30 October 1975. It won the Booker Prize that year. The Merchant Ivory film, with her screenplay, came in 1983.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A woman who comes to India to trace Olivia's story); Olivia (The wife of a British civil servant in the 1920s); The Nawab (The charming ruler of a small state who attracts Olivia); Harry (An Englishman who lives at the Nawab's palace and cannot leave)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator comes to India to learn about Olivia, from old letters.
In the 1920s, Olivia is the bored wife of a British official.
A Nawab (a local prince) draws Olivia into his world.
A pregnancy and an abortion cause a scandal, and Olivia leaves her husband.
The narrator also becomes pregnant and goes to the hill town where Olivia lived.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Bog poems set the killings of the Troubles beside ancient buried bodies.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1975 is correct. Faber published it in London. Bog Poems, a small press book, appeared the same year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (A speaker torn between private art and public violence)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber published North in 1975, after Heaney had left Belfast.
The first part uses bog bodies (ancient dead kept in peat).
Poems such as Punishment and Bog Queen link old victims to new ones.
He asks if looking at violence makes the poet a voyeur (a watcher).
Later poems, including Singing School, turn to his own schooling.
Fosterage in that sequence is for his mentor Michael McLaverty.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In early twentieth century New York, invented families meet real celebrities, and a Black pianist demands justice.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1975 is correct. Random House published the novel in 1975. It won the National Book Critics Circle Award that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Coalhouse Walker (A proud Black ragtime pianist who turns to violence for justice); Sarah (The mother of Coalhouse's child, killed while trying to help him); Tateh (A Jewish immigrant who later becomes a film maker); Mother (The New Rochelle wife who grows more independent); Mother's Younger Brother (A restless young man who joins Coalhouse and later goes to Mexico)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A rich family in New Rochelle is pulled into a crisis of race and class.
Coalhouse Walker, a Black pianist, wants justice after racists wreck his car.
Sarah, the mother of his child, is killed while she tries to help him.
Tateh, a Jewish immigrant, rises from street poverty into the movie business.
Real people such as Houdini, Ford, and Emma Goldman enter the same story.

items.title: "Self-Portrait in a Convex Mirror" (1975) — John Ashbery

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1975 book whose long title poem thinks about a curved mirror painting.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1975 is the book year. The National Book Foundation lists the National Book Award in 1976. Wikipedia dates the Pulitzer Prize and the critics' prize to 1976 as well.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viking Press published the book in 1975.
The long title poem is the heart of the book.
It answers a painting by Parmigianino of a face in a curved mirror.
In 1976 the book won the Pulitzer Prize for Poetry.
The same year it won the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Magician Magnus Eisengrim tells a film crew the hard life behind his wonders.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1975 is correct. Macmillan of Canada published the novel in 1975. It closes the Deptford Trilogy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Magnus Eisengrim (Paul Dempster grown up, a master magician who narrates most of his life); Dunstan Ramsay (Eisengrim's friend, who adds context and was the narrator of Fifth Business); Liesl (Eisengrim's partner in the magic show, who questions his story); Willard (The carnival magician who abducts the boy and trains him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A film crew is making a picture about the French magician Robert Houdin.
Magnus Eisengrim tells his own life during the breaks in filming.
As a boy he is Paul Dempster, taken from home by the carnival magician Willard.
Willard abuses him and also teaches him the craft of illusion.
Ramsay and Liesl listen, and the mystery of Boy Staunton's death is faced at last.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Later poems claim Bombay as home and include hymns, gurus, and Indian English voices.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1976 is correct. Oxford University Press published Hymns in Darkness in 1976, in the New Poetry in India series.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Most of the poems were written in the early 1970s.
Background, Casually tells his own life as a Jewish poet in India.
Island says he cannot leave Bombay, because he was born there.
Guru and the goodbye party poem use satire of speech and holy men.
The title hymns answer old Vedic hymns, read in a dark room.
Oxford University Press published the book in 1976.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A visitor walks through the temple town of Jejuri and questions stone and god.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1976 is correct. Clearing House in Bombay published Jejuri in 1976. It won the Commonwealth Poetry Prize in 1977. Wikipedia says he visited the town in 1963 and that a quarterly printed poems in 1974. The exam year for the book is 1976.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The visitor (A modern speaker who walks the town and will not settle the question of God); Khandoba (The local god of Jejuri, worshipped as a form of Shiva); The old woman (A beggar whose stare seems to crack the hills and the temples)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A bus brings a doubtful visitor to the town of the god Khandoba.
He sees priests, small shrines, and stones that people treat as gods.
One poem says a huge rock is Khandoba's wife, struck and turned to stone.
An old woman begs, and the hills seem to crack around her eyes.
A yellow butterfly, with no legend on it, holds the dry hills under its wings.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A frank autobiography of her childhood, marriage, and life as a writer.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The English edition is 1976. Wikipedia names Sterling Publishers, New Delhi. Britannica agrees on 1976 for My Story. The book was first written in Malayalam as Ente Katha. The database calls this work poetry. It is an autobiography.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kamala Das (The author telling her own life, with some fictional parts); K. Madhava Das (Her husband, a bank officer, whom she married young)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
She first wrote the life story in Malayalam as Ente Katha.
The English book is called My Story.
Sterling Publishers in New Delhi issued the English edition in 1976.
The book speaks openly about marriage, desire, and pain.
She compares such honesty to taking off every cover.
She later said that some parts were fictional.
The catalog calls it poetry, but it is an autobiography.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first full poetry book sets short, modern English poems inside Indian scenes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1976 is correct. Clearing House in Bombay published it. This is a book of his own English poems, not a translation. The database translation flag is wrong.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book gathers early poems written after his little magazine years.
The lines are spare, with sudden images rather than a story plot.
City life, the body, and odd juxtapositions (things placed sharply side by side) recur.
He uses the plain speech he learned from American modern poets.
The poems are his own English work, issued by a poets' cooperative in Bombay.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1976 selection of his poems, later enlarged in 1982.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1976 matches the first selected edition. Angus and Robertson published it. A larger edition in 1982 is titled The Vernacular Republic: Poems 1961-1981. Do not replace 1976 with 1982.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Angus and Robertson published Selected Poems: The Vernacular Republic in 1976.
The title points to poetry in the speech of ordinary Australians.
The book gathers earlier work and shows his range.
In 1982 an enlarged edition covered poems from 1961-1981.
Readers sometimes mix the 1976 book with that 1982 edition.

items.title: "Will You Please Be Quiet, Please?" (1976) — Raymond Carver

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Will You Please Be Quiet, Please?

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first major story collection, about quiet damage in ordinary American lives.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1976 is correct. McGraw Hill published the book in 1976. It was a National Book Award finalist in 1977.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ralph (A teacher who learns that his wife was unfaithful and cannot stay calm); Marian (Ralph's wife, who admits the old affair and waits for him)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book gathers twenty two stories from his early writing years.
In the title story, Marian tells Ralph she was unfaithful years before.
Ralph drinks, wanders the city, and hides from her in the bathroom.
Other stories, such as Neighbors and Fat, show small events that unsettle a life.
The people often cannot say what they feel.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A screenwriter returns to England and to the woman he loved at Oxford.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: He began it in 1969, drafted again from 1974, and finished revisions in March 1977. Jonathan Cape published it in 1977. The database year 1977 is correct. It is an original English novel, not a translation. The same year saw the revised Magus, which is a different book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Daniel Martin (A playwright and screenwriter looking back at his English life); Jane (Anthony's wife and the woman Daniel has loved since Oxford); Nell (Jane's sister and Daniel's former wife); Anthony (Daniel's dying friend, married to Jane); Caro (Daniel's daughter by Nell)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Daniel Martin, a playwright and Hollywood screenwriter, is called back to England.
His dying Oxford friend Anthony asks him to look after Anthony's wife Jane.
Flashbacks show Oxford, Daniel's marriage to Jane's sister Nell, and one night with Jane.
Daniel and Jane travel through Egypt, Syria, and Lebanon, and they fall in love again.
He leaves his younger girlfriend, and the lovers come together at the end.

items.title: "India: A Wounded Civilization" (1977) — V. S. Naipaul

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His second India book reads the Emergency as a sign of a deeper wound.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1977 is correct. London: Andre Deutsch. Essays on the Emergency appeared in The New York Review of Books in 1976. It is not a translation.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: V.S. Naipaul (The traveller reading India during the Emergency)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
III. India: A Million Mutinies Now - It consists of an essay entitled "Indian Autobiography".
This is the middle book of the India trilogy.
Naipaul returned during the Emergency declared in 1975.
People were afraid to talk, so he read papers, magazines, and books.
He treats the crisis as more than a short political fight.
Andre Deutsch published the book in London in 1977.
It is travel and essay prose in English, not a translation.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four people in Ilmorog are pulled into a murder case in independent Kenya.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Heinemann published it in 1977 in the African Writers Series. The catalog year 1977 is correct. He wrote it in English. The catalog translation flag is wrong. Detention followed the Gikuyu play of the same year, not a translation of this novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Munira (A teacher in Ilmorog who later sets the fire); Wanja (A barmaid and later a brothel keeper, granddaughter of Nyakinyua); Abdulla (A one legged shopkeeper who fought in the Mau Mau war); Karega (A young teacher who turns toward workers' politics)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Three directors die in a fire, and the police question four people.
Munira, Abdulla, Wanja, and Karega have gathered in the village of Ilmorog.
Drought drives the villagers on a hard walk to Nairobi.
The new elite use the road, the bar, and the land.
New Ilmorog grows, and Wanja's brothel becomes the fire.
The novel asks if independence only copied colonial power.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Milkman Dead travels south and finds a family song about flying.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1977 is correct for the novel. Knopf published it in 1977. It won the National Book Critics Circle Award. Wikipedia dates that award to 1978, so do not replace the book year with the prize year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Macon Dead III (Milkman) (The hero, who grows from a selfish son into a seeker); Pilate Dead (Milkman's aunt, a singer and keeper of family memory); Macon Dead Jr. (Milkman's father, a harsh landlord); Guitar Bains (Milkman's friend, who later turns against him); Hagar (Pilate's granddaughter, who loves Milkman and is rejected)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Macon Dead III is born in Michigan and nicknamed Milkman.
His father loves property, while Aunt Pilate keeps the family past.
Milkman and Guitar steal a bag they think holds gold.
The bag holds bones, so Milkman travels south to learn why.
In Shalimar he hears children sing of an ancestor who flew.
The song is his own family story, and he learns how to leap.

items.title: "The Passion of New Eve" (1977) — Angela Carter

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A cruel Englishman is remade as a woman in a broken America.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: She began the book in January 1972. Victor Gollancz published it in 1977. The database year 1977 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Evelyn, later Eve (The English narrator, changed from a man into a woman); Leilah, later Lilith (A dancer whom Evelyn harms, later a rebel leader); Mother (A surgeon who rules the women's city of Beulah); Tristessa (A silent film star who is discovered to be a man); Zero (A brutal one eyed cult leader with several wives)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Evelyn, an Englishman, arrives in a violent, decaying New York.
He uses Leilah, then flees into the desert.
Mother, a surgeon goddess, changes his body into a woman's body.
The new Eve is captured by Zero and meets the film star Tristessa.
Tristessa is revealed as a man, and Eve later leaves by sea.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A seven year affair is shown from the end back to the start.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1978 is correct. Eyre Methuen published the play in 1978. It opened at the Lyttelton Theatre, National Theatre, London, on 15 November 1978. The story uses Pinter's affair with Joan Bakewell.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Emma (Robert's wife and Jerry's lover); Robert (Emma's husband and Jerry's friend); Jerry (A literary agent who hides the affair)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is set between years 1968-77, but actually the action takes place in reverse chronology.
The scenes run from 1977 back to 1968.
Jerry has had an affair with Emma, who is married to Robert.
Jerry is also Robert's close friend.
Each scene shows another kind of lie among the three.
The last scene on stage is the earliest meeting, in 1968.

items.title: "A Bend in the River" (1979) — V. S. Naipaul

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Salim, an Indian shopkeeper, watches an African town rise and break.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1979 is correct. The US edition is Alfred A. Knopf, May 1979. A catalog label that calls the book poetry is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Salim (An Indian Muslim shopkeeper and the narrator); Ferdinand (Zabeth's son, later an official who frees Salim); The Big Man (The president who never appears but rules the town)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It was shortlisted for Booker prize in 1979.
Opening lines: "The world is what it is; men Who are nothing, who allow themselves to become nothing have no place in it."
It is set in an unnamed African country after independence and the narrator is Salim, an ethnically Indian Muslim and a shopkeeper.
Salim observes the rapid changes in the Africa with an outsider distance.
Salim, the protagonist grows in the Indian community on the east coast of Africa but he feels insecure about his future in East Africa and buys a business from Nazruddin in a town, at " a bend in the river", in the heart of Africa.
When he moves there he found the town as "Ghost town".
Salim leaves the east coast and buys a shop inland.
The town sits at a bend in a great river in an unnamed country.
After independence the bush, the army, and a Big Man reshape the town.
Salim has an affair with Yvette, the wife of a European adviser.
His shop is taken.
A young official, Ferdinand, tells him to flee.
The novel was published in 1979 and shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A two-act play that links a Victorian colony with sexual freedom in 1979 London.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Joint Stock workshopped the play in 1978. It premiered at Dartington College of Arts on 14 February 1979. The Royal Court opened it on 29 March 1979. Database year 1979 matches the premiere.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Clive (A colonial administrator and Betty's husband in Act 1); Betty (Clive's wife, played by a man in Act 1 and by a woman in Act 2); Edward (Their son, played by a woman in Act 1); Joshua (An African servant, played by a white actor)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Act 1 is set in a British colony in Africa in Victorian times.
Clive rules the house, while his wife Betty is played by a man.
Their son Edward is played by a woman, and the servant Joshua by a white actor.
Act 2 moves to a London park in 1979.
For the family, only 25 years have passed, and the casting changes.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems of marriage, Glanmore, and elegies after he left the North.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1979 is correct. Faber published the book. The same year a small press printed sonnets from Glanmore.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (A husband and elegist speaking after the move south)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber published Field Work in 1979.
Heaney was then living in Dublin after years in Wicklow.
The Glanmore Sonnets praise married life in the countryside.
Elegies remember people killed in the Troubles.
Casualty is one of those elegies for a dead friend.
The book is more open in feeling than the packed lines of North.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first book of poems, sharp sketches of Goan Catholic family life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1979 is correct. Newground, a Bombay poets' collective, published Fix in 1979. It was her first book of poems.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Father X. D'Souza (The boastful Catholic father in Catholic Mother, called a pillar of the Church); The Mother (The silent wife in that poem, present in the family picture but given no speech); The Bride (The woman in Marriages Are Made, examined for health, teeth, and caste before marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poets' group Newground published Fix in Bombay in 1979.
The poems are short, ironic, and often one speaker's voice.
In Catholic Mother a proud father boasts of seven children in seven years.
The mother in that poem is almost silent.
The father takes the credit.
Marriages Are Made lists a bride checked like goods before a wedding.

items.title: "If on a winter’s night a traveler" (1979) — Italo Calvino

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: If on a winter’s night a traveler

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A reader tries to finish a novel that keeps breaking off into other novels.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Einaudi published the Italian novel in 1979. William Weaver's English translation appeared in 1981. The first publication is 1979. The database English year is the translation date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Reader (The you of the story, who tries to finish the book); Ludmilla (Another reader, who joins the search and becomes the love interest); Ermes Marana (A translator who mixes up texts and spreads false books); Silas Flannery (A novelist troubled by unfinished stories)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel speaks to you, the reader, in the second person (the word you).
You begin a book, but the pages are out of order.
You meet another reader, Ludmilla, and you both hunt the missing text.
Between those chapters come the openings of ten different novels.
Each of those novels stops at a tense moment.
A crooked translator, Ermes Marana, and a writer, Silas Flannery, enter the plot.
Read in order, the ten broken titles make one long sentence.
The real subject is reading itself.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Old Barth characters write letters to one another and to the author.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1979 is correct. Putnam published the novel that year. It is fiction in letters, not a volume of real correspondence.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Author (John Barth, writing as a character inside his own novel); Todd Andrews (The lawyer from The Floating Opera, now older); Jacob Horner (The paralysed teacher from The End of the Road); Ambrose Mensch (The boy from Lost in the Funhouse, now a blocked novelist); Lady Amherst (A new character, not taken from an earlier Barth novel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Putnam published this long novel in 1979.
Seven writers send letters, and Barth himself is one of them.
Todd Andrews, Jacob Horner, and Ambrose Mensch return from earlier books.
Lady Amherst is the new character among the letter writers.
The dates of the letters hide the word LETTERS.
It is fiction, not real mail.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ten dark fairy tales retold so that women see, choose, and fight back.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Gollancz published the British book in 1979. Harper and Row published it in the United States. The database year 1979 is correct. The Sadeian Woman, a prose study, also came out in 1979.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The young bride (The pianist narrator of the title story); The Marquis (A Bluebeard figure who murdered his earlier wives); The bride's mother (The woman who rides in and saves her daughter); The piano tuner (A blind young man who stays with the bride)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The long title story follows a young bride and a rich Marquis.
He gives her keys but forbids one room.
She opens it and finds the bodies of his earlier wives.
He plans to kill her, but her mother arrives and shoots him.
The other nine stories rewrite Beauty and the Beast, Puss in Boots, and Red Riding Hood.

items.title: "The Book of Laughter and Forgetting" (1979) — Milan Kundera

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Book of Laughter and Forgetting

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Seven linked stories about memory, laughter, and life under Czech communism.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The English year 1980 is correct. The first book was the French edition in 1979. The Czech book from 68 Publishers in Toronto is 1981, not 1979.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mirek (A man who tries to erase an old love and is jailed); Tamina (A woman in exile who wants her lost letters and diaries); The narrator (A voice like Kundera that steps in with essays and jokes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book has seven parts, not one straight plot.
It opens with a photograph from which a fallen leader is erased.
Mirek tries to recover old love letters and is arrested.
Tamina, in exile, wants the diaries she left in Prague.
Kundera explains the Czech feeling litost (pain at the sudden sight of one's own misery).
Laughter can be joy, or it can force people into one official idea.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Nnu Ego gives her life to her children in colonial Lagos and dies alone.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Allison and Busby published it in London in 1979. Heinemann's African Writers Series issued it in 1980. Database year 1979 is the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nnu Ego (An Igbo woman whose worth is measured by the sons she bears); Nnaife (Her husband in Lagos, who washes clothes for a white employer); Nwokocha Agbadi (Her father, a proud and wealthy local chief)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nnu Ego is the daughter of Chief Nwokocha Agbadi and Ona.
Her first marriage fails when she seems unable to bear a child.
She goes to Lagos and marries Nnaife, a laundryman for a white family.
She bears children, but war, poverty, and absent sons wear her down.
She dies lonely in her village, and her children later fund a grand funeral.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short report that defines the postmodern as disbelief in grand stories.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: French publication 1979, Les Editions de Minuit. English 1984, University of Minnesota Press, translated by Geoffrey Bennington and Brian Massumi.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jean-François Lyotard (The philosopher writing a report on knowledge)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The government of Quebec asked for a report on knowledge.
Lyotard says modern thought trusted grand stories such as progress.
He defines the postmodern as disbelief in those grand stories.
Knowledge splits into many language games with different rules.
Science is then judged by usefulness and profit, not only by truth.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Das siblings meet again in Old Delhi and face a family split by time and Partition.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1980 is correct. Heinemann published the novel in 1980. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bimla Das (Bim) (The elder sister who stays in the Old Delhi house and teaches history); Tara (Bim's younger sister, married to a diplomat and living abroad); Raja (Their brother, who loves Urdu poetry and moves to Hyderabad); Baba (Their brother, who stays with Bim and plays the same old records); Aunt Mira (The widowed aunt who raises the Das children)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel is primarily set in Old Delhi. The story describes as adults and moving back into their lives throughout the novel.
The novel is split into 4 sections covering the 'Das' family set at various times during partition on Old Delhi the tension between Hindu and Muslims. It is a partition novel.
In this novel, Quotes from various poets are used as T.S. Eliot's (The Wasteland and Burnt Norton), Alfred Tennyson, Lord Byron, Muhammad Iqbal, D.H. Lawrence.
Tara returns to the old family house in Delhi and meets her sister Bim.
Bim teaches history and cares for their brother Baba, who lives in a small private world.
Their brother Raja now lives in Hyderabad, and Bim still resents an old letter.
The middle of the novel goes back to the 1940s, illness, and the flight of their Muslim landlords.
Aunt Mira, who raised the children, dies, and Tara escapes by marriage.
Bim's anger breaks, and she chooses to forgive Raja.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poetry book that turns office language into strange, broken lyric.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1980 is correct for the first Roof Books edition. The catalogue marks the book as a translation. It is an English original.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Roof Books published Controlling Interests in New York in 1980.
The poems borrow memos, slogans, and business talk.
Long lines and lists replace one smooth personal voice.
A poem such as Matters of Policy asks who controls language.
Roof printed the book again later.
The first year remains 1980.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An aged gay novelist recalls a century while the church weighs his brother in law for sainthood.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1980 is correct. Hutchinson published it in October 1980. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize and lost to William Golding's Rites of Passage.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kenneth Toomey (An 81 year old novelist, partly suggested by Somerset Maugham); Carlo Campanati (Toomey's brother in law, who becomes Pope Gregory XVII in the novel); Hortense (Toomey's sister, married into the Campanati family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In this novel 81 year old hero Kenneth Toomey tells the story of his life in 82 chapters.
He is the autobiographical narrator who starts familiarity with James Joyce, C. Day Lewis, Ford Maddox Ford and Rudyard Kipling.
It starts with the sentence : "It was the afternoon of my eighty first birthday and I was in bed with my Catamite when Ali announced that the archbishop had come to see me".
On his 81st birthday, Kenneth Toomey is asked to help a saint's case.
The dead man is Carlo Campanati, Toomey's brother in law, a fictional pope.
Toomey's memoirs cross the First World War, fascism, and later horrors.
He struggles with Catholic teaching and his life as a homosexual writer.
The book treats memory as unreliable, full of small false details on purpose.

items.title: "Inglan Is a Bitch" (1980) — Linton Kwesi Johnson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Creole poem-book about hard, low-paid work for a Caribbean migrant in London.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1980 is right. Race Today published the book in London. The title poem was also performed and recorded.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The migrant speaker (A Caribbean man who moves from job to job in London)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Race Today Publications brought out the book in London in 1980.
The title poem follows a man who has just come to London.
He works on the Underground, in a hotel, and later in a factory.
After fifteen years the factory sends him away without work.
Each stanza returns to the same angry refrain.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His first poetry book, mixing his own poems with a few translations.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1980 matches the private edition. Britannica also says 1980. Writers Workshop issued the first public edition in 1981. Penguin India reprinted a revised text in 1994. The database calls the book fiction, but it is poetry.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Seth drafted many of these poems while he was a writing fellow at Stanford.
A private edition of about 150 copies appeared in 1980.
Writers Workshop in Calcutta issued the first public edition in 1981.
The poems move through India, China, and California in many small forms.
Penguin India reprinted a revised text in 1994.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An experimental autobiography in prose sentences that she kept expanding as she aged.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The catalog year 1980 is right for the first Burning Deck edition. Sun and Moon published the expanded book in 1987. My Life in the Nineties, a further volume, appeared in 2003.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (Hejinian recalling ordinary moments from her own life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The 1980 book has 37 sections because she was 37.
Each of those sections has 37 sentences.
The 1987 edition grows to 45 sections of 45 sentences.
Repeated phrases stitch together memories of childhood, family, and daily life.
There is no straight plot.
The reader must connect the gaps.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long poem in twelve parts about the poet's bond with the past of Odisha.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Greenfield Review Press in New York published Relationship in 1980. The Sahitya Akademi Award followed in 1981. The database year 1980 is the publication year, not the award year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (The poet's voice, searching his land and his past)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker enters the history and myths of Odisha.
Stones, temples, and childhood memories press on him.
He feels guilt for living apart from his own origins.
The poem tries to give his home a large epic voice.
It won the Sahitya Akademi Award for English in 1981.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young gentleman's sea journal records how shame destroys a clergyman.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1980 is correct. Faber published Rites of Passage in 1980, and it won the Booker Prize that year. Close Quarters (1987) and Fire Down Below (1989) complete the sea trilogy (a set of three books).

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Edmund Talbot (A young gentleman who writes the journal); Reverend Colley (The parson who dies after public shame)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Edmund Talbot sails toward Australia in the early nineteenth century.
He writes a journal for his godfather about the ship and its classes.
Reverend Colley is a clumsy clergyman whom the crew and gentlemen mock.
A humiliating rite breaks Colley.
He hides in his cabin and dies.
Talbot has to face his own part in the cruelty.
The novel won the Booker Prize in 1980 and opens a sea trilogy (a set of three books).

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A hill girl gives up a prized blue umbrella and heals a jealous shopkeeper.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Encyclopedia.com dates the illustrated book, with pictures by Trevor Stubley, to 1974. The database year is 1980, and a Wikipedia page also says 1980. Use 1974 for the first edition. A Hindi film by Vishal Bhardwaj came in 2005 and won a National Film Award.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Binya (A village girl who owns the blue umbrella); Ram Bharosa (The shopkeeper who becomes jealous of the umbrella); Rajaram (A boy from the next village who works in the shop)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Binya lives in a Garhwal village with her mother and her brother.
She trades a leopard claw pendant for a beautiful blue umbrella.
The shopkeeper Ram Bharosa wants the umbrella and tries to buy it.
His helper Rajaram tries to steal it and is caught.
The village turns against the shop.
Binya gives him the umbrella.

items.title: "The Name of the Rose" (1980) — Umberto Eco

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In 1327, friar William of Baskerville hunts a murderer inside a monastery library.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Italian publication 1980 is the right first date. English by William Weaver is 1983. The database calls the book poetry. It is a novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William of Baskerville (A Franciscan friar and former inquisitor who solves the deaths); Adso of Melk (A young Benedictine novice who tells the story years later); Jorge of Burgos (A blind monk who guards a forbidden book and starts the fire)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Italian title is Il nome della rosa, published by Bompiani in 1980.
William Weaver's English translation appeared in 1983.
William of Baskerville and the novice Adso investigate deaths at a Benedictine abbey.
The trail leads into a labyrinth library and a poisoned book.
The blind monk Jorge of Burgos has hidden a lost book of Aristotle on laughter.

items.title: "Waiting for the Barbarians" (1980) — J. M. Coetzee

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A frontier magistrate learns what his empire does to the people it fears.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1980 is correct. Secker and Warburg published it on 27 October 1980. It won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize and the Geoffrey Faber Memorial Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Magistrate (The narrator, a frontier official who turns against the torture); Colonel Joll (The officer who leads the Third Bureau); The barbarian girl (A tortured prisoner the magistrate tries to return home)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An unnamed magistrate governs a small town at the edge of the Empire.
Colonel Joll of the Third Bureau tortures prisoners called barbarians.
The magistrate cares for a barbarian girl who has been blinded and hurt.
He takes her back to her people and is then jailed as a traitor.
The army's campaign fails, and the soldiers leave before winter.
The title comes from a poem by Constantine Cavafy.

items.title: "Ake: The Years of Childhood" (1981) — Wole Soyinka

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A memoir of Soyinka's boyhood in the parsonage at Ake, Abeokuta, before he left for school in Ibadan.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Rex Collings published it in London in 1981, and Random House published the American edition the same year. The catalog year 1981 is correct. The catalog genre Fiction is loose. This is autobiography. It won an Anisfield Wolf Book Award in 1983.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Wole (The child narrator, later the writer); Samuel Ayodele Soyinka (His father, an Anglican minister and headmaster, called Essay in the family); Grace Soyinka (His mother, a trader and activist from the Ransome Kuti family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The child Wole grows up in Ake, part of Abeokuta.
His father is an Anglican headmaster, and his mother keeps a shop and joins protests.
The memoir follows the years before and during World War II.
School, church, market women, and Yoruba home life share one memory.
In 1946 he leaves for Government College, Ibadan.
The book is the clearest gate into his later plays.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A white family hides with their former servant during an imagined revolt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1981 is correct. The Nobel bibliography lists a New York Viking edition in 1981.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: July (The former servant who shelters the Smales family); Maureen Smales (The white woman who must live by July's rules); Bamford Smales (Maureen's husband, once the head of a liberal city home)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel imagines a violent end to white rule in South Africa.
Maureen and Bamford Smales flee the city with their children.
They hide in the village of July, their long-time servant.
July's family and the Smales family must share one poor place.
Old roles of master and servant begin to break.
The book asks how people choose when race and fear close in.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A boy born at the midnight of India's freedom tells the nation's story through his own life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1981 is correct. Jonathan Cape published it in 1981, and it won the Booker Prize that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Saleem Sinai (The narrator, born at the midnight of independence); Shiva (The baby swapped with Saleem, later his rival); Padma (The listener to whom Saleem tells his story); Mary Pereira (The nurse who switches the two babies)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Saleem Sinai is born at midnight on 15 August 1947, as India becomes free.
A nurse swaps him at birth with another baby, Shiva.
Saleem can hear the minds of other children born in that hour.
His body and family misfortunes echo wars, partition, and later politics.
He tells the tale to Padma, who listens and interrupts.
The novel won the Booker Prize in 1981.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A theory book on copies, media, and a real world replaced by models.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First publication is the 1981 French book. Sheila Faria Glaser's complete English translation appeared in 1994. The database genre Poetry is wrong. This is theory, not a poem.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Baudrillard retells a Borges story in which a map becomes as large as the land.
He says today the map, or the model, comes before the real territory.
Images move through stages until they no longer point to any original.
He calls this hyperreality.
Disneyland is one of his examples of a staged fake.
The French book is 1981. Sheila Faria Glaser's English translation is 1994.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A rich Bombay businessman hunts a meaning he cannot buy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The novel was published in 1981. It won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1982. The database year 1981 is the book year. The award year is the usual trap.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Som Bhaskar (A Bombay industrialist and the hungry narrator); Anuradha (The woman in Banaras who draws Som beyond business); Geeta (Som's wife, mother of his two children)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Som Bhaskar is a millionaire who still feels a hunger he calls I want.
Business, marriage, and affairs do not quiet that cry.
His search takes him from Bombay to the lanes of Banaras.
Anuradha and a hill shrine pull him toward mystery rather than money.
The book leaves him between reason and a wonder he cannot prove.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Marxist book that tells critics to read every narrative through history.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Cornell University Press published the book in 1981. The database year 1981 is correct. It is literary theory, not a poem. The database genre label Poetry is a catalog error.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens with the slogan, Always historicize.
Jameson studies the frames people use to interpret stories, not only the plots.
He treats history as the widest horizon of literary and cultural analysis.
Hidden class conflict leaves small traces in form, theme, and genre.
He argues that Marxist criticism can hold other methods inside a larger history.

items.title: "What We Talk About When We Talk About Love" (1981) — Raymond Carver

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: What We Talk About When We Talk About Love

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Seventeen very short stories about love, hurt, and talk that fails.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1981 is correct for the Knopf book. Lish's cuts are part of that text. Beginners (2009) restores earlier versions. The Bath in this book is the short form of A Small, Good Thing.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mel McGinnis (A cardiologist who leads the talk about what love is); Terri (Mel's wife, who defends the violent love of her former boyfriend); Nick (The narrator, married to Laura, who listens and drinks); Laura (Nick's wife, a legal secretary at the table)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Two couples sit in Albuquerque and drink gin in the afternoon.
Terri says her old boyfriend loved her so much that he tried to kill her.
Mel, a heart doctor, will not call that violence love.
Mel tells of an old couple smashed up in a car crash.
The talk goes on until the room grows dark and nobody moves.

items.title: "A History of Indian English Literature" (1982) — M. K. Naik

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A History of Indian English Literature

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical history of Indian writing in English from 1809 to 1979.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1982 is right for the first Sahitya Akademi edition. Wikipedia notes a revised edition in 1989. The story inside the book stops at the end of 1979.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Naik says no full critical history of this field had yet been written.
He starts with C. V. Boriah's English account of the Jains in 1809.
The Pagoda Tree chapter runs from the beginnings to 1857.
Later chapters cover 1857 to 1920, the Gandhian years, and Independence.
Each period looks at prose, poetry, drama, fiction, and the short story.

items.title: "A Pale View of Hills" (1982) — Kazuo Ishiguro

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Etsuko, in England, recalls Nagasaki and the daughter who later kills herself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1982 is correct. Faber published it in February 1982. It won the Winifred Holtby Memorial Prize. It grew from his East Anglia thesis.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Etsuko (The narrator, a Japanese woman living in England); Niki (Etsuko's younger daughter by her English husband); Keiko (Etsuko's elder daughter, who kills herself in England); Sachiko (A woman in the Nagasaki memories, mother of Mariko)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber published this first novel in February 1982.
Etsuko, a Japanese widow in England, talks with her daughter Niki.
Her elder daughter, Keiko, has recently died by suicide.
Etsuko remembers postwar Nagasaki, her husband Jiro, and a woman named Sachiko.
Sachiko's daughter Mariko is as solitary as Keiko.
The two stories blur, so the memory may be hiding Etsuko's own guilt.

items.title: "Distance in Statute Miles" (1982) — Arvind Krishna Mehrotra

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A second poetry book measures memory, family, and place in land miles.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1982 is correct. Clearing House in Bombay published it. The title means land miles, not sea miles. This book is also original English poetry.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title uses statute miles, the ordinary land mile, not the sailor's sea mile.
The poems look at distance from people and from the cities of his life.
Family figures, including the uncle who raised him, enter the personal poems.
The tone stays dry, exact, and short, with fewer dream pictures than before.
Clearing House in Bombay published this book six years after Nine Enclosures.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A study of the Bible as the code behind Western literature.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1982 is correct. The Canadian Encyclopedia and the Dictionary of Canadian Biography both date The Great Code to 1982. Words with Power (1990) is the sequel.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Frye argues that a student of English who does not know the Bible will miss many meanings.
He links the Bible's stories and images to the conventions of Western literature.
The title comes from Blake.
Blake called the Old and New Testaments the Great Code of Art.
The book grew out of his long Bible course at Victoria College.
Words with Power (1990) is the second Bible study, not this book.

items.title: "The Keeper of the Dead" (1982) — Keki N. Daruwalla

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1982 poetry book that won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1984.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1982 is the publication year. Oxford University Press issued the book. The Sahitya Akademi Award came in 1984, not in 1982.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The keeper (A figure in the title poem who stays with the dead)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems return to death, memory, and history.
The title points to a person who keeps watch over the dead.
Oxford University Press published the book in 1982.
The national letters prize followed in 1984.
In 2015 he gave that prize back, as a protest.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Stories of love, parents, and daughters, ending with a father near death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1982 is correct for the book. Macmillan of Canada published The Moons of Jupiter in 1982. The title story first appeared in The New Yorker on 22 May 1978. Do not use 1978 as the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Janet (A middle-aged writer visiting her father before his operation); Janet's father (A dying man who recites the moons of Jupiter from memory)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title story follows Janet, a divorced writer, in a Toronto hospital.
Her dying father changes his mind and agrees to a risky operation.
She goes to a planetarium (a dome that shows the stars) to steady herself.
There she hears that old facts about the planets can be replaced.
She asks him to name the moons of Jupiter, fearing these are last words.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Marlene celebrates a promotion with famous women, then faces the daughter she left behind.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It premiered at the Royal Court Theatre, London, on 28 August 1982. Max Stafford-Clark directed. Database year 1982 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Marlene (A tough career woman newly promoted at the Top Girls agency); Joyce (Marlene's working-class sister, who raises Angie); Angie (Marlene's daughter, brought up by Joyce); Pope Joan (A dinner guest, a woman said to have ruled as pope)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Marlene gives a dinner for women from history, myth, and art.
The guests include Pope Joan, Isabella Bird, Lady Nijo, Dull Gret, and Patient Griselda.
Later scenes show her employment agency in Thatcher's Britain.
Her sister Joyce has raised Angie, who is really Marlene's daughter.
The last scene, set a year earlier, shows the sisters quarrel about class.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A masked anarchist fights a fascist British state and trains a young woman to follow him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says serialized 1982-1989 and collected 1988-1989. Warrior ran from March 1982 into 1985 and stopped unfinished. DC finished the story in ten issues from September 1988 to May 1989. A table note dates the first collected book to May 1990. Britannica gives the shorter span 1982-1986. For the exam, start at 1982 and keep 1988-1989 as the DC finish.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: V (An anarchist in a Guy Fawkes mask, once a prisoner at Larkhill camp); Evey Hammond (A young woman whom V saves and who later takes his role); Adam Susan (The lonely leader of Norsefire, tied to the Fate computer); Eric Finch (A detective who hunts V and finally walks away from the state)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After a nuclear war, the Norsefire party rules Britain as a police state.
On Guy Fawkes Night, V saves Evey Hammond from state police.
V wears a Guy Fawkes mask and kills the staff of the old Larkhill camp.
He stages a prison so that Evey will choose death over betrayal.
V dies, Evey takes the mask, and the crowd must choose the next government.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Twelve later stories, wider in feeling, including a blind man and a drawn cathedral.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 1983 is correct for the first US edition from Knopf. Collins published a London edition in 1984. The book was a finalist for the 1984 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A husband who scorns blindness and then draws a cathedral with closed eyes); The wife (The narrator's wife, and an old friend of the blind man); Robert (A blind man whose visit changes the narrator)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The narrator dreads a visit from Robert, a blind friend of his wife.
He feels jealous of their closeness and uneasy about blindness.
Robert stays with the couple for a few days.
They begin to talk about what a cathedral looks like.
By sharing that picture, the husband and Robert reach a new bond.

items.title: "Life & Times of Michael K" (1983) — J. M. Coetzee

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Michael K tries to carry his dying mother home through a civil war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1983 is correct. Ravan Press published it in Johannesburg. It won the Booker Prize. A catalog label that calls it poetry is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Michael K (A quiet gardener who wants to live without a trace); Anna K (His sick mother, a domestic servant); The medical officer (A camp doctor who comes to envy K's freedom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Michael K is a gardener in Cape Town with a cleft lip.
War and martial law close the roads.
He builds a cart to take his mother, Anna, toward Prince Albert.
She dies on the way.
He carries her ashes onward.
Camps, soldiers, and a doctor try to hold him.
He keeps escaping.
The novel won the Booker Prize in 1983.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A dark comic tale of shame, power, and two rival families in a country like Pakistan.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1983 is correct. Shame was published in 1983, between Midnight's Children and The Satanic Verses.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Omar Khayyam Shakil (A man at the edge of the action, raised by three mothers); Sufiya Zinobia (A daughter in whom shame turns into violence); Iskander Harappa (A charming politician based on a Pakistan leader); Raza Hyder (A general who seizes power)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is set in a country that stands for Pakistan.
Omar Khayyam Shakil grows up hidden in a house of three mothers.
Two public men, like Bhutto and Zia, fight for power.
Sufiya Zinobia carries the family's shame and becomes violently strong.
Rushdie links shame with violence, and violence with more shame.
The book came two years after Midnight's Children.

items.title: "The Colour of Magic" (24 November 1983) — Terry Pratchett

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A failed wizard must guide the Disc's first tourist and his walking luggage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Colin Smythe published the British hardcover on 24 November 1983. That printing was about 506 copies. St. Martin's Press also issued it in the United States in 1983. The database year 1983 is correct. The database genre Poetry is not. This is the first Discworld novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rincewind (An incompetent wizard who knows one dangerous spell and mostly runs away); Twoflower (The Disc's first tourist, cheerful, rich, and unaware of danger); The Luggage (Twoflower's savage pearwood chest, which follows him on hundreds of little legs); Death (The skeleton who comes for the dying and speaks in capital letters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rincewind, a cowardly failed wizard, is forced to guide Twoflower.
Twoflower is a rich tourist from the Agatean Empire, and his chest, the Luggage, walks on many legs.
A tavern fire, started for the insurance money, burns much of Ankh-Morpork.
They meet imagined dragons, a barbarian hero, and the nation of Krull at the world's edge.
Rincewind falls off the Disc.
The next novel, The Light Fantastic, continues the fall.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A hard book on conflicts that no shared rule of speech can judge fairly.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: French publication 1983, Les Editions de Minuit. English 1988, University of Minnesota Press, translated by Georges Van Den Abbeele.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jean-François Lyotard (The philosopher defining the differend)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lyotard studies phrases, meaning units of speech, even silence.
Different kinds of phrases cannot be translated into one another.
A differend happens when one side's harm cannot be said in the court's words.
Using only the winner's rules makes the victim silent.
He asks readers to witness that silence instead of smoothing it away.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A history teacher tells his class the sad story of his family in the Fens.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1983 is correct. William Heinemann published the novel in 1983. It won the Guardian Fiction Prize and was shortlisted for the Booker. A film came in 1992.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tom Crick (The history teacher who narrates the book.); Mary Crick (Tom's wife, who takes a baby and is put in hospital.); Dick Crick (Tom's brother, who dies in the water.); Freddie Parr (A boy Dick pushes into the river.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tom Crick has taught history for many years at a school in Greenwich.
A crisis at home pushes him out of the job, so he tells stories instead.
The stories cross the Fens and two families joined by a secret.
As teenagers, Mary has an abortion and cannot have a child later.
Dick pushes Freddie Parr into the river, and Freddie drowns.
Years later Mary takes a baby and is sent to a mental hospital.
Dick learns a dark fact about his birth, rides into the water, and dies.

items.title: "Blood and Guts in High School" (1984) — Kathy Acker

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Blood and Guts in High School

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A collage novel about Janey Smith and words taken from older books.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1984 is the first publication. She wrote the book in the 1970s. It was copyrighted in 1978. Picador and Grove Press both issued it in 1984. The first printings swapped the last two sections. A 2017 edition restored her order.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Janey Smith (A young American girl whose life is broken by violence and travel); Jean Genet (A real French writer who appears as a character on Janey's journey)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Janey Smith lives with her father, who then sends her away to school in New York.
She is kidnapped and sold, and she later travels in North Africa.
In the story she meets the French writer Jean Genet, and then she dies.
The book joins letters, poems, drawings, and pieces of other books.
It reuses parts of The Scarlet Letter by Nathaniel Hawthorne.
The first printings in 1984 reversed the last two sections by mistake.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A retired doctor hunts the stuffed parrot that once sat on Flaubert's desk.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Jonathan Cape published it in 1984. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 1984. It won the Geoffrey Faber Memorial Prize in 1985 and the Prix Medicis Essai in 1986.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Geoffrey Braithwaite (A retired doctor and amateur Flaubert expert, the narrator); Gustave Flaubert (The real French novelist whose life Braithwaite cannot fix in one story); Louise Colet (Flaubert's lover, given her own chapter in the novel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Geoffrey Braithwaite, a widowed English doctor, visits Flaubert places in France.
Two museums each claim to own the stuffed parrot from Flaubert's desk.
He learns that the bird might be one of about fifty parrots.
Chapters use timelines, lists, criticism, and a bestiary (an animal catalogue).
The book looks like a biography, but the narrator is invented.
His own grief for his dead wife slowly comes into view.
He never gets one simple true parrot.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A lecture on nation language, the Caribbean English shaped by African speech rhythms.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Some lists date the lecture to 1979. New Beacon Books published the full essay in 1984. The database year 1984 matches that book. The database calls it Poetry, but the work is criticism.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kamau Brathwaite (The lecturer explaining nation language)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Brathwaite says standard English beats cannot carry a hurricane.
He calls that speech nation language, not broken English.
Its rhythm comes from African speech, calypso, and songs performed aloud.
He gives examples from Caribbean poets and popular singers.
The aim is a poetry that sounds like Caribbean life.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Hindi lecturer tries to record a great Urdu poet and finds only mess and loss.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1984 is correct. Heinemann published the novel in 1984, and it was shortlisted for the Booker Prize that year. The Merchant Ivory film came in 1993.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Deven Sharma (A Hindi lecturer who loves Urdu and is easily used by others); Nur Shahjahanabadi (An ageing Urdu poet whose life has fallen into disorder); Murad (Deven's editor friend, who pushes the interview and exploits him); Sarla (Deven's unhappy wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Deven Sharma teaches Hindi in a small college, but he loves Urdu poetry.
His friend Murad sends him to interview Nur, a famous and now broken Urdu poet in Old Delhi.
Deven hopes the meeting will lift him out of his dull life.
Nur is surrounded by quarrels, drink, and people who want money.
A cheap tape recorder and unpaid bills ruin the interview plan.
Deven is left holding the poet's decline, like a man who has taken a prisoner into his care.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A blues band waits in a Chicago studio while pride and theft explode.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A staged reading took place at the O'Neill Center in 1982. The Yale Repertory Theatre opened the play in April 1984. Broadway opened at the Cort Theatre on 11 October 1984. The database year 1984 matches that public premiere, not the 1982 reading.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ma Rainey (The blues singer who controls the session on her own terms); Levee (A hot tempered trumpeter who wants fame and his own songs); Toledo (The pianist, killed by Levee at the end); Cutler (The trombonist who defends the old way of playing); Sturdyvant (The white studio owner who exploits the musicians)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1927, Ma Rainey's band waits in a Chicago recording studio.
The young trumpeter Levee wants his own band and a new style.
The older players want to stay loyal to Ma's music.
White producers delay the session and underpay Black art.
Ma fires Levee, the producer rejects his songs, and Levee stabs Toledo.

items.title: "Metafiction: The Theory and Practice of Self-Conscious Fiction" (1984) — Patricia Waugh

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Metafiction: The Theory and Practice of Self-Conscious Fiction

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short theory book that defines fiction which knows it is fiction.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The British national record lists Methuen, London, 1984. Routledge later reissued the book and holds the 1984 copyright line. The database year 1984 is correct. The book is theory about fiction, not a poem.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book asks what metafiction is, and why some critics dislike it.
Metafiction means fiction that draws attention to itself as a made object.
Waugh reads writers such as John Fowles, Jorge Luis Borges, Muriel Spark, Kurt Vonnegut, and John Barth.
She uses Russian Formalism (a theory of how literary forms change) to explain parody.
She argues that parody and popular forms can expose tired rules and suggest new ones.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A winged circus star tells her life to a journalist who joins the show.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chatto and Windus published it on 4 March 1984. It won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize for fiction that year. The database year 1984 is correct.
