fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sophie Fevvers (A Cockney aerialiste who claims she has real wings); Jack Walser (An American journalist who becomes a circus clown); Lizzie (Fevvers's adoptive mother and sharp adviser); Colonel Kearney (The circus owner who trusts his fortune telling pig)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In London, Jack Walser interviews Sophie Fevvers, a famous aerialiste.
Fevvers says she hatched from an egg and grew real wings.
Walser joins Colonel Kearney's circus as a clown to test her story.
The tour runs through Petersburg and then into a wreck in Siberia.
At the dawn of the new century, Fevvers laughs that she fooled him.

items.title: "Postmodernism, or, The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism" (1991) — Fredric Jameson

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Postmodernism, or, The Cultural Logic of Late Capitalism

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jameson's account of postmodern culture as the logic of late capitalism.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: An essay with this title appeared in New Left Review in 1984. Duke University Press published the book in 1991. The database genre label Fiction is a catalog error. This is cultural theory, not a novel.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A long essay with this title appeared in New Left Review in 1984.
Jameson then expanded it into a book published by Duke in 1991.
He links postmodern art to a global, financial stage of capitalism.
He describes a crisis of historicity, a waning of affect, and pastiche.
Huge hotels and airports become hyperspace, space people cannot mentally map.

items.title: "The Unbearable Lightness of Being" (1984) — Milan Kundera

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about Tomas, Tereza, Sabina, and Franz during and after the Prague Spring.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: English 1984 is correct, and so is the French first edition of 1984. The Czech book is 1985, from 68 Publishers in Toronto. A Prague edition waited until 2006. The film is 1988.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tomas (A surgeon and womanizer who loves only Tereza); Tereza (His wife, a photographer who feels the weight of the body); Sabina (A painter and mistress who chooses betrayal and lightness); Franz (A Geneva professor who idealizes Sabina); Karenin (The couple's dog, named with a man's name)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tomas, a Prague surgeon, lives by lightness and many affairs.
Tereza comes from a small town and loves only him.
The Soviet invasion of 1968 wrecks the Prague Spring.
The couple try Zurich, then return to a harder Prague.
Tomas loses his post as a surgeon and washes windows.
Sabina keeps moving, while Franz dies far from her.
Tomas and Tereza die together in a country road accident.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A girl in Antigua loves her mother, then breaks away and leaves home.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chapters first appeared in The New Yorker. The book came out in March 1985. The database year 1985 is the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Annie John (The girl who tells her own story of growing up); Annie's mother (The beloved parent who later feels like a rival); Gwen (Annie's close school friend); The Red Girl (A wilder girl who stands for freedom)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Annie grows up in Antigua and adores her mother.
She learns that she must one day live apart from her mother.
At school she loves her friend Gwen, then admires the freer Red Girl.
She grows angry, ill, and distant from her mother.
At the end she leaves Antigua for nursing school in England.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eight stories that retell the lives of famous or half hidden people.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chatto and Windus published Black Venus in London in 1985. The United States edition is Saints and Strangers. The database year 1985 is correct. Do not confuse it with The Bloody Chamber of 1979.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jeanne Duval (The Black Venus of the title story, Baudelaire's lover); Charles Baudelaire (The French poet linked with Jeanne in the title story); Edgar Allan Poe (A writer reimagined in The Cabinet of Edgar Allan Poe); Lizzie Borden (The figure in the story The Fall River Axe Murders)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title story looks at Jeanne Duval, lover of the poet Baudelaire.
Other stories recast Edgar Allan Poe and Lizzie Borden.
One story rewrites music for A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Peter and the Wolf and a kitchen tale sit beside those histories.
The book prefers sidelong lives over the famous man's version.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The kid rides with Glanton's scalp hunters and is haunted by Judge Holden.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Random House published it in April 1985. Early reviews were mixed. Many readers now call it his greatest novel. Database year 1985 is correct. It is not part of the Border Trilogy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The kid (A nameless youth from Tennessee who rides with the scalp hunters); Judge Holden (A huge, learned, violent man who seems untouched by time); John Glanton (Leader of the historical gang of scalp hunters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The kid runs away from Tennessee and drifts into Texas.
He joins John Glanton's gang, which is paid for Apache scalps.
The gang kills widely, including villagers, and is later destroyed.
Judge Holden, a huge hairless man, treats war as a lasting law.
In 1878 the kid, now a man, meets the Judge again in a Texas fort.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A bitter garbage man builds a fence and blocks his son's chance.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Wilson wrote the play in 1983. Yale Repertory Theatre premiered it in 1985. Britannica dates a publication to 1986. Broadway opened on 26 March 1987 and won the Tony Award and the Pulitzer Prize that year. The database year 1985 is the premiere, not the Pulitzer.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Troy Maxson (A garbage collector and former baseball player, father of Cory); Rose Maxson (Troy's wife, who agrees to raise the baby but not to take Troy back); Cory Maxson (Their son, blocked from college football); Gabriel Maxson (Troy's wounded brother, who believes he talks to heaven); Jim Bono (Troy's friend and fellow garbage worker)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1957 Pittsburgh, Troy Maxson collects garbage and remembers baseball.
He forbids his son Cory to take a football scholarship.
Troy had been a star in the Negro leagues and feels the major leagues shut him out.
He tells Rose that another woman is pregnant, and that woman dies in childbirth.
Years later Troy is dead, and Cory comes home for the funeral.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An eighteenth century church builder and a modern detective share one pattern of murders.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Hamish Hamilton published it in 1985. The catalog year 1985 is correct. It won the Whitbread Novel Award and the Guardian Fiction Prize. It is a novel, not a biography of the historical Nicholas Hawksmoor.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nicholas Dyer (A fictional architect based on Nicholas Hawksmoor, who builds churches with sacrifices); Nicholas Hawksmoor (A modern detective investigating murders at Dyer's churches); Sir Christopher Wren (The historical architect who stands for reason against Dyer's secret faith)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nicholas Dyer builds London churches and hides a human sacrifice in them.
He works under Sir Christopher Wren and hides a dark faith.
In the 1980s, murders happen at the same churches.
Detective Nicholas Hawksmoor investigates and finds no ordinary clues.
Past and present start to occupy one another.
Ackroyd said this history is his own invention, not a strict historical novel.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical book on the novel and society in India, including novels in Indian languages.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Oxford University Press, Delhi, published it in 1985. The catalog year 1985 is correct. The catalog genre Poetry is wrong. This is criticism of the novel.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book asks how the novel meets Indian social life.
It does not stay inside novels written in English.
It reads major novelists in Indian languages beside the English tradition.
It asks what realism (lifelike detail) can and cannot show.
Society, not a borrowed Western plot, is the test of the form.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two women face greed, weak rights, and the Emergency in New Delhi.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: First published in London by Heinemann in 1985. The United States edition from Norton came in 1986. The Sahitya Akademi Award followed in 1986. The Sinclair Prize was in 1985.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rose (A British woman who came to India as Ram's second wife); Sonali (An Indian civil servant who questions the Emergency and helps Rose); Ram (Rose's husband, a businessman already married to Mona); Dev (Ram's son, who wants Rose removed and the property kept)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A historical and political fiction novel.
Set in New Delhi during the chaotic time between 1932 and the mid 1970's. It follows the lives of two female protagonists Rose and Sonali and their fight to live in a time of a political upheaval and social re-organization.
Ram is Rose's husband who is already married to Mona, when they wed.
Dev is Ram's spoiled son. 2. Prison and Chocolate Cake: A Time to be Happy (Memoir; 1954)
It is the fascinating memoir of Sahgal that talks about India and her struggle for Independence from point of a view of a young woman. 3. Relationship; Collection of letter between Sahgal & E.N. (her husband) Mangat Raj. 4. Before Freedom: Nehru's Letter to his Sister (edited by Nayantara Sehgal).
The story is set in New Delhi during the Emergency (a pause on many citizen rights).
That pause ran from June 1975 to March 1977.
Rose, a British woman, is the second wife of the businessman Ram.
Sonali, a civil servant and Rose's friend, loses her place in the new order.
Dev, Ram's son by his first wife, schemes to take the money and push Rose out.
It also looks back at sati (a widow's death on her husband's fire) and at women's thin rights.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1985 novel about a young Caribbean family that migrates to England.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Faber and Faber published the British edition in 1985. Penguin published an American edition the same year. The catalog year 1985 is correct. It won the Malcolm X Prize in 1985.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Leila Preston (A young woman who leaves the island for England with her child); Michael (Leila's unreliable husband, drawn to drink and other women); Calvin (The small son who travels with Leila and Michael)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1958, Leila Preston plans to leave a small Caribbean island.
She goes with her husband Michael and their son Calvin.
Her sick mother has already left for England for treatment.
In London they face poor rooms, racism, and a failing marriage.
Her mother dies, and Leila sees that Michael will not stay with her.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In Gilead, fertile women are forced to bear children for commanders.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1985 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published it in 1985. Britannica dates Atwood's Governor General's Award for this novel to 1986. The sequel is The Testaments in 2019.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Offred (The Handmaid whose name means she belongs to Fred); The Commander (The powerful man of the house, Fred); Serena Joy (The Commander's Wife); Nick (The chauffeur who becomes Offred's secret ally); Moira (Offred's old friend, who resists and is punished); Aunt Lydia (A trainer of Handmaids who returns in the sequel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The United States has become the Republic of Gilead, a religious tyranny.
Offred is a Handmaid, kept to produce a child for a Commander.
She remembers her husband, her child, and her lost name.
The Commander's house, the Wife, and the Eyes control her days.
A later historical note shows scholars studying her taped story.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three New York tales in which a watcher or a writer loses his own name.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database span 1985-1986 matches the three separate books. City of Glass is 1985. Ghosts and The Locked Room are 1986. Faber gave them the trilogy title in 1987. The US Penguin collection followed in 1990.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Daniel Quinn (A mystery writer who takes a case meant for Paul Auster); Blue (The detective in Ghosts, paid to watch Black); Fanshawe (The missing writer in The Locked Room); The narrator of The Locked Room (Fanshawe's friend, who publishes the missing man's work)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sun and Moon Press published City of Glass in 1985, then Ghosts and The Locked Room in 1986.
Faber and Faber gathered the three as The New York Trilogy in 1987.
In City of Glass, the writer Quinn answers a wrong call and plays the detective Paul Auster.
In Ghosts, Blue is hired by White to watch a man named Black.
In The Locked Room, a narrator searches for the missing writer Fanshawe.
Each book starts like a crime story and ends as a question about identity.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A professor of Hitler studies faces a toxic cloud and the fear of death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1985 is correct. Viking published the book on 21 January 1985, and it won the National Book Award that year. DeLillo first wanted the title Panasonic, but the company objected.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jack Gladney (The narrator, a professor who invented Hitler studies); Babette (Jack's wife, who secretly takes the drug Dylar); Murray Jay Siskind (A colleague who talks with Jack about death, media, and Elvis)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viking published the novel on 21 January 1985.
Jack Gladney teaches Hitler studies at the College on the Hill.
He and his wife Babette both fear which of them will die first.
A chemical spill releases a black toxic cloud over their town.
Babette seeks Dylar, an experimental drug meant to cure the fear of death.
The book won the National Book Award for fiction in 1985.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A travel book on the United States as desert, speed, and simulation.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Grasset published Amerique in 1986. Verso published America in 1988. The database genre Poetry is wrong. This is travel prose.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Baudrillard travels in the United States and writes in short, sharp sections.
He searches for astral America, the America of freeways, deserts, and images.
New York, Los Angeles, and the desert become signs of a hyperreal country.
He says there is no single truth of America hidden under the images.
The French book Amerique appeared in 1986. Chris Turner's English America appeared in 1988.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays from 1975 to 1984 on poetry, meaning, and official verse culture.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1986 is correct for the first Sun and Moon edition. A reprint appeared in 2001. The translation flag in the catalogue is wrong. The essays were written in English.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charles Bernstein (The essayist writing about poetry, reading, and institutions)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sun and Moon Press published the essays in Los Angeles in 1986.
The pieces were written from 1975 to 1984.
Bernstein names official verse culture, the narrow world of prizes and reviews.
He argues that a plain sincere lyric can hide how language works.
Northwestern University Press printed the book again in 2001.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays that tell African writers to leave European languages and use African ones.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: James Currey published it in 1986. The catalog year 1986 is correct. The catalog calls it fiction and a translation. Both notes are wrong. He wrote the essays in English. The book itself says farewell to English.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ngugi wa Thiong'o (The essayist arguing for African languages in literature)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ngugi calls the book a farewell to English as his writing language.
He says language carries culture, memory, and a people's values.
Colonial schooling split the language of home from the language of school.
He names that split colonial alienation (being cut off from yourself).
He asks writers to decolonise the mind by choosing African languages.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Art interviews his father Vladek, whose story runs from prewar Poland to the gates of Auschwitz.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1986 is the Pantheon book of the first six chapters. Serialization in Raw began in December 1980. A three page version appeared in 1972. Do not use 1972 or 1980 as the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Art Spiegelman (The son and cartoonist, drawn as a mouse, who records the interviews); Vladek Spiegelman (Art's father, a Polish Jewish survivor, careful, stubborn, and haunted); Anja Spiegelman (Art's mother, also a survivor, who died by suicide in 1968); Richieu Spiegelman (The first son, killed in 1943 before Art was born)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In Queens, adult Art asks Vladek to tell the war story.
Vladek recalls marriage to Anja and the Nazi attack on Poland.
They send their first son, Richieu, to an aunt for safety.
The aunt kills herself and the children, including Richieu, to escape the camps.
Vladek and Anja hide, are betrayed, and are taken toward Auschwitz.
A reprinted strip faces Anja's suicide in 1968.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A later English book about double vision, between India, Chicago, and the body.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1986 is correct. Oxford University Press in New York published it. The database marks it as a translation. That flag is wrong. Second Sight is his own English poetry.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker of Chicago Zen (A city walker whose ordinary sight suddenly opens into vision)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Oxford University Press published Second Sight in 1986.
The title means seeing twice, or seeing in a new way.
Poems move between Indian memory and life in an American city.
Chicago Zen places a Himalayan vision on a Chicago street.
The book continues his mix of science, family, and myth.

items.title: "The Book of a Thousand Eyes" (2012) — Lyn Hejinian

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Book of a Thousand Eyes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 2012 book of night poems, dreams, and stories, written in honor of Scheherazade.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The catalog year 1986 does not match this title. Omnidawn published The Book of a Thousand Eyes in 2012. A shorter related book, The Little Book of a Thousand Eyes, appeared in 1996.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Scheherazade (The storyteller from The Arabian Nights whom the book honors)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book honors Scheherazade, who told stories each night to stay alive.
The pieces include lullabies, fairy tales, dream notes, and playful songs.
They move through sleep, waking, and imagination.
A concern for women's lives runs under the many forms.
The poems keep a stubborn love of life, even while they mourn.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young weaver is blamed for a blast and flees across the Indian Ocean.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1986 is correct. Hamish Hamilton published the British edition in 1986. It won France's Prix Medicis for a foreign book in 1990, not in 1986.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alu (Nachiketa Bose) (The young weaver who is wrongly accused and must keep moving); Balaram Bose (Alu's uncle, a rationalist obsessed with skulls and cleanliness); Zindi (A woman who shelters Alu while he is on the run)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Main Characters - Balram, Nachiketa Bose.
Alu, an orphan with an oddly large head, goes to live with his uncle Balaram.
Balaram trusts phrenology (reading character from the shape of a skull) and pure reason.
After an explosion, a local officer frames Alu as a terrorist.
Alu flees to a Gulf oil town and then to North Africa.
The book has three parts, Satwa, Rajas, and Tamas, and the chase comes full circle.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel in verse about young friends, love, and loss in 1980s San Francisco.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1986 is correct. Random House in the United States published the first edition. The form follows Charles Johnston's translation of Eugene Onegin. The Sahitya Akademi Award came in 1988.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Brown (A lonely computer professional in San Francisco and the central figure.); Janet Hayakawa (John's sculptor friend, who places a lonely hearts advertisement for him.); Elisabeth Dorati (A trial lawyer, called Liz, who answers the advertisement and loves John.); Phillip Weiss (John's friend, called Phil, who later marries Liz.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The work is a novel in verse composed of 590 Onegin stanzas (sonnets written in iambic tetra meter with the rhyme scheme following abab ccdd effe gg pattern of Eugene Onegin).
It was inspired by Charles Johnston's translation of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin.
It brought Seth, Sahitya Akademi Award in 1988.
Protagonist-John Brown.
Random House published it in 1986.
It has 590 stanzas of 14 lines, in the form of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin.
John Brown, a quiet computer worker, is nudged toward love by his friend Janet Hayakawa.
The lawyer Liz Dorati answers, and they live together until the bond breaks.
Liz later marries John's friend Phil Weiss, and Janet dies in a car crash.
The book won India's Sahitya Akademi Award for English in 1988.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Retired and outlawed heroes uncover a plot while nuclear war threatens an alternate 1985.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The monthly series ran from September 1986 to October 1987. DC collected it as a book in 1987. The film is 2009. Do not use 2009 as the comic's year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rorschach (Walter Kovacs, a masked vigilante who will not compromise); Doctor Manhattan (Jon Osterman, the one hero with real superhuman power); Ozymandias (Adrian Veidt, who kills millions to force the superpowers to unite); Nite Owl (Daniel Dreiberg, a retired hero who returns to the hunt); Silk Spectre (Laurie Juspeczyk, daughter of the Comedian); The Comedian (Edward Blake, a government hero whose murder opens the story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In October 1985, Rorschach finds that the murdered Edward Blake was the Comedian.
He warns Nite Owl, Doctor Manhattan, Silk Spectre, and Ozymandias.
Doctor Manhattan leaves for Mars after a charge that he causes cancer.
Adrian Veidt, once Ozymandias, has already faked an attack on New York.
Most heroes hide the truth to keep peace.
Rorschach refuses and is killed.
His journal may still reach a newspaper.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three childhood friends navigate tyranny, betrayal, and violence in a corrupt military-ruled West African nation.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published by Heinemann in 1987, twenty-one years after A Man of the People. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sam (His Excellency) (A British-trained army officer who becomes an insecure and ruthless military dictator.); Chris Oriko (Commissioner for Information and Sam's old schoolmate who gets murdered while on the run.); Ikem Osodi (Outspoken poet and editor of the National Gazette who is assassinated by security forces.); Beatrice Okoh (A brilliant female civil servant who unites the survivors and embodies moral hope.); Elewa (Ikem's working-class market girlfriend who gives birth to his posthumous daughter.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In the fictional West African state of Kangan, military dictator Sam rules with growing paranoia.
Chris Oriko serves as Commissioner for Information, trying to moderate the regime's brutality.
Ikem Osodi edits the national newspaper and openly publishes fierce editorials against injustice.
Sam suspends Ikem, and government soldiers soon kidnap and murder the fiery editor.
Chris goes into hiding, helps expose the regime's corruption, and flees to the countryside.
A coup topples Sam, but Chris is killed by a rogue policeman during the chaotic aftermath.
Beatrice Okoh gathers surviving women and friends to hold an unconventional naming ceremony for Ikem's baby.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sethe is haunted by the baby she killed to keep her from slavery.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1987 is correct for the novel. Knopf published it on 16 September 1987. Wikipedia says the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction came the next year, 1988. It is the first novel of the loose Beloved trilogy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sethe (A formerly enslaved mother haunted by the child she killed); Beloved (The ghostly young woman who seems to be that dead child); Denver (Sethe's living daughter, who later seeks help from the town); Paul D (A man from Sethe's old plantation who tries to build a new life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After slavery, Sethe lives at 124 Bluestone Road in Cincinnati.
The house is haunted by the baby she lost.
Years earlier, slave catchers came, and Sethe killed that child.
She meant to save her children from a return to slavery.
A young woman called Beloved appears and claims Sethe's love.
The past will not stay buried, and the town finally drives Beloved out.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A modern poet finds papers that suggest Thomas Chatterton faked his death and kept writing.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Hamish Hamilton published it in 1987. The catalog year 1987 is correct. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize. It is a novel about Chatterton, not a biography that settles how he died.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charles Wychwood (A young poet who hunts the Chatterton papers); Thomas Chatterton (The eighteenth century poet and forger whose death the novel reopens); Harriet Scrope (A novelist afraid that her plagiarism will be found)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Charles Wychwood, a poor poet, finds a portrait of an older Chatterton.
History says Chatterton died at seventeen, by arsenic, in poverty.
A manuscript hints that the death was a trick and the poems continued.
The novelist Harriet Scrope fears that her own copying will be exposed.
Research, forgery, and illness mix the eighteenth century with modern London.
The novel shows that each age rebuilds Chatterton for its own use.

items.title: "Modern Indian Poetry in English" (1987) — Bruce King

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A critical history of Indian poetry in English since Independence.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Oxford University Press published the first edition in Delhi and New York in 1987. Persee records a revised edition in 2001. An Oxford India paperback page dates one printing to 2005. The exam year for the first edition is 1987.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King surveys poets, journals, publishers, and readers after 1947.
He discusses poetry circles in cities such as Bombay and Delhi.
He gives chapters to Ezekiel, Ramanujan, Kolatkar, Mahapatra, and others.
Charts at the back list careers, anthologies, awards, and important poems.
A revised edition in 2001 adds later poets, including new women poets.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1987 theory book that separates modernist knowing from postmodern worlds.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Methuen published it in London and New York in 1987. Later reprints came from Routledge. The catalog year 1987 is correct. The database label Fiction is misleading, because the book is theory.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
McHale borrows the idea of the dominant, the feature that organizes a work.
He says the dominant of modernist fiction is epistemological.
Modernist stories ask how we know, and how sure that knowledge is.
He says the dominant of postmodernist fiction is ontological.
Postmodern stories ask which world this is, and how worlds are made.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse satire on greed in the London stock market of the 1980s.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was first staged at the Royal Court in March 1987, directed by Max Stafford-Clark. It then transferred to Wyndham's Theatre. The database calls it fiction, but it is a play. Database year 1987 is the premiere year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: City dealers (Traders whose greed the verse play mocks)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dealers in the City chase fast trades and huge profits.
The play looks at LIFFE, the London futures and options exchange.
Much of the talk is in rhyming couplets (paired rhyming lines).
Ian Dury wrote music for the show.
It opened at the Royal Court in March 1987 and later moved to the West End.

items.title: "The Broom of the System" (1987) — David Foster Wallace

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Lenore Beadsman hunts her missing great grandmother in a strange Cleveland.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1987 is correct. Viking published the finished novel in Wallace's lifetime. The catalogue flags for an unfinished posthumous book belong to The Pale King (2011), which is not this work.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lenore Beadsman (The young switchboard operator who searches for her great grandmother); Lenore Beadsman the elder (The missing great grandmother, once a student of Wittgenstein); Rick Vigorous (Lenore's boss and jealous boyfriend, who tells her stories)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viking published the novel in 1987.
It grew from Wallace's English thesis at Amherst College.
Young Lenore works a switchboard in a 1990 Cleveland.
Her great grandmother, once a student of Wittgenstein, leaves a nursing home.
A talking bird and a jealous boss pull language into the plot.
The catalogue calls this book unfinished and posthumous.
That note fits The Pale King, not this novel.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Early poems about exile, family memory, and a Kashmir that fits on a postcard.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1987 is correct. Wesleyan University Press published the book in 1987. Postcard from Kashmir is the prologue. The line about paper is from the poem Stationery in this book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet-speaker (A Kashmiri voice far from home, holding a postcard and family memories)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens with Postcard from Kashmir, where home shrinks to a small card.
The poet holds the half-inch Himalayas in his hand and calls that card home.
Later poems recall family portraits, Delhi, and the journey to America.
Memory looks bright on the card, but he fears it will blur.
The closing mood is loss, with a wish that someone still write to him.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A later book of parables, alphabets, and sonnets for his dead mother.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1987 is correct. Faber published it. Clearances belongs here, not in Field Work.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (A son remembering his mother and his schooling)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber published The Haw Lantern in 1987.
His mother had died in 1984, and his father in 1986.
Clearances is a set of eight sonnets in her memory.
Alphabets looks back at the move from farm work to school.
The Nobel biographical note places Alphabets in this book.
Many poems are short parables (simple stories with a hard meaning).

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A brother and sister fight over a carved family piano and the land it could buy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: A staged reading came at the O'Neill Center in 1987. Yale Repertory Theatre premiered the play on 26 November 1987. Broadway followed in 1990. The Pulitzer Prize for Drama came in 1990. The database year 1987 is the premiere, not the prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Berniece (The sister who keeps the piano and finally plays it); Boy Willie (The brother who wants to sell the piano and buy land); Doaker Charles (Their uncle, who tells the history of the piano); Maretha (Berniece's daughter, who is learning to play)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1936, Boy Willie comes to Pittsburgh to sell the family piano.
He wants the money to buy Sutter's land, where their people were enslaved.
His sister Berniece refuses, because ancestors are carved into the wood.
Doaker tells how the piano was stolen and how their father died for it.
Berniece plays again, the ghost is faced, and Boy Willie leaves the piano.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A theory book that names historiographic metafiction and explains postmodern art.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1988 is correct. This is criticism, not a poem. The catalog unit for this title is literary criticism, which fits better than poetry.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hutcheon asks what postmodernism means in fiction, history, and theory.
She says many postmodern novels return to the past.
They also show that any story about the past is partial.
She names this double habit historiographic metafiction.
Parody lets a new work use an old form and question it at the same time.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A fierce essay on tourists, corruption, and the colonial past of Antigua.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1988 is correct. Farrar, Straus and Giroux published this essay in 1988. It is not a novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (Kincaid, remembering the Antigua of her childhood); The tourist (The reader, addressed as you)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker talks to you, a tourist arriving in Antigua.
She says tourists enjoy the island and miss its poverty.
She remembers British rule.
Antigua became independent in 1981.
She attacks corrupt leaders and the broken public library.
She says the island is small, beautiful, and marked by slavery.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A future story of Thivai and Abhor in a broken Paris.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1988 is correct. Grove Press in New York and Picador in London both published it in 1988. Acker called it a turning point because the borrowing is quieter.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thivai (A would be pirate who tells part of the story); Abhor (A being who is part human and part machine)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The tale is set in a near future after revolt and disease.
Thivai wants to be a pirate and seeks a drug and a kind of freedom.
Abhor is part human and part machine, and she travels with him.
Algerian fighters take over Paris, and the old order falls apart.
The novel still borrows other books, but the borrowing is less obvious than before.
It reworks bits of Huckleberry Finn and of Neuromancer by William Gibson.

items.title: "English, August: An Indian Story" (1988) — Upamanyu Chatterjee

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young civil servant drifts through a dull year in the small town of Madna.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1988 is correct. Faber and Faber published the novel in 1988. One Wikipedia page says January and the author page says June. The safe exam year is 1988. A film adaptation came in 1994.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Agastya Sen (A young Indian Administrative Service trainee posted to Madna)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Agastya Sen, a city youth, is posted to the district town of Madna.
He is training as an officer, but the work bores him.
His mind stays on books, women, and soft drugs.
The year becomes a comic picture of government life.
He remains an outsider in the town he is meant to serve.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three editors invent a Templar conspiracy and then start to believe the game.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Italian publication is October 1988. English by William Weaver is 1989. Eco rejected the idea that the title points to Michel Foucault. Who is in his place is a question from Karl Popper used in the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Casaubon (The narrator, a researcher who helps invent the Plan); Jacopo Belbo (An editor who is hanged from the pendulum's cable); Diotallevi (The third editor, who links his cancer to the game)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Italian title is Il pendolo di Foucault, published by Bompiani in 1988.
William Weaver's English translation appeared in 1989.
Casaubon, Belbo, and Diotallevi work with occult manuscripts in Milan.
They build a fake master plot called the Plan, using a computer named Abulafia.
Believers kidnap Belbo, and the story ends at the real pendulum in a Paris museum.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about Lee Harvey Oswald and a plot against President Kennedy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1988 is correct for the Viking edition of 15 August 1988. It won the Irish Times International Fiction Prize the next year. It is a novel, not a nonfiction report.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lee Harvey Oswald (The historical gunman, imagined here as a lonely man pulled into a plot); Nicholas Branch (A CIA archivist who cannot finish the secret history); Win Everett (A CIA plotter who helps shape the false attack)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viking published the novel on 15 August 1988.
One thread follows Oswald from boyhood to Dallas in 1963.
Another thread follows CIA men who want a false attack blamed on Cuba.
Nicholas Branch, a later CIA archivist, tries to sort the records.
The plot grows beyond a staged miss and moves toward murder.
DeLillo says the book does not give factual answers about the killing.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A neglected wife finds love with a cobra that visits her in her husband's shape.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1988 matches the play. During Karnad's Chicago visit of 1987-88, the first performance used his English text at the Guthrie Theater in Minneapolis. Oxford University Press published the English book Naga Mandala, Play with Cobra, in 1990. The database marks the work as a translation, which fits the English text.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rani (The young wife who is locked in and later tested by the village); Appanna (Rani's husband, cold by day and absent by night); Naga (A cobra who takes Appanna's form and becomes Rani's lover); Kurudavva (A blind woman who gives Rani the love root); Kappanna (Kurudavva's son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
6. Flowers (2012). Short Play.
Rani is a young bride whose husband Appanna locks her in the house.
He spends his nights with another woman and ignores Rani.
A love root meant for Appanna is poured out and reaches a king cobra.
The cobra, called Naga, visits Rani in the shape of Appanna and loves her.
She becomes pregnant, and the village orders a snake ordeal (a dangerous truth test).
She holds the cobra and lives, so the village treats her as innocent.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Shona girl fights for school while family power and colonial rule strain the women around her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1988 is correct. The Women's Press in London published it. It won the Commonwealth Writers Prize for the Africa region in 1989. It is often called the first English novel published by a Black woman from Zimbabwe.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tambudzai Sigauke (The narrator, a Shona girl who hungers for school. She is called Tambu.); Nhamo (Tambu's brother. His death opens the mission school place for her.); Babamukuru (Tambu's educated uncle and the strict head of the extended family.); Nyasha (Babamukuru's daughter. English life and her father's control make her ill.); Maiguru (Babamukuru's educated wife, who still has little power at home.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Women's Press in London published the novel in 1988.
Tambudzai, called Tambu, tells the story in her own voice.
She is not sorry when her brother Nhamo dies, because his school place can pass to her.
Her uncle Babamukuru, a mission headmaster, pays for that schooling.
She grows close to her cousin Nyasha, who has lived in England and later breaks down.
Tambu learns that success in an English school can also wound a girl.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two men fall from a blown up plane and live through angelic, devilish, and dream stories.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1988 is correct for publication. The book was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 1988. The fatwa was issued in February 1989, not in 1988.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gibreel Farishta (A film star who survives the fall and is linked with visions); Saladin Chamcha (A voice actor who survives and is transformed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is the most controversial work of Rushdie. Inspired in a part by the life of Muhammad.
The title refers to Satanic Verses, a group of Quranic Verses, that allow intercessory prayers to be made to three Pagan Meccan goddesses: Allal, Uzza and Menat.
The part of the story that deals with Satanic Verses, was based on accounts from the historians "al Waqdi and al Taberi".
Harold Bloom named it Rushdie's largest aesthetic achievement.
A jet bound for London is blown apart over the sea.
Gibreel Farishta and Saladin Chamcha fall and survive.
One man takes on an angelic glow, and the other grows devilish.
Dream chapters tell stories about a prophet and a city of faith.
Many Muslims called the book an insult.
India banned its import.
In February 1989 a fatwa (a religious death order) called for Rushdie to be killed.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A family story shows how borders, memory, and riots cross Calcutta, Dhaka, and London.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1988 is correct for the Ravi Dayal first edition. An Oxford study edition with essays came in 1995. The Sahitya Akademi Award was given in 1989.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A Calcutta boy who later studies the past through other people's memories); Tridib (The narrator's storytelling cousin, killed in a Dhaka riot); Thamma (The strict grandmother who crosses to Dhaka for her uncle); Ila (The narrator's London cousin, whom he loves without success); May Price (The English woman Tridib loves)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Got Sahitya Akademi Award for it. (it is in 2 parts - Going Away & Coming Home; Protagonist Tridip).
An unnamed boy in Calcutta grows up on stories told by his cousin Tridib.
His grandmother, Thamma, wants to bring her old uncle home from Dhaka.
The family is tied to the Price family in London, including May and Nick.
In the riots of 1964, Tridib is killed in Dhaka while trying to help May.
The narrator later learns that maps cannot hold the lines people live by.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Travel essays on how American films, music, and goods show up across Asia in the 1980s.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1988 is correct for the first Knopf edition in July 1988. A British Black Swan edition followed in 1989. The database translation flag is wrong. Iyer wrote the book in English.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pico Iyer (The traveller and essayist who reports what he sees)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Knopf in New York published the book in July 1988.
The full title adds And Other Reports from the Not So Far East.
Iyer travels through Asian cities and watches local life remix American pop culture.
Videos, Hollywood heroes, and fast food appear far from the United States.
He writes as an outsider who is also at home in several cultures.
The book is reportage (eyewitness prose), not a novel and not a translation.

items.title: "Women in Dutch Painting" (1988) — Eunice de Souza

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her second book of poems, on quiet women and the lives hidden under a calm surface.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1988 is correct. Women in Dutch Painting is her second collection, after Fix (1979) and before Ways of Belonging (1990).

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Speaker (A woman looking at painted wives and at real wives who look just as still); The Painted Women (Figures who look calm and pregnant while their choices stay very small)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book was published in 1988.
The title poem looks at women who seem calm in old Dutch paintings.
Those painted women are also like wives running neat Indian homes.
They do not answer their husbands, and they do not seek public fame.
Bovine means like a cow, dull and passive.
She refuses that picture of women.

items.title: "“Can the Subaltern Speak?”" (1988) — Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An essay asking if the poorest colonized people can be heard.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: An earlier version, with the subtitle Speculations on Widow Sacrifice, appeared in the journal Wedge in 1985. The standard citation is the 1988 chapter. A revised text is inside A Critique of Postcolonial Reason (1999). The database year 1988 is the standard date.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Spivak takes subaltern from Antonio Gramsci, then turns it toward colonial India.
She says Western thinkers often keep Europe as the subject who knows.
Scholars who claim to let the oppressed speak may still speak for them.
She studies sati (a widow's death on her husband's pyre) and British colonial law.
Her hard conclusion is that the subaltern cannot speak inside these elite frames.

items.title: "A History of the World in 10½ Chapters" (1989) — Julian Barnes

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: A History of the World in 10½ Chapters

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Linked pieces that retell history through ships, wrecks, and doubt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Jonathan Cape published the British book in 1989. Alfred A. Knopf published the American book in October 1989. The half chapter is an essay on love. The catalog slug drops the half, but the title keeps it.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The woodworm narrator (A stowaway on Noah's Ark who questions the official flood story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is a collection of short stories in different styles in 10 chapters.
A woodworm tells the story of Noah's Ark from the side.
Later pieces include a hijacked ship and a trial of woodworms.
One chapter studies Gericault's painting The Raft of the Medusa.
A half chapter, called Parenthesis, is an essay on love.
Ships, survival, and the telling of history link the parts.
The book refuses any single story of the world.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Bronx teenager joins the real gangster Dutch Schultz and learns the cost of that glamour.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1989 is correct. Random House published the novel in 1989. It won the 1990 PEN Faulkner Award and was a Pulitzer runner up.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Billy Bathgate (The narrator, a Bronx boy who joins the gang and whose last name is borrowed from a street); Dutch Schultz (The real New York gangster who leads the crew); Drew Preston (A rich socialite who becomes Schultz's companion and Billy's lover); Otto Berman (Schultz's accountant, who brings Billy into the gang); Bo Weinberg (Schultz's lieutenant, killed for a suspected betrayal)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Billy is a poor boy of fifteen in the Bronx.
Dutch Schultz, a real gangster, takes him in after seeing him juggle.
Billy watches the murder of Bo Weinberg and grows close to Drew Preston.
He helps Drew escape when Schultz wants her killed.
After gunmen shoot the gang, Billy finds the clue to Schultz's hidden money.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A family play about a male Bharatanatyam dancer and strict rules of manhood.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The catalog date 1989 is the first staging, at the Deccan Herald Theatre Festival in Bangalore. Printed collection dates come later. Do not use a film year for the play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jairaj (A Bharatanatyam dancer whose father tries to stop his career); Ratna (Jairaj's wife, an ambitious dancer and Lata's teacher); Amritlal (Jairaj's father, who sees a male dancer as unmanly); Lata (Their daughter, a young dancer preparing for a performance); Viswas (Lata's fiance, who watches the family history unfold)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In the present, Jairaj and Ratna prepare their daughter Lata for the stage.
Lata's fiance Viswas hears old family quarrels come back.
In the past, Jairaj's father Amritlal calls a male dancer unmanly.
Amritlal uses Ratna's wish for fame to weaken Jairaj.
Ratna gives their baby too much opium so she can practise, and the baby dies.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The weak Night Watch must stop a summoned dragon that has made itself king.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Victor Gollancz published it in London in 1989. The US edition from Roc came later, in 1991. The database year 1989 matches the British first edition. It is a novel, not a poem. BBC Radio 4 broadcast a six-part adaptation from 23 November to 28 December 1992.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Samuel Vimes (Captain of the Night Watch, cynical, drunk at the start, and stubborn about the law); Carrot Ironfoundersson (A tall new recruit raised by dwarfs, honest to the point of taking words literally); Sybil Ramkin (A noblewoman who breeds small swamp dragons and later stands with Vimes); Havelock Vetinari (The Patrician, the cool ruler whom the dragon plot removes and then restores)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A secret brotherhood summons a huge dragon to overthrow the Patrician of Ankh-Morpork.
Captain Samuel Vimes leads a scorned Night Watch: Carrot, Colon, and Nobby.
Carrot is a human raised by dwarfs, and he believes the law should be obeyed literally.
Lady Sybil Ramkin, who breeds swamp dragons, gives the Watch a small dragon named Errol.
Errol drives off the great dragon.
Vimes tells Carrot to throw the book at the plotter, and Carrot does it literally.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Orphan Marco Fogg survives New York, then learns the hidden story of his father and grandfather.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1989 is correct. Viking Press, New York, published it in February 1989.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Marco Stanley Fogg (The narrator, an orphan searching for his family); Kitty Wu (The woman who rescues Marco and becomes his lover); Thomas Effing (A blind old man, once the painter Julian Barber); Solomon Barber (Marco's father, and Effing's son); Uncle Victor (The uncle who raised Marco and left him books)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viking published the novel in February 1989, in the shadow of the moon landing summer.
Marco Stanley Fogg is an orphan whose uncle Victor has died.
He becomes homeless in Central Park until Kitty Wu saves him.
He reads to a blind old man, Thomas Effing, once the painter Julian Barber.
Effing's life in the American desert hides Marco's grandfather.
Solomon Barber, Marco's unknown father, completes the three generation puzzle.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her first poetry book looks at the veil, shame, and life between worlds.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1989 matches the poet's own list and South Asian Britain: Oxford University Press, 1989. The Open British National Bibliography lists an edition in 1988. The poems were written in English. A database translation tag is wrong.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Purdah is the curtain or veil that limits how a woman is seen.
The poems show girls being taught shame and silence.
They also show movement between countries and faiths.
The poet's own drawings appear with the poems.
This was her first collection, from Oxford University Press.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Mahabharata is retold as the political history of modern India.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1989 is correct. Wikipedia and Tharoor's site date the Viking Press edition to 24 August 1989. The title puns on Mahabharata, the great tale of India, and on the idea of a great national novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ved Vyas (The aged narrator who dictates this comic history); Ganapathi (The scribe who writes down Ved Vyas's words); Gangaji (The Gandhi figure, a leader of vows, fasts, and protest); Dhritarashtra (The Nehru figure, who becomes prime minister); Priya Duryodhani (The Indira Gandhi figure, daughter of the prime minister's house); Mohammed Ali Karna (The Jinnah figure, leader of the demand for Karnistan)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The old narrator Ved Vyas dictates the book to a scribe, Ganapathi.
The novel has 18 books, like the 18 books of the epic.
Gangaji, the Gandhi figure, fasts, marches, and is killed.
Dhritarashtra, the Nehru figure, becomes prime minister.
Pandu, the Bose figure, fights the British and dies in a plane.
Priya Duryodhani, the Indira figure, gathers power after them.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short theory book on the politics of postmodern images, stories, and parody.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1989 is correct for the first edition. A later reprint is 2002. The catalog genre Poetry is wrong. This is literary theory.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hutcheon asks whether postmodern art can still make a political point.
She studies fiction, photography, and popular images.
She says postmodern works install an old form and also ironize it.
Parody can support what it copies and undercut it in the same move.
She argues that this habit can reopen history instead of emptying it.

items.title: "The Remains of the Day" (1989) — Kazuo Ishiguro

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Butler Stevens drives west and sees the life he gave to Lord Darlington.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1989 is correct. Faber published the UK edition in May 1989. Knopf published the US edition on 4 October 1989. The film is 1993.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Stevens (The butler and narrator, loyal to a fault); Miss Kenton (The housekeeper, later Mrs Benn); Lord Darlington (The former owner, ruined by his politics); Mr Farraday (The American who now owns the hall)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1956 Stevens, butler at Darlington Hall, motors toward Cornwall.
He hopes the former housekeeper, Miss Kenton, may return.
On the road he recalls the 1920s and 1930s under Lord Darlington.
Darlington tried to appease Germany and once dismissed Jewish maids.
Stevens chose dignity over love and over his own judgment.
Miss Kenton, now Mrs Benn, will not come back.
The novel won the 1989 Booker Prize.

items.title: "A Million Mutinies Now" (1990) — V. S. Naipaul

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The last India book listens to many voices in a country that is changing.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1990 is correct. London: Heinemann. It is English travel writing, not a translation, and it closes the India trilogy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: V.S. Naipaul (The traveller who records many Indian speakers)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This is the third and last book of the India trilogy.
Heinemann published it in 1990.
It is a travelogue (a journey book) built from talks with many people.
Naipaul still doubts many Indian habits.
He also sees economic change and people claiming a share of power.
The title links those claims with the Mutiny of 1857. The tone is more hopeful.

items.title: "All You Who Sleep Tonight" (1990) — Vikram Seth

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1990 poetry book on love, travel, history, and quiet shared grief.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1990 is correct for the first edition. Faber published it in London and Knopf in New York that year. Vintage issued a paperback on 18 June 1991. Some catalogue boxes show only that 1991 paperback. The database calls the book fiction, but it is poetry.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber in London and Alfred A. Knopf in New York published it in 1990.
The poems fall into groups: love, other voices, places, quatrains, and meditations.
A quatrain is a stanza of four lines.
One voice is a doctor in Hiroshima on the day of the atomic bomb.
The title poem stands last and tells the lonely sleeper that others grieve too.
A Vintage paperback in 1991 is a later printing, not the first edition.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young West Indian woman works as an au pair and fights to become herself.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1990 is correct. Farrar, Straus and Giroux published the book in September 1990.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lucy Josephine Potter (The young narrator and au pair); Mariah (Lucy's employer, a wealthy American mother); Lewis (Mariah's unfaithful husband); Peggy (The friend Lucy later lives with)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lucy leaves the West Indies to work as an au pair in America.
She cares for the children of Mariah and Lewis.
Mariah is kind, but Lucy feels ruled, as she did by her mother.
She will not open her mother's letters.
Then her father dies.
She moves out, begins to take photographs, and still feels alone.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A son tells how his father's affair and the struggle tear the family.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1990 is correct. It was written near the end of the State of Emergency. The Nobel press release of 1991 discusses it.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Will (Sonny's son and one of the narrators); Sonny (A Coloured teacher who becomes an activist and takes a lover); Aila (Sonny's wife, later charged as a courier for the movement)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sonny is a schoolteacher classed as Coloured under apartheid law.
He is drawn into the fight against white rule.
He begins an affair with a white woman he can talk to.
His son Will finds out and tells part of the story.
Sonny's wife Aila is charged with hiding weapons.
She leaves the country.
The family house is later burned.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Caribbean epic that retells Homeric rivalry among island fishermen.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1990 is correct. Farrar, Straus and Giroux published the poem in 1990. It won the WH Smith Literary Award in 1991. The Nobel Prize followed in 1992.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Achille (A Saint Lucian fisherman, one rival for Helen); Hector (A fisherman who leaves the sea and becomes a taxi driver); Helen (A housemaid, and also a figure for Saint Lucia, once called Helen of the West Indies); Major Plunkett and Maud (A retired English officer and his wife living on the island); Seven Seas (A blind man who stands for Homer); Philoctete (A wounded fisherman, named from Homer's injured hero)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Fishermen Achille and Hector quarrel over Helen, a housemaid.
Major Plunkett and his wife Maud face the British past of the island.
Achille dreams a voyage back through the slave ship toward Africa.
The blind man Seven Seas stands for Homer, and the poet also enters the story.
The poem moves among Saint Lucia, Brookline, and cities of Walcott's travels.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two modern scholars uncover a secret Victorian romance and fall in love themselves.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1990 is correct. Chatto and Windus published it in 1990, and it won that year's Booker Prize. A film followed in 2002.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Roland Michell (A poor modern scholar who steals the draft letters and starts the hunt); Maud Bailey (A LaMotte scholar who learns she descends from the hidden child); Randolph Henry Ash (A famous Victorian poet, partly drawn from Browning and Tennyson); Christabel LaMotte (A woman poet, partly drawn from Christina Rossetti)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Roland Michell finds draft letters by the poet Randolph Henry Ash in a library.
The trail leads to Christabel LaMotte, a woman poet of the same age.
He joins Maud Bailey, a scholar and a distant relative of LaMotte.
Letters show a brief affair, a hidden child, and a companion's death.
In the great storm of 1987 they open a grave and misread a lock of hair.
An epilogue shows that the hair came from the child, not from LaMotte.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A play about conjoined twins separated by surgery that favors the boy.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Written and first staged in Bangalore in 1990 as Twinkle Tara. Alyque Padamsee staged it in Mumbai in 1991 as Tara. The catalog year 1990 matches the first staging.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tara (The girl twin, bright and disabled after the separation surgery); Chandan (Dan) (Tara's twin, who later writes the play from a room in London); Bharati (Their mother, who chose the boy in the surgery and is consumed by guilt); Patel (Their father, who finally tells the twins the truth about the operation); Doctor Thakkar (The surgeon who separated the twins and sits above the action)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Main characters are Tara and Chandan.
The story of the play is about the twins Tara and Chandan, they are born as joint twins with three legs and blood supply to third leg is from the baby girl's body.
Only one of the twins could have two legs and other have to survive with only one leg.
It is decided to fix the third leg on the male baby's body so as to complete male baby. This decision was taken on the ground of gender discrimination in our society.
The Siamese twins Tara and Chandan had to go through surgical operation to get separated.
Against the wish of doctor the third leg was separated with Chandan but it goes rotten with the passage of time as there was no blood supply in it.
Ultimately both the child becomes freaks. 4. Dance Like a Man.
Patriarchy has been brought out effectively in this novel.
Jairaj and Ratna are the main characters and they come under the pressure of patriarchy.
Jairaj wanted to pursue his career as a Bharatnatyam dancer but his father Amrital Parekh's autocracy doesn't allow him to be dancer. 5. Bravely Fought the Queen.
This play revolves around Trivedi family which consists of Jiten, Baa, Nitin Trivedi, Dolly and Alka.
The play depicts the exploitation of women in the family and home confined identity.
Indian society considers women as uncivilized, rude and ill-mannered needing to be polished.
Violence is the tool that is used for the socialization of women.
Dolly suffers in the hand of her mother in law who provokes her son to beat her.
Jiten and Nitin gratify their sexual desire with market girls.
The issue of homosexuality is also depicted in the play as Nitin has homosexual relationship with Praful.
At the end of the play Alka and Dolly both rebels against the male dominance and their husbands realize their mistakes.
'Bonsai' in the play symbolizes the limited freedom to women. 6. On a Muggy Night in Mumbai.
The play is full of lesbian and homo sexual relationships. 7. Thirty days in September.
The story revolves around Mala and Shanta and the play reveals the betrayal in blood relationship.
Mala, is sexually abused by her maternal uncle at the age of six. She suffers continuous molestation sexually which leads her to the arms of any man who she comes into contact with.
Ultimately she fights against this exploitation with the help of Deepak with whom she was to marry.
She also came to know that her mother Shanta was also suffering from the same exploitation by her brother, but she never dared to reveal the truth because Indian society does not permit such relationships. 8. Seven Steps Around the Fire Protagonist - Uma.
Chandan, now called Dan, tries to write a play about his dead twin Tara.
As children, Tara and Chandan shared three legs.
The family and Doctor Thakkar gave the better chance of two legs to the boy.
Tara is left disabled, and she later dies.
Dan writes in London to face his guilt and his mother's choice.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Karim Amir, a mixed race teenager, leaves a London suburb to chase acting and a new self.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Faber and Faber published the novel in 1990. It won the Whitbread Award (a British book prize) for the best first novel. The BBC made a four part series in 1993.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Karim Amir (The mixed race narrator who wants to become an actor); Haroon Amir (Karim's Indian father, called a Buddha by London society); Eva (A woman chasing a higher place in London society); Eleanor (Karim's richer lover from the theatre world)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Karim lives in a south London suburb with an Indian father and an English mother.
London friends call Haroon a guru (a spiritual guide), the Buddha of the suburb.
Karim follows love, pop music, and theatre into the city.
In plays, he is pushed to perform a narrow Indian type.
He goes to New York, then returns as Britain nears the 1979 election.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Hill District diner faces demolition while its regulars ask for a fair price.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Yale Repertory Theatre premiered it on 27 March 1990. Broadway opened at the Walter Kerr Theatre on 13 April 1992. It was a Pulitzer finalist in 1992 and did not win. The database year 1990 is the premiere.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Memphis Lee (The owner who demands his price before the city takes the diner); Risa (The waitress, the only woman in the play); Sterling (A young man newly out of prison who wants the rally); Hambone (A man who repeats his demand for a promised ham); Holloway (An older regular who explains the neighbourhood's history)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1969, Memphis Lee's restaurant is marked for city demolition.
He fights to be paid what he thinks the building is worth.
Risa, Sterling, Holloway, Wolf, West, and Hambone use the room as a meeting place.
Sterling, just out of prison, pushes a rally for racial justice.
Hambone still wants the ham he was promised years ago.

items.title: "A Strange and Sublime Address" (1991) — Amit Chaudhuri

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A ten year old boy from Bombay spends holidays in his uncle's Calcutta house.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1991 is correct. The Spectator reviewed the Heinemann edition on 18 May 1991 and called it that year's Betty Trask winner. Wikipedia also lists a Penguin edition in 1991. Keep 1991 as the first year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sandeep (A ten year old boy from Bombay who watches Calcutta closely); Sandeep's mother (She travels with him from Bombay to her relatives); The uncle (The Calcutta relative whose rambling house holds the visit); Abhi (Sandeep's cousin in the Calcutta house)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Sandeep lives in a Bombay high rise with his parents.
In summer he travels to Calcutta with his mother.
He stays with his aunt, his uncle, and his cousin Abhi.
Heat, rain, meals, and family visits fill the days.
The family returns in winter and meets a harder turn.
Sandeep learns that wonder can sit inside ordinary life.

items.title: "Angels in America: Millennium Approaches" (1992) — Tony Kushner

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In Reagan-era New York, Prior Walter has AIDS, his lover leaves, and an angel calls him a prophet.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Eureka Theatre in San Francisco premiered it in May 1991, directed by David Esbjornson. A workshop of material had been seen in Los Angeles in May 1990. That workshop is not the premiere. London opened on 23 January 1992. Broadway opened on 4 May 1993. The Pulitzer Prize for Drama, 1993, is for this part. The database year 1991 matches the San Francisco premiere.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prior Walter (A gay man with AIDS who is visited by ancestors and then by an angel); Louis Ironson (Prior's lover, who cannot bear the illness and leaves); Roy Cohn (A powerful closeted lawyer, based on the historical Roy Cohn, who denies he has AIDS); Joe Pitt (A Mormon Republican clerk who is hiding that he is gay); Harper Pitt (Joe's anxious wife, lost in Valium visions); The Angel (A messenger who names Prior a prophet at the end of this part)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Louis Ironson abandons his lover Prior Walter as Prior's AIDS gets worse.
Joe Pitt, a closeted Mormon lawyer, is pulled toward Roy Cohn and toward Louis.
Joe's wife Harper flees into pills and visions, and she meets Prior inside a dream.
Roy Cohn is dying of AIDS but tells the world he has liver cancer.
An angel crashes through Prior's ceiling and says the Great Work has begun.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1991 novel about slavery on a Caribbean plantation, told in clashing voices.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Bloomsbury published it in Britain in 1991. Knopf published the American edition in 1992. The catalog year 1991 matches the British first edition. It is a novel, not poetry.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Emily Cartwright (An Englishwoman sent to report on her father's Caribbean estate); Cambridge (An enslaved man, once called David Henderson, who tells his own life); Arnold Brown (The plantation overseer, also called Mr Brown); Christiana (An enslaved woman whose story changes with each narrator)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The tale sits between the end of the slave trade and the freeing of the enslaved.
Emily Cartwright comes from England to see her father's estate.
She meets the overseer Brown and an enslaved man called Cambridge.
Cambridge tells how he was taken from Africa and later enslaved again.
The voices clash about a death, so the reader cannot trust one story.

items.title: "Changes: A Love Story" (1991) — Ama Ata Aidoo

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A career woman in Accra leaves her husband and becomes a second wife, then loses that freedom too.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1991 is the London Women's Press first edition. The New York Feminist Press edition is 1993. The Commonwealth Writers' Prize for Best Book (Africa) came in 1992, so the book was already out.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Esi Sekyi (A highly educated career woman who wants space inside love); Oko Sekyi (Esi's first husband, a school headmaster); Ali Kondey (A charming travel agent who takes Esi as a second wife); Fusena Kondey (Ali's first wife, who gave up study for marriage); Opokuya Dakwa (Esi's friend, a nurse who stays inside her own marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Esi Sekyi works as a data analyst in Accra and neglects her marriage.
Her husband Oko forces sex on her.
She calls it marital rape.
She divorces Oko and falls in love with Ali Kondey.
Ali already has a wife, Fusena.
Esi agrees to be the second wife.
She hopes polygamy (marriage to more than one wife) will leave her free.
Ali drifts away.
Gifts replace his presence.
They do not divorce.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A book length poem from 1991 that drifts through memory, talk, and art.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1991 is correct. The Academy of American Poets and the Flow Chart Foundation both give 1991.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Knopf published Flow Chart in 1991.
It is one long poem, not a set of separate short poems.
The lines wander, as talk wanders in a long conversation.
Memory, daily speech, and other poems enter and leave.
It is much later than Self-Portrait, so do not date it 1975.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A prose selection of oral tales from many languages of India.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1991 is correct. It is a selection of oral tales. Sources differ on whether the subtitle says twenty languages or twenty two. The safe exam point is 1991 and many Indian languages.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Many village tellers (The oral sources behind tales of animals, fools, gods, and families)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book was published in 1991.
Ramanujan selected and retold oral tales, not one continuous story.
The tales come from many regions and many Indian languages.
His notes show how oral tales and written classics echo each other.
This is scholarship and storytelling together.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three young friends in the desert quit dull jobs and tell modern tales.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1991 is correct. St. Martin's Press published the book in March 1991. The phrase Generation X was used before Coupland, but this novel made it a common label.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
