fields.value: Andy (The narrator, one of the three friends who left ordinary careers); Dag (A friend from Toronto who quits a job and comes to the desert); Claire (The third friend, who shares the storytelling)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
St. Martin's Press published the book in 1991.
The subtitle is Tales for an Accelerated Culture.
Andy, Dag, and Claire live near Palm Springs.
They work McJobs (low pay service jobs with no future).
They tell each other strange stories about love, death, and malls.
Page margins add comic definitions, including the word McJob.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A hidden novelist meets crowds, news images, and a hostage crisis.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1991 is correct for publication. The PEN Faulkner Award came in 1992. Do not swap those two years.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bill Gray (A reclusive novelist who leaves hiding and travels toward danger); Karen (A young woman married in the mass wedding at the start)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viking published the novel in 1991.
It opens at a mass wedding in Yankee Stadium.
Bill Gray is a famous novelist who hides from the public.
He is drawn toward a writer held hostage in Lebanon.
The title comes from Andy Warhol's screen prints of Mao.
The book won the PEN Faulkner Award in 1992.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Vladek's story continues through Auschwitz and the road home, while Art faces fame and guilt.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Maus II itself was published by Pantheon in 1991. The Complete Maus, both volumes in one book, was published on 19 November 1996. Do not answer 1996 as the first year of Maus II. The special Pulitzer, for the finished work, came in 1992.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Art Spiegelman (The cartoonist, now guilty about the success of the first volume); Vladek Spiegelman (The father, whose camp story fills the book and who dies before it is done); Anja Spiegelman (The mother, separated in the camps and reunited after the war); Francoise Mouly (Art's wife, drawn as a mouse after she converts to Judaism); Mala Spiegelman (Vladek's second wife, also a survivor)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The second book opens inside the camps.
Vladek survives hunger, selections, and the long march by wit and luck.
He and Anja find each other after liberation.
Art, now known for the first book, talks with a survivor psychiatrist.
Vladek grows tired and calls Art by the dead brother's name.
Vladek died in 1982. The book ends at the parents' grave.

items.title: "Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra" (1991) — Ruskin Bond

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A story collection of childhood memories from Dehra, its people, and its trees.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1991 is correct for the book. Encyclopedia.com lists Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra in 1991. Wikipedia records the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1992 for this collection. The award year is not the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A boy much like the young Bond, remembering Dehra)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The pieces look back at Bond's early years in Dehra.
Trees, houses, and people from that time fill the book.
The tone is memory, not a single adventure plot.
Penguin published the collection in 1991.
It won the Sahitya Akademi Award for English in 1992.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Gustad Noble, a Parsi bank clerk in Bombay, is pulled into a secret money plot during the 1971 war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1991 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published it in 1991. It won the Governor General's Award and the Commonwealth Writers Prize, and it was a Booker shortlist.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gustad Noble (A Parsi bank clerk trying to hold his family together); Dilnavaz Noble (Gustad's wife); Sohrab Noble (The elder son who refuses the IIT place); Jimmy Bilimoria (Gustad's old friend, whose letter pulls him into a secret plot); Tehmul (A disabled neighbour who shows Gustad's kinder side)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The year is 1971, during the war that led to Bangladesh.
Gustad Noble wants a decent life for his wife Dilnavaz and their children.
His son Sohrab refuses a place at the Indian Institute of Technology.
His daughter Roshan falls ill, and the household grows anxious.
An old friend, Major Jimmy Bilimoria, draws Gustad into a secret transfer of money.
The wall outside his building and the neighbour Tehmul keep the public world close.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Azaro, a spirit child, chooses to stay in a hard living world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1991 is correct. Jonathan Cape published The Famished Road in 1991. It won the Booker Prize that year. The database file lists this novel under drama. That label is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Azaro (The spirit child who chooses the living world and tells the story); Mum (Azaro's mother, who loves him and gives him his short name); Dad (Azaro's father, a labourer and boxer called Black Tyger in the story)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens on a river that becomes a road and stays hungry.
Azaro is an abiku, a child who can die and return to the spirits.
This time he chooses to stay, and his mother shortens Lazaro to Azaro.
The family lives poor in a Nigerian city around the time of independence.
His father boxes and fights, while spirits keep calling the boy back.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1991 selected poems book, mixing older hits with new political poems.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1991 is right for this Bloodaxe selected poems book. Many famous poems inside it first appeared in the 1975 and 1980 books. The author's page dates the Bloodaxe book to 5 December 1991.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet-speaker (Johnson's public voice, commenting on Black Britain and world politics)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Bloodaxe Books published Tings an' Times in 1991.
It reprints work from his 1974, 1975, and 1980 books.
It also adds poems about racism, riots, and police oppression.
New Cross Massahkah recalls the 1981 New Cross fire.
Mi Revalueshanary Fren answers the fall of hard-line rule in Eastern Europe.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Twin chorus girls tell the messy stage history of the Hazard family.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chatto and Windus published it in 1991. It was her last novel. She already knew she had lung cancer. The database year 1991 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dora Chance (The narrator, a seventy five year old chorus twin); Nora Chance (Dora's twin and partner on the stage); Melchior Hazard (A famous Shakespeare actor who long denies the twins); Peregrine Hazard (Melchior's twin, the loving uncle who may be more than an uncle); Grandma Chance (The guardian who raises Dora and Nora)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Dora and Nora Chance turn seventy five on the same day.
That day is also the hundredth birthday of Melchior Hazard, the actor.
Dora looks back at music hall, Hollywood, and a failed Dream film.
Melchior at last owns the twins as his daughters.
Peregrine returns alive, and the twins are given two babies to raise.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: John Grady Cole rides into Mexico, loves Alejandra, and loses the old ranch world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Knopf published it in May 1992. It won the National Book Award and the National Book Critics Circle Award. The Crossing (1994) and Cities of the Plain (1998) complete the trilogy. Database year 1992 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: John Grady Cole (A sixteen-year-old Texan who lives for horses); Lacey Rawlins (John Grady's friend on the ride into Mexico); Alejandra (Daughter of the ranch owner, who loves John Grady and then refuses him); Jimmy Blevins (A young runaway who is executed by the police)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1949, John Grady leaves Texas after his grandfather's ranch is to be sold.
He and Lacey Rawlins ride south and meet the runaway Jimmy Blevins.
On a Mexican ranch he trains horses and falls in love with Alejandra.
The police kill Blevins, and the friends are jailed until her aunt frees them.
Alejandra refuses him, and John Grady returns toward Texas with the horses.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two Victorian novellas, one about a naturalist in a great house and one titled The Conjugial Angel.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1992 is correct. Chatto and Windus published the pair in 1992. The film Angels and Insects (1995) adapts Morpho Eugenia only.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: William Adamson (A naturalist who loses his Amazon collections and depends on a patron); Eugenia Alabaster (Sir Harold's daughter, whom William marries); Matty Crompton (The sharp governess who studies insects with William and leaves with him); Edgar Alabaster (Eugenia's brother, and the father of the children William thought were his)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book holds two novellas (short novels), Morpho Eugenia and The Conjugial Angel.
In Morpho Eugenia, William Adamson returns poor from the Amazon.
He marries Eugenia, daughter of his rich host Sir Harold Alabaster.
With Matty Crompton he studies ants and publishes a book.
He learns that Eugenia's children are her brother Edgar's, and he leaves with Matty.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1992 theory book that treats postmodernism as something critics build.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Routledge published it in London and New York in 1992. The catalog year 1992 is correct. The database genre label Poetry is wrong. This is a theory book.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
McHale says postmodernism is not a found object.
He calls it a manufactured artifact, made by readers and critics.
He offers several overlapping accounts, not one fixed list of features.
He reads novels by Thomas Pynchon, Umberto Eco, James Joyce, and others.
He also links those novels to television, film, and cyberpunk.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ghosh joins his stay in Egyptian villages to the trail of a twelfth century merchant and his Indian slave.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1992 is correct. Ravi Dayal published it in India. This book is nonfiction, though some lists file it with his novels.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Amitav Ghosh (The narrator, a student of anthropology in Egypt); Abraham Ben Yiju (A twelfth century Jewish merchant reconstructed from old letters); Bomma (Ben Yiju's Indian slave, later his agent)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
As a student, Ghosh lives in the Nile villages of Lataifa and Nashawy.
He is hunting a twelfth century Jewish merchant, Abraham Ben Yiju.
Ben Yiju's letters survived in the Cairo Geniza, a store of old papers.
Ghosh traces Ben Yiju's Indian slave, whom he comes to call Bomma.
The modern village story and the medieval trade story run side by side.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In 1920s Harlem, Joe Trace kills young Dorcas, and Violet answers with a knife.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1992 is correct. Knopf published the novel in 1992. Wikipedia gives 21 April 1992. It is the second book of the Beloved trilogy, before Paradise in 1997. The Nobel Prize came a year later, in 1993.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Joe Trace (A travelling cosmetics seller who kills Dorcas); Violet Trace (Joe's wife, nicknamed Violent after the funeral); Dorcas (Joe's young lover, shot at a party); Alice Manfred (Dorcas's aunt, who later talks with Violet)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens on Joe and Violet Trace in Harlem.
Joe, a cosmetics seller, shoots his young lover Dorcas at a party.
At the funeral, Violet cuts the dead girl's face.
The narrator circles back through their Southern childhoods.
Violet later seeks out Dorcas's aunt, and a hard friendship starts.
The telling imitates jazz, with repeats, solos, and changed memories.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Peter Aaron reconstructs how his friend Benjamin Sachs became a bomber called the Phantom of Liberty.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1992 is correct for publication. The database unit label Non Fictional Prose is a catalog error. Leviathan is a novel from Viking Press. Do not confuse it with Hobbes's Leviathan of 1651.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Peter Aaron (The narrator, a writer telling his friend's story); Benjamin Sachs (A novelist who becomes the bomber called the Phantom of Liberty); Fanny (Sachs's wife); Maria Turner (An artist whose projects pull the friends into danger)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Viking published this novel in 1992. It is fiction, not a political essay.
The title recalls the Bible and Thomas Hobbes, but the book is Auster's story.
Benjamin Sachs dies when a bomb he is building explodes.
His friend Peter Aaron writes the book to explain Sachs before the police do.
After a killing on a lonely road, Sachs takes another man's money and papers.
He then bombs small copies of the Statue of Liberty and is called the Phantom of Liberty.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Prior wrestles the angel, refuses the order to stop moving, and chooses more life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The Mark Taper Forum in Los Angeles premiered it on 8 November 1992. Staged readings came earlier, in 1991 and May 1992. Broadway joined it to Millennium Approaches on 23 November 1993. It won the 1994 Tony Award for Best Play. Kushner dated the work complete in 1995 after more cuts. The database year 1992 matches the Los Angeles premiere, not the Broadway year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Prior Walter (The prophet who refuses Heaven's order and stays among the living); The Angel (Heaven's messenger, who wants mankind to stop progress); Roy Cohn (The dying lawyer who tricks Ethel Rosenberg even on his deathbed); Belize (A nurse and Prior's friend, who cares for Roy and steals the drug stash); Hannah Pitt (Joe's Mormon mother, who helps Prior and stays in his chosen family)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The angel tells Prior that God has left Heaven and that humans must stop moving.
Roy Cohn dies in hospital, still cruel, after the ghost of Ethel Rosenberg watches him.
Belize and Louis take Roy's hidden AZT for Prior.
Prior climbs to Heaven, rejects the angels, and demands more life.
In 1990, Prior speaks to the audience at Bethesda Fountain.
The Great Work continues.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The great god Om is trapped in a tortoise because only one novice still believes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Victor Gollancz published the British edition in 1992. Colin Smythe's chronology dates that publication 21 May 1992. Encyclopedia.com also lists the Gollancz edition as 1992, with a later HarperCollins US edition. The database year 1992 is correct. It is a novel, not a poem.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Brutha (A patient novice who cannot read but remembers every word he hears); Om (The god of Omnia, stuck in a tortoise because belief has dried up); Vorbis (Head of the Quisition, who mistakes his own inner voice for the god); Didactylos (A blind Ephebian philosopher who wrote the book called The Turtle Moves)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Om tries to return in power and instead appears as a tortoise.
Only Brutha, a novice with a perfect memory, can hear him.
Vorbis, head of the Quisition (a cruel church police), plans a holy war on Ephebe.
In the desert, Om learns that a god dies when belief dies.
Brutha becomes the new prophet, stops torture, and makes the god obey rules too.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In a ruined Italian villa in 1945, a burned man, a nurse, a thief, and a sapper share the war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1992 is correct. It shared the Booker Prize that year with Sacred Hunger by Barry Unsworth. It also won the Governor General's Award. The film by Anthony Minghella is 1996. In 2018 it won the Golden Man Booker.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Count Almasy (The burned patient, a Hungarian mapmaker mistaken for an Englishman); Hana (A young Canadian nurse who will not leave him); Kip (Kirpal Singh, a Sikh bomb disposal soldier); Caravaggio (A Canadian thief and spy, friend of Hana's father); Katharine Clifton (The Englishwoman Almasy loves in the desert)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
McClelland and Stewart published the novel in September 1992. It is a loose sequel to In the Skin of a Lion.
Hana, a young Canadian nurse, stays in a bombed villa to care for a burned man.
The patient is thought to be English.
He is the Hungarian desert explorer Count Almasy.
Caravaggio, a Canadian thief whose thumbs were cut off, comes to uncover him.
Kip, a Sikh sapper (a soldier who makes bombs safe), falls in love with Hana.
Almasy's affair with Katharine Clifton, and the bombs on Hiroshima, break the group apart.

items.title: "The Thousand Faces of Night" (1992) — Gita Hariharan

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Devi returns from America to Madras and faces marriage, myth, and the lives of other women.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1992 is correct for the first edition. It won the Commonwealth Writers Prize for best first book in 1993. A later Penguin India page shows a 2018 reprint.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Devi (The young woman who returns from America and enters an arranged marriage); Sita (Devi's mother, who has lived as a dutiful wife and mother); Mayamma (The old family servant who survives by bending with circumstances)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Devi comes back to Madras with a degree from America.
Her mother Sita draws her into a suitable but hollow marriage.
An unsuitable lover offers Devi only a brief escape.
Old stories, music, and myth show women how to endure or how to leave.
Mayamma, the old family servant, also sees another possible life through Devi.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A huge 1993 novel about a mother hunting a husband for her daughter in 1950s India.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1993 is correct. Phoenix House issued the British edition in March 1993. HarperCollins issued the United States edition in May 1993. The setting is the invented state of Purva Pradesh in 1951 and 1952.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lata Mehra (A university student of English whose marriage is the main question.); Mrs Rupa Mehra (Lata's determined mother, who wants a suitable boy for her.); Kabir Durrani (A student Lata loves, from a Muslim family.); Amit Chatterji (A poet and one of the men offered to Lata.); Haresh Khanna (A practical shoemaker and another of Lata's suitors.); Maan Kapoor (The lively son of a state minister, whose own love story runs beside Lata's.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is one of the longest novels ever published in a single volume in the English language.
It is set in newly post-independence, post partition India.
It follows the story of four families over a period of 18 months and centers on Mrs. Rupa Mehra's effort to arrange the marriage of her younger daughter Lata to a suitable boy. Her suitors are Kabir, Haresh and Amit.
Lata finally finds Haresh as a suitable boy.
An Equal Music (1999)
A Suitable Girl (upcoming)
Phoenix House in Britain published it in March 1993.
HarperCollins published the United States edition in May 1993.
Mrs Rupa Mehra tells her younger daughter Lata that she will choose the boy.
The story runs through 1951 and 1952 in Brahmpur, a city Seth invented.
Lata is drawn toward Kabir Durrani, the poet Amit Chatterji, and Haresh Khanna.
Around four families, the book also shows law, land, and the new nation's election.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An Indian student at Oxford remembers two loves, his parents' Bombay, and a music teacher.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1993 matches the Heinemann edition reviewed in The Independent on 11 July 1993. The Encore Award, for a second novel, was given in 1994. Do not date the book 1994.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A Bengali student at Oxford who tells the story in the first person); Two women in Oxford (The pair between whom his feelings are divided); The music teacher (A master singer, now dead, who taught the narrator and his mother)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A nameless narrator looks back at lonely student days in Oxford.
His affection is split between two women.
Memory also moves to Bombay, where his parents live.
Calcutta, the city of his birth, returns in the same weave.
A dead music teacher, who taught him and his mother, haunts the book.
An afternoon raag (a melodic pattern for late day) gives the book its time.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: One Derbyshire house joins 1809 and the present in a single story.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1993 is correct. The Royal National Theatre premiered it at the Lyttelton Theatre on 13 April 1993. It won the Olivier Award for Best New Play in 1993.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomasina Coverly (A brilliant girl in 1809 who sees that spilled heat cannot be restored); Septimus Hodge (Her tutor, a friend of Byron, later the hermit of the park); Hannah Jarvis (A modern writer researching the hermit and the garden); Bernard Nightingale (A professor who rushes out a wrong theory about Byron); Valentine Coverly (A mathematician in the present who reads Thomasina's notes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1809, pupil Thomasina Coverly studies with tutor Septimus Hodge.
She asks about love, heat, and shapes that cannot be undone.
Lord Byron is a guest offstage, and a silly duel is threatened.
In the present, Hannah Jarvis and Bernard Nightingale study that past.
Bernard falsely claims Byron killed a poet in a duel.
The two times meet on stage as Thomasina's lost ideas return.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1993 novel in which an African father tells the scattered lives of three children.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Bloomsbury published it in Britain in 1993. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 1993. It won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize in 1994. A 1985 BBC radio play has the same title, but it is not this novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The ancestor (A father figure, like the voice of Africa, who sold his children); Nash Williams (A freed man sent to Liberia as a missionary, where he dies); Martha Randolph (A woman who runs from slavery toward California and dies on the way); Travis (A Black American soldier in Britain during the Second World War); Joyce (An Englishwoman who loves Travis and later meets their son); James Hamilton (A slave ship captain whose journal records the trade)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An African ancestor says his crops failed, so he sold three children.
Nash is sent from America to Liberia as a Christian teacher.
Martha flees slavery and dies before she can reach California.
In the Second World War, the soldier Travis loves the Englishwoman Joyce.
Separate stories show how the slave trade still shapes later lives.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A play about a Hindu family that shelters two Muslim youths during a riot.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The catalog year 1993 matches the first staging in Bangalore. A December 1992 premiere at the Deccan Herald festival was cancelled after the Babri Masjid was destroyed. The 1998 Sahitya Akademi Award was for the printed book Final Solutions and Other Plays.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Smita (A young woman in the Hindu family); Babban (A Muslim youth who seeks shelter in the house); The Hindu family (The household that must decide whether to hide the two youths)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
During a communal riot, two Muslim youths ask a Hindu family for shelter.
The family argues about fear, faith, and memories of Partition.
An older woman remembers violence from the time of Partition.
Young Smita feels love for Babban, one of the sheltered men.
The play shows how a public riot enters a private home.

items.title: "Green Grass, Running Water" (4 March 1993) — Thomas King

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Coyote and four ancient Indians try to fix a Blackfoot world blocked by a dam.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Houghton Mifflin published the hardcover on 4 March 1993. It was a finalist for the 1993 Governor General's Award for fiction and won the 1994 Canadian Authors Award. The database year 1993 is correct. The title points to treaty language that promised land while the grass is green and the water runs.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Coyote (A trickster whose dream gets loose and whose dancing shakes the dam); Lionel Red Dog (A drifting salesman pulled between family, Alberta, and a tidier life); Eli Stands Alone (Lionel's uncle, a former professor who will not leave the cabin in the dam's way); Alberta Frank (A professor who wants a baby but does not want a husband); The four old Indians (Escaped elders who retell creation under the names of Western heroes)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book opens with Coyote, a dream that thinks it is God, and too much water.
Four old Indians escape a hospital.
They call themselves the Lone Ranger, Ishmael, Robinson Crusoe, and Hawkeye.
Each tells a creation story that bumps into the Bible and a famous Western book.
In Alberta, Lionel drifts, and Alberta wants a child without a husband.
Eli lives in a cabin that blocks a dam.
Coyote's dancing helps break the dam.
The water returns to its old path, and the telling starts again.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Jamun returns to a middle class family and stays while his parents fail.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1993 is correct. Faber and Faber published the book on 16 August 1993. It is his second novel. A sequel, Way to Go, came much later and is a different book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jamun (The drifting younger son who returns to the family home); Urmila (Jamun's mother, who is ill in hospital); Shyamanand (Jamun's ageing father); Burfi (Jamun's elder brother); Joyce (Burfi's wife)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jamun is a young man without steady work, living away from home.
He comes back when his mother, Urmila, is in hospital.
The house holds his father Shyamanand, his brother Burfi, and Burfi's wife Joyce.
He stays as illness, money, and old quarrels press on the family.
The book moves back and forth in time through their shared past.

items.title: "The Odyssey: A Stage Version" (1993) — Derek Walcott

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Walcott's stage retelling of Homer's Odyssey.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1993 is correct for the published play. It is a stage version of Homer's Odyssey, not a book of poems. The database genre label Poetry is a catalog error.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Odysseus (The wandering hero of Homer's Odyssey, retold by Walcott for the stage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The play puts Homer's voyage of Odysseus on the modern stage.
It belongs with Walcott's long habit of reusing classical stories.
Like Omeros, it joins Greek epic to a Caribbean imagination.
The published text appeared in 1993, three years after Omeros.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic novel about two boys in a Mumbai chawl (a crowded block of small homes).

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1994 is correct for the English novel. He had started a Marathi version and then completed the book in English. Sequels came in 2012 and 2015.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ravan (A Hindu boy whose babyhood accident ties him to Eddie's family); Eddie (A Catholic boy who grows up in the same chawl)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ravan is Hindu, and Eddie is Catholic, and both live in one chawl.
When Ravan is a baby he falls, and that fall kills Eddie's father.
The boys grow up side by side, but the two communities barely meet.
The story uses jokes, film dreams, and the press of city life.
Nagarkar began the book in Marathi and finished it in English.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Black gravedigger who looks like Lincoln lets customers pretend to shoot him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: She wrote it in 1993. The world premiere ran at Yale Repertory Theatre from 13 January to 5 February 1994, directed by Liz Diamond. The Public Theater then played it from 22 February 1994. Theatre Communications Group published it in 1995 in The America Play and Other Works. The database year 1994 matches the premiere.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Foundling Father (A gravedigger, also called the Lesser Known, who impersonates Abraham Lincoln); Lucy (His wife, a mourner who keeps the secrets of the dying); Brazil (Their son, who weeps, digs, and hunts for wonders in the hole)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Foundling Father looks like Abraham Lincoln and works as his impersonator.
Customers pay a penny and play John Wilkes Booth.
He calls the missing Black past the Great Hole of History.
His wife Lucy and his son Brazil dig and mourn at a copy of that hole.
Lines repeat, as in jazz, and the story of the past never settles.

items.title: "The Location of Culture" (1994) — Homi K. Bhabha

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays on how colonial power slips when cultures mix, copy, and talk back.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1994 is correct for the book. Routledge first published it in 1994. Some essays had appeared earlier in journals. Of Mimicry and Man is linked to 1984, and The Other Question to 1983. A Routledge Classics reprint came in 2004.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Homi K. Bhabha (The critic whose essays explain these terms.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
3) Edward Said Continuing the Conversation (2005)
The book gathers essays on identity, nation, and colonial rule.
Bhabha says culture is made in between, not in one pure place.
Hybridity is the blend that appears in that gap.
Mimicry copies the colonizer but stays almost the same, not quite.
A stereotype, a frozen picture of a people, tries to stop that change.
The Third Space is the in between place where a new culture can start.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A widow, two tailors, and a student share a flat while the Emergency destroys their chances.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1995 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published it in 1995. It won the Giller Prize (a top Canadian novel prize) that year. The Booker shortlist was 1996. A Faber paperback is listed as 1996, so do not call 1996 the first year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Dina Dalal (A widow fighting to stay independent in her flat); Ishvar Darji (A tailor who escaped caste violence and later loses his legs); Omprakash Darji (Ishvar's nephew, a young tailor maimed by the forced campaign); Maneck Kohlah (A student from the mountains who boards with Dina)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The main action is the middle of the 1970s, under the Emergency.
Dina Dalal, a Parsi widow, hires two tailors so she can keep her flat.
Ishvar and his nephew Om come from a low caste (a group fixed by birth).
They learned tailoring to leave the leather trade.
Maneck Kohlah, a student from the hills, boards with Dina.
Slum clearance, forced labour, and forced sterilisation (surgery to stop births) break the tailors.
Years later the survivors meet again, and Maneck's despair ends in suicide.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Short stories about Indian and Indian American women facing marriage, migration, and choice.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Anchor Books published the collection in 1995. It won an American Book Award. Sources differ on whether that prize was 1995 or 1996, so the prize year is not fixed here. Database year 1995 is the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Immigrant wives and daughters (Women caught between Indian family rules and life in America)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The stories move between India and the United States.
Women face arranged meetings, new husbands, and lonely new homes.
Some want love or work that their families will not allow.
Clothes and household customs show what they keep and what they lose.
The book won an American Book Award and a PEN Josephine Miles Award.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An unseen young man seeks visibility and learns a different secret.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1995 is correct. The author's site and Wikipedia give Weidenfeld and Nicolson as the 1995 publisher. A Spectator review dated 1 April 1995 names Phoenix House. Both records keep the year 1995.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The unnamed hero (A young man born invisible who searches for the secret of being seen); The invisible guides (Voices and beings who lead him through the tests of the island)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The unnamed hero reads that he and his people are missing from history.
He leaves home to find the people who count as visible.
After seven years he reaches an island of invisible beings.
Guides he cannot see set him tests of fire, water, and desire.
He learns that being unseen can be a hidden creative power.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A hotel room in Leeds turns from a private assault into a war zone.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1995 is the premiere. Wikipedia dates the Royal Court opening to 12 January 1995, directed by James Macdonald. Bloomsbury also places that production in 1995. A separate first book year is not fixed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ian (A middle aged tabloid journalist, racist and violent); Cate (A young, fragile woman whom Ian tries to control); Soldier (An unnamed fighter who brings the war into the room)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ian, a crude middle aged journalist, brings young Cate to a hotel in Leeds.
He presses her for sex.
She is ill and afraid.
A bomb breaks the room, and a soldier enters.
The soldier attacks Ian and leaves him blind.
Cate later returns with food, and Ian thanks her.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Microsoft coder keeps a computer journal of work, fear, and friendship.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1995 is correct for the HarperCollins novel. A shorter version appeared in Wired in January 1994. The catalogue unit label Poetry is wrong. This is fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Daniel Underwood (The narrator, a young programmer who keeps a computer journal); Karla (A coworker who becomes close to Daniel)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A short version was the cover story in Wired in January 1994.
HarperCollins published the full novel in June 1995.
Daniel Underwood writes the book as notes on his computer.
He and his friends code at Microsoft in Redmond.
The group later tries a startup in Silicon Valley.
The catalogue calls this book poetry.
It is a novel.

items.title: "Red Earth and Pouring Rain" (1995) — Vikram Chandra

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A typing monkey and a young student tell stories so that death will wait.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Penguin India, Faber and Faber, and Little, Brown all published the novel in 1995. It won the Commonwealth Writers Prize for Best First Book and the David Higham Prize. The title comes from the Kuruntokai, a classical Tamil anthology.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Abhay (A young Indian just back from college in America); Sanjay (A nineteenth century poet whose soul lives in the wounded monkey); Yama (The god of death, who bargains for Sanjay's soul); Hanuman (The monkey god who helps Sanjay win time to tell stories); Sikander (A soldier in the nineteenth century story, drawn from James Skinner)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Abhay, home from America, shoots a monkey that stole his clothes.
The monkey holds the soul of Sanjay, a poet from the nineteenth century.
Yama, the god of death, comes to claim that soul.
Sanjay may live if his typed story keeps the listeners interested.
The tale joins colonial India, including the soldier Sikander, with Abhay's modern road.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A near future search uncovers a secret history behind Ronald Ross and malaria research.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1995 is the year often printed in lists. The Ravi Dayal copyright page says 1996. Inside the story, Murugan disappears in 1995. That story year is not the publication year. The Clarke Award came in 1997.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Antar (An Egyptian clerk in near future New York who starts the search); L. Murugan (A researcher who disappears in Calcutta in 1995); Urmila Roy (A Calcutta journalist pulled into the same mystery); Ronald Ross (The historical scientist whose malaria work the novel reopens)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Set in Calcutta, Protagonist - Murugan, Antar. 4. The Glass Palace (2000) Protagonist - Rajkumar,.
It is a Historical novel, set in Burma, Bengal, India & Malaya spans a century from the fall of Konbaurg Dynasty in Mandalay through WW II to modern times. 5. The Hungry Tide (2004) Protagonist - Fokir, Kanai Dutt.
Important Quote from the novel: "How do you lose a word? Does it vanish into your memory like an old toy in a cupboard, and hidden in the cobwebs and dust waiting to be cleaned out or rediscovered". 6. Sea of Poppies Protagonist - Deeti 7. River of Smoke (2011)
Antar, a clerk in New York, finds a trace of his missing colleague Murugan.
Murugan had vanished in Calcutta in 1995 while chasing the history of malaria.
He believed Ronald Ross did not solve the mosquito puzzle alone.
A journalist, Urmila Roy, follows strange stories in the same city.
The searches meet, and science turns into a mystery about hidden knowledge.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mixed Bombay family tells a wild story of art, trade, and a city falling apart.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1995 is correct. The novel was published in 1995, while Rushdie was still living under the fatwa.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Moraes Zogoiby (The narrator, nicknamed the Moor); Aurora Zogoiby (His mother, a powerful painter); Abraham Zogoiby (His father, a trader who grows dangerous)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is set in Bombay and Cochin. It refers to the fifteenth century Spain as a starting point.
The title is taken from the story of Bobadil (Abu Abdullah Muhammad), the last Moorish king of Hranada, who is also mentioned in it.
The mother of narrator and an artist friend of mother, each makes a painting which they call "The Moor's Last Sigh".
It traces four generations of the narrators family and ultimate effects upon the narrator, Mores Zogoiby who is called 'Moor'.
The Ground Beneath Her Feet (1999)
Shalimar the Clown (2005)
The Enchantress of Florence (2008)
Two Years Eighty Months And Twenty Eight Nights (2015)
Moraes Zogoiby, called the Moor, narrates his family's story.
His mother Aurora is a famous painter.
His father deals in spices.
The family mixes Jewish, Christian, and Indian lines.
The title recalls the last Muslim ruler of Granada and his sigh.
The plot runs from older Cochin trade to modern Bombay.
Rushdie wrote and published it while he was still in hiding.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A novel about Grace Marks and the Canadian murders of 1843.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1996 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published it in September 1996. It won the Giller Prize and was shortlisted for the Booker Prize. The murders it retells are from 1843.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Grace Marks (The servant whose guilt remains uncertain); Dr Simon Jordan (A fictional doctor who studies Grace's memory); James McDermott (The fellow servant who was hanged); Nancy Montgomery (The housekeeper who was killed); Thomas Kinnear (The gentleman who was killed)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1843 Thomas Kinnear and Nancy Montgomery were murdered.
Servants Grace Marks and James McDermott were convicted.
McDermott was hanged.
Grace was sent to prison for life.
Atwood invents Dr Simon Jordan, who questions Grace years later.
Grace sews quilts and will not give one settled confession.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A huge novel about a film so pleasing that viewers cannot stop watching.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1996 is correct. Little, Brown published the finished book on 1 February 1996, while Wallace was alive. Excerpts appeared in magazines in 1995. The Pale King, not this novel, was unfinished and came out in 2011.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hal Incandenza (A brilliant young tennis player at Enfield Tennis Academy); James Incandenza (Hal's dead father, who made the fatal film called the Entertainment); Joelle van Dyne (An actress in the film who later seeks treatment at Ennet House)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Little, Brown published the novel on 1 February 1996.
Most of the story sits in the Year of the Depend Adult Undergarment.
Hal Incandenza trains at the Enfield Tennis Academy.
Addicts try to recover at Ennet House in Boston.
A film called the Entertainment grips viewers until they waste away.
A Quebec separatist group hunts a master copy.
Many plots stay open.
Hundreds of endnotes are part of the novel, not an optional extra.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four London friends carry a dead butcher's ashes from Bermondsey to Margate.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1996 is correct. Picador published it on 26 January 1996. It won the Booker Prize and shared the James Tait Black Memorial Prize. The film is 2001.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jack Dodds (The dead butcher whose ashes go to Margate.); Amy Dodds (Jack's widow, who stays away from the trip.); The four friends (The men from Bermondsey who carry out the wish.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jack Dodds, a butcher, has died.
His last wish is to have his ashes scattered at Margate.
Four old friends drive there from Bermondsey, in south London.
His widow Amy does not join the journey.
On the road, the men remember war, love, debt, and regret.
The title also means the last drinks called in a pub.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A modern, brutal retelling of the Phaedra myth, centred on Hippolytus.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1996 is correct for the premiere. Wikipedia dates the Gate Theatre opening to 15 May 1996, directed by Kane. Bloomsbury agrees on the Gate Theatre in 1996. A separate first book year is not fixed here.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hippolytus (The prince at the centre, cold and sexually cruel); Phaedra (The queen and stepmother who desires him and then dies); Strophe (Phaedra's daughter, who tries to warn her); Theseus (The king and father, who returns and joins the killing)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Queen Phaedra loves her stepson Hippolytus.
He is lazy, cruel, and bored with everyone.
She confesses her love.
He rejects her.
She kills herself and leaves a note that accuses him.
A crowd kills Hippolytus on stage.
Theseus sees the truth too late.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Young Londoners buy, sell, and use one another when love has no price except money.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1996 is the first performance, on 26 September 1996 at the Royal Court Theatre Upstairs. Methuen later printed the play in Plays 1 (2001). The names echo the band Take That and the singer Lulu.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mark (A young man who leaves rehab and still wants control); Lulu (A young woman in the household who takes risky work); Robbie (Mark's lover, who loses money that is not his); Gary (A teenage sex worker who asks to be owned); Brian (A violent businessman who wants his money back)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This was Ravenhill's first long play.
A reading was given at the Finborough Theatre in 1995.
Out of Joint and the Royal Court opened it on 26 September 1996.
Mark, Lulu, and Robbie try to live as a small household after Mark leaves rehab.
They fall into debt with Brian, a hard businessman.
Gary, a teenage sex worker, says he wants to be owned, not loved.
The play shows sex, drugs, and care all treated as shopping.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A historical novel about the husband of the saint poet Mira in Mewar.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1997 is correct. HarperCollins India published it. He won the Sahitya Akademi Award for this novel. Reports give that prize as 2000 or as 2001.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Maharaj Kumar (The narrator, heir of Mewar, based on Prince Bhoj Raj); Mira (His wife, the poet saint who treats Krishna as her husband)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is set in the Rajput kingdom of Mewar in the 1500s.
The narrator is Maharaj Kumar, a prince based on Bhoj Raj.
His wife Mira gives her love to the god Krishna, not to him.
He tries to win her while wars press on the kingdom.
The book asks who will rule after the Maharana dies.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A poor Mumbai family sells organs to a rich Western buyer.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1997 is the Onassis prize year, and the play is copyright 1997. The author says she wrote it in 1996 and that Kali for Women published it in early 1998. Wikipedia dates that Kali book to 1997. Delhi performances began in 1999. A Greek performance followed in Athens in January 2000.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Om Prakash (A jobless clerk who agrees to sell his organs); Jaya (Om's wife, who resists Virgil at the end); Ma (Om's mother, pulled in by the new comforts); Jeetu (Om's younger brother, taken by mistake for the operation); Ginni (A young woman on the video screen, later shown to be an image); Virgil (The old Western man who is the real organ receiver)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The play is set in Mumbai in 2010, in one small room.
Om has lost his clerk's job and signs with InterPlanta.
The firm will pay the family if a body stays fit for harvest.
Ginni appears on a video module and controls their food and home.
The guards take Jeetu, Om's brother, and Jaya finds that Virgil is the real receiver.

items.title: "Love and Longing in Bombay" (1997) — Vikram Chandra

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Five Bombay stories told by a retired civil servant in a bar.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 1997 by Penguin India, Faber and Faber, and Little, Brown. Sartaj Singh appears here in Kama, before Sacred Games.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Subramaniam (A retired civil servant who tells the five stories); Sartaj Singh (A Sikh police inspector in the story Kama, later the hero of Sacred Games); Jago Antia (The wounded soldier in Dharma who meets a ghost at home)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Subramaniam tells the stories over evenings at the Fisherman's Rest.
Dharma follows a wounded soldier and a ghost in his old house.
Shakti follows two rich families split by a long feud.
Kama follows Inspector Sartaj Singh into a murder and city corruption.
Artha and Shanti turn to love, loss, and Subramaniam's own past.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic historical novel about the surveyors Charles Mason and Jeremiah Dixon.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1997 is correct. Henry Holt published the novel on 30 April 1997. The title uses an ampersand: Mason & Dixon.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charles Mason (An English astronomer, one of the two surveyors); Jeremiah Dixon (The surveyor who works with Mason); Wicks Cherrycoke (A clergyman who narrates their adventures as a tall tale)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Henry Holt published the novel on 30 April 1997.
Reverend Wicks Cherrycoke tells the tale in Philadelphia in 1786.
Mason and Dixon meet in England and sail to observe the Transit of Venus.
They later survey the line that will divide American colonies.
The prose copies the spelling and rhythm of the eighteenth century.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems that lend God a human voice, with pictures of fragile city homes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1997 is the Bloodaxe edition, which also reprints Purdah. The poet's site and the Open British National Bibliography list a Viking edition in 1994. That is the first publication. The poems are in English, not in translation. The database genre Fiction is wrong. This is poetry.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The God speaker (A voice in the title poems, close to human doubt.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title poems let God speak like someone sending messages.
In one poem God is nothing but a space that someone must fill.
Living Space, placed in this book by Bloodaxe, watches a shaky house.
Other poems question faith, home, and the noise of prayer.
The 1997 Bloodaxe edition also reprints the earlier book Purdah.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1997 poetry book on the Caribbean home and his mother's death.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1997 is correct. Britannica says the poems are mostly about his Caribbean home and his mother's death. Wikipedia lists The Bounty among the 1997 poetry books.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet speaker (Walcott mourning his mother and returning in verse to Saint Lucia)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Most of the poems turn back to Walcott's Caribbean home.
Grief for his mother runs through the book.
Praise of island light sits beside mourning.
The book comes after Omeros and before Tiepolo's Hound.

items.title: "The Country Without a Post Office" (1997) — Agha Shahid Ali

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Country Without a Post Office

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems on the Kashmir conflict, closed post offices, and letters that never arrive.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1997 is correct for the first book. Poets.org lists a Ravi Dayal edition in 1997. The same note lists a Norton edition in 1998. The database file places this poetry book under drama. That label is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet-speaker (A Kashmiri poet looking at the conflict from exile, often from Delhi); Rizwan (A young man killed in the conflict, whose father must not be told)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An armed rising in Kashmir around 1990 shut post offices for months.
Letters piled up, and news from home could not get out.
The speaker, far away, follows a dead boy named Rizwan through the streets.
The book also mourns Kashmiri Pandits who had to leave.
The poet still hopes the soldiers will return the keys and peace will come.

items.title: "The God of Small Things" (1997) — Arundhati Roy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Twins in a Kerala family are broken by caste, a death, and a forbidden love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1997 is correct. Roy began the book in 1992 and finished it in 1996. It won the Booker Prize in 1997. IndiaInk published the Indian edition.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rahel (One twin, who returns to Ayemenem as an adult); Estha (Rahel's twin brother, later silent from trauma); Ammu (Their divorced mother, punished for loving Velutha); Velutha (A skilled Dalit carpenter and a secret communist); Baby Kochamma (The twins' bitter grandaunt, who pushes the false charge)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It centers around a tragedy that sends a family apart and its lasting effects on the twins who were at the heart of it.
The book explores how the small things affect people's behavior and their lives.
The story is set in Ayemenem (Kerala).
Fraternal twins Rahel and Esthappen are seven years old in 1969.
Ammu is the most important female character. 'Baba' is Rahel & Estha's father who is divorced by Ammu when the children were very young.
The story enters in 1990 as the young women Rahel returns to her village to be re-united with her twin brother Esthappen at the age of 31.
The twins used to call themselves as "Me" or "Us".
The day before Margaret and Sophie arrived, the family visits a theatre to see "The Sound of Music" where Estha is molested by the "Orangedrink Lemondrink Man" a beverage vendor.
Velutha is an untouchable, a dalit. His family has been working for the IPE family for generations.
Rahel and Estha form an unlikely bond with Velutha and come to love him, despite his untouchable status.
When Ammu's relationship with Velutha is discovered, Ammu is locked in her room and Velutha is banished.
In her rage, Ammu blames the twins for her misfortune and calls them "Millstones around her neck".
The story moves between 1969, when the twins are children, and their return as adults.
Rahel and Estha live in Ayemenem with their mother Ammu, who is divorced.
Their cousin Sophie Mol arrives from England, and the family prepares a grand welcome.
Ammu loves Velutha, a Paravan (a Dalit caste treated as untouchable) who works for the family.
Sophie drowns, Velutha is beaten and dies after a false charge, and the twins are separated.

items.title: "The Mistress of Spices" (1997) — Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Tilo, a magic spice seller in Oakland, breaks her vows when she falls in love.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Doubleday published it on 6 February 1997. The film adaptation came out in 2005. Database year 1997 is the book year, not the film year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tilo (A trained mistress of spices who runs a shop in Oakland); Raven (The American man Tilo loves, against the rules of her order)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Tilo keeps a spice shop in Oakland and senses what people need.
Her training forbids her to leave the shop or to love a man.
She falls in love with an American man called Raven.
The spices punish her, and an earthquake destroys the shop.
She lives, and she and Raven start to build a life again.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Rei Shimura finds a businessman's wife dead in the snow and hunts the killer in Japan.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1997 is correct. Wikipedia says HarperCollins published it in the United States in 1997. Massey's site and Wikipedia record the Agatha Award for best first novel. She began the book while living in Japan in the early 1990s.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rei Shimura (A Japanese American English teacher who becomes an amateur detective); Setsuko Nakamura (The murdered wife of a Japanese company executive); Hugh Glendinning (A Scottish lawyer who asks Rei to investigate)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Rei Shimura is a Japanese American English teacher in Tokyo.
She is 27, and she is half Japanese and half American.
On a New Year trip to the Japanese Alps, she finds a body in the snow.
The dead woman is Setsuko Nakamura, wife of a company man.
Hugh Glendinning, a Scottish lawyer, presses Rei to help.
The search moves back to Tokyo and into office life and family secrets.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A huge novel follows a 1951 baseball and America's Cold War waste.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1997 is correct for the Scribner novel. The prologue appeared in Harper's in 1992 as Pafko at the Wall, and again as a small book in 2001. Do not date the whole novel 1992 or 2001.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nick Shay (A waste executive from the Bronx who ends up with the baseball); Cotter Martin (The boy who catches the 1951 home run ball); Klara Sax (An artist who paints old war planes in the desert)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Scribner published the novel in 1997.
The prologue retells Bobby Thomson's home run on 3 October 1951.
That game scene first appeared as Pafko at the Wall in Harper's in 1992.
Nick Shay, a waste executive, later owns the winning baseball.
The story moves backward through waste, bombs, and private guilt.
A separate small book of the prologue appeared in 2001.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A red winged boy named Geryon loves Herakles in the modern world and is left heartbroken.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1998 is correct. Alfred A. Knopf published it in 1998. A sequel, Red Doc>, came in 2013.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Geryon (A shy red winged boy, the monster retold as a modern lover and artist); Herakles (The charismatic young man who breaks Geryon's heart); Ancash (Herakles's later boyfriend, who sees Geryon's wings)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Carson rewrites the ancient Geryoneis of Stesichorus.
In the myth, Herakles kills the red monster Geryon and steals his cattle.
Here Geryon is a red winged boy who writes and later takes photographs.
At fourteen he falls in love with Herakles, who then leaves him.
Years later they meet in Buenos Aires, where Herakles has a boyfriend, Ancash.
The three travel toward Peru, and Geryon flies once, toward a volcano.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eighty eight poems in which Hughes finally writes to Sylvia Plath about their marriage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1998 is correct. Faber published it months before his death on 28 October 1998. It is not a posthumous book. The database flag is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ted Hughes (The speaker, addressing Sylvia Plath as you); Sylvia Plath (The dead poet to whom the poems are written)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poem won Forward Poetry Prize in 1998.
It is a collection of poems released only months before Hughes death.
It has 88 poems and widely considered to be Hughes most explicit response to the suicide of his estranged wife Sylvia Plath in 1953, and to their widely discussed politicized and explosive marriage.
Faber published Birthday Letters in 1998.
For many years Hughes had said almost nothing in public about Plath.
These poems speak to her about their meeting, marriage, and her death in 1963.
The last poem is Red, about the colours in her life.
Their daughter Frieda made the cover art.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A tycoon builds a theme park England on the Isle of Wight.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Jonathan Cape published it on 27 August 1998. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 1998. It did not win. The database year 1998 is correct.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Martha Cochrane (The heroine, who helps build the island and later leaves it); Sir Jack Pitman (The entrepreneur who creates the theme park England); Paul Harrison (Martha's colleague and lover on the project)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
England, My England is a collection of short stories by D. H. Lawrence, while England, My England is also a poem by William Ernest Henley.
It was shortlisted for Booker's Prize.
Barnes himself described the novel as "a semi- force.
It has dystopian and farcical elements.
It is divided into three parts entitled.
England.
England England and,.
Anglia.
It first parts focuses on protagonist Martha Co Chnance and her childhood memoirs.
The second part is set in the near future Martha is now 40's and gets employed by sir jack pitman for megalomaniac project.
The third part is set decades later and depicts Martha who has returned to a village in old England after many years of wandering abroad Love etc. (2000)
It is a sequel to Talking it Over.
Martha Cochrane remembers a childhood broken when her father leaves.
Sir Jack Pitman hires her for a huge tourist project.
He copies famous English sights onto the Isle of Wight.
The park is called England, England, and tourists prefer the copy.
Martha rises to lead the island, then she is forced out.
The real England grows poor and returns to a simple rural life.
The novel asks what stays real when the copy wins.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A verse novel about Fred Boettcher, who loses the sense of touch.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1998 is the first book publication. Duffy and Snellgrove issued it in Australia, and Carcanet issued a hardcover in 1998. Parts had appeared in PN Review before the book. Some lists use 1999 for a later printing.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Fred Boettcher (A German Australian sailor, also called Fredy, who loses his sense of touch)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Fred Boettcher is a German Australian sailor.
In World War I he sees Armenian women burned by a mob in Trabzon.
Shock takes away his sense of touch.
The loss hides him and also gives him huge strength and no pain.
He travels through both world wars, the 1929 crash, and many countries.
At the end his feeling returns.

items.title: "Hullabaloo in the Guava Orchard" (1998) — Kiran Desai

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Sampath Chawla leaves his job, lives in a guava tree, and is treated as a holy man.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1998 is correct. Faber and Atlantic Monthly Press both brought it out in 1998. It won the Betty Trask Award for a first novel by a young writer.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sampath Chawla (A young man who escapes adult life by living in a guava tree)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is set in the fictional town of Shahkot.
Sampath Chawla is tired of work and of adult duties.
He climbs into a guava tree in an orchard and stays there.
He uses gossip from his old post office job to sound like a seer (a person who claims hidden knowledge).
The town crowds around the tree and a comic fuss begins.
Desai took the idea from Kapila Pradhan, a man who really lived in a tree.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: On one sad night, Jay decides to leave his partner and their two young sons.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Faber published Intimacy in 1998. A film with the same title appeared in 2001. That film is only loosely based on the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jay (The narrator, a writer about to leave his home); His partner (The woman he has lived with, and the mother of his two sons)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jay spends his last night at home before he walks out.
He thinks about his partner, their sons, a lover, and his friends.
He has lived with this woman for years and now wants no more of that life.
The whole story covers about one day and one night.
Many readers took Jay as a harsh portrait of Kureishi himself.

items.title: "A Critique of Postcolonial Reason" (1999) — Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A long book that rethinks postcolonial reason and the native informant.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1999 matches Harvard University Press. The history chapter revises the 1988 essay. This book is not the first printing of that essay.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Spivak tracks the native informant through philosophy, history, and literature.
A native informant is a local person treated as a source for Western knowledge.
She reads Kant, Hegel, and Marx, and also colonial archives and literature.
She reworks the subaltern essay inside the history chapter.
The book warns that postcolonial talk can repeat the old colonial frames.
Harvard University Press published it in 1999.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 1999 novel about a London violinist and a pianist who is losing her hearing.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1999 is correct. Phoenix House published the London edition and Broadway Books the New York edition in that year. The title quotes John Donne. It is not a second part of A Suitable Boy.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Michael Holme (The narrator, a second violinist haunted by a failure in Vienna.); Julia McNicholl (A pianist, now married, who is losing her hearing.); The Maggiore Quartet (Michael's string group, with players named Piers, Helen, and Billy.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Phoenix House in London and Broadway Books in New York published it in 1999.
Michael Holme plays second violin in the Maggiore Quartet.
He meets Julia McNicholl again, the pianist he loved and left in Vienna.
They become lovers again, though Julia is married and is going deaf.
The quartet works on Bach, and Julia joins them for Schubert's Trout Quintet.
The title comes from a sermon by John Donne about one equal music.

items.title: "Brief Interviews with Hideous Men" (1999) — David Foster Wallace

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Stories in which men answer hidden questions about sex, ego, and shame.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1999 is correct for the Little, Brown book. Some pieces appeared earlier in magazines, including The Paris Review. The catalogue posthumous and unfinished flags do not fit this 1999 collection.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The interviewer (A questioner whose words are omitted and marked only as Q); The hideous men (Male speakers whose answers expose ego and cruelty)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Little, Brown published the collection on 28 May 1999.
It holds many short pieces, including four sets of interviews.
In those interviews the questions appear only as the letter Q.
The men talk about women, sex, and their own egos.
Some pieces appeared in magazines before the book.
The book came out while Wallace was alive.
It is not The Pale King.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: David Lurie loses his post, then cannot protect his daughter on her farm.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1999 is correct. Secker and Warburg published the UK edition on 1 July 1999. It won that year's Booker Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: David Lurie (A twice-divorced professor who loses his post); Lucy Lurie (His daughter, who farms in the Eastern Cape); Melanie Isaacs (The student at the centre of Lurie's disgrace); Petrus (The neighbouring farmer whose power on the land is rising)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
David Lurie teaches in Cape Town after apartheid.
He forces a relationship on his student Melanie Isaacs and will not repent.
He resigns and goes to his daughter Lucy's farm in the Eastern Cape.
Three men attack the farm, rape Lucy, and burn Lurie.
Lucy stays, becomes pregnant, and will not live by her father's plan.
The novel won the Booker Prize in 1999.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Nine stories about Indians and Indian Americans caught between two homes.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 1999 is correct. Houghton Mifflin published the book in 1999. It won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2000.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Mr Kapasi (A tour guide who also translates for a doctor); Mrs Das (An Indian American visitor who confesses a secret); Shoba and Shukumar (A couple in A Temporary Matter mourning a stillborn child); Lilia (The girl who watches Mr Pirzada wait for news of his daughters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book holds nine stories of love, loss, and migration.
In the title story, the guide Kapasi drives the Das family in India.
Mrs Das tells him a private guilt and wants him to explain her pain.
He cannot give the comfort or the romance she seems to offer.
Other stories show failing marriages, war news, and children between cultures.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Nick leaves prison after 15 years and finds that 1980s protest politics has faded.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 1999 is correct. First performance was 30 September 1999 at the Theatre Royal, Bury St Edmunds. The London run opened on 14 October 1999. Methuen published the play in 1999.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nick (A former activist just released after 15 years in prison); Helen (Nick's old comrade, now a Labour councillor); Nadia (A young dancer who talks in self help phrases); Tim (A young man living with AIDS); Victor (A Russian dancer whom Tim has brought over); Jonathan (The businessman Nick once attacked)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Out of Joint first performed the play on 30 September 1999 in Bury St Edmunds.
It reached the New Ambassadors Theatre in London on 14 October 1999.
Nick was jailed for a political attack on the businessman Jonathan.
His old comrade Helen is now a Labour councillor.
He meets Nadia, Tim, who is living with AIDS, and Victor, a Russian dancer.
The young people chase pills and a happy ending that never quite arrives.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young student in Benaras is drawn to books, solitude, and Western glamour.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The first UK edition is Picador, London, 1999. The British national record and the novel's own reference page agree on 1999. Mishra's website dates the novel 2000, which fits a later edition. It won the Los Angeles Times Art Seidenbaum Award for first fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Samar (The young narrator, a student newly arrived in Benaras); Catherine (A Western woman whose life pulls Samar out of his solitude)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Samar, a young narrator, arrives at a boarding house in Benaras (the holy city also called Varanasi).
He hopes for books and quiet, but the city wakes his hidden wants.
He is drawn to Catherine and to the shine of Western lives.
The novel watches caste (birth rank), class, and the meeting of East and West.
It is a growing up story, told with irony (a gap between what is said and what is meant).

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two brothers named Lincoln and Booth share one room, a card hustle, and a gun.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The play opened at the Public Theater on 26 July 2001. Jeffrey Wright played Lincoln, and Don Cheadle played Booth. Broadway opening was 7 April 2002 at the Ambassador Theatre. Mos Def replaced Cheadle. Parks won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama on 8 April 2002. A 2023 revival won the Tony Award for Best Revival of a Play.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Lincoln (The older brother, a former card hustler who now impersonates Abraham Lincoln); Booth (The younger brother, a shoplifter who wants Lincoln's old card skill)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Lincoln dresses as Abraham Lincoln in an arcade, and customers shoot blanks at him.
He lives with his younger brother Booth after his wife throws him out.
Booth practices three-card monte (a fast street card trick) and dreams of being the dealer.
Their parents left each boy five hundred dollars, then vanished.
Lincoln wins Booth's hidden money.
Booth then shoots him.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A broken last play about depression, with no named characters.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database says 2000, after her death. That year is the premiere. Wikipedia and Bloomsbury place the Royal Court opening in June 2000. Wikipedia gives the day as 23 June 2000. She died on 20 February 1999. Wikipedia dates the Methuen Complete Plays text to 2001.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The text has no named people and no fixed place.
The voices speak of pain, medicine, love, and the wish to die.
A repeated hospital test counts backward by sevens.
The title is the early hour when Kane often woke.
She finished the play just before she died.
It was first staged in 2000, after her death.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Forensic scientist Anil Tissera returns to Sri Lanka to name one victim of the civil war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2000 is correct. It shared the Giller Prize with Mercy Among the Children by David Adams Richards. It also won Canada's Governor General's Award for fiction.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anil Tissera (A Sri Lankan forensic anthropologist who returns from abroad); Sarath Diyasena (A local archaeologist who works with Anil and knows the risk); Palipana (An old, blind epigraphist (a reader of ancient writings)); Ananda (An artisan who rebuilds faces for the unidentified dead); Sailor (The nickname of the skeleton whose identity they seek)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel was published in 2000, including by McClelland and Stewart in Canada.
Anil, educated in the West, is sent by a human rights group to investigate killings.
With the archaeologist Sarath Diyasena she studies a skeleton they call Sailor.
The blind scholar Palipana and the eye painter Ananda help them read the bones.
Naming the dead becomes dangerous in a war of hidden bodies.
It shared the 2000 Giller Prize and won the Governor General's Award.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A short play in which fear and war spread from one house to all of nature.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: It was first performed at the Royal Court Jerwood Theatre Upstairs in November 2000. Nick Hern Books publishes the text. Database year 2000 is correct. It opened before the attacks of September 2001.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Joan (A girl who later makes hats for condemned prisoners); Harper (Joan's aunt, who hides the violence in the house); Todd (Joan's co-worker and love interest at the hat factory)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Young Joan sees her uncle loading hurt people into a lorry at night.
