Her aunt Harper says he is saving them, and tells Joan to stay silent.
Years later, adult Joan makes fancy hats for prisoners.
The prisoners are marched in the hats, and the hats are burned with the bodies.
In the last scene, rivers, animals, and weather seem to take sides in a war.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A thematic biography of London from early Britain to the end of the twentieth century.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Chatto and Windus published it in London in 2000. The catalog year 2000 is correct. The catalog genre Poetry is wrong. This is nonfiction prose. It later won a South Bank Show literature award.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ackroyd treats London as a living body, not only as a list of dates.
The book refuses one straight timeline from start to finish.
Chapters take up light, silence, childhood, speech, and drink.
He links present streets with older customs that still shape them.
The city is the main character of his novels and his biographies.

items.title: "Men in the Off Hours" (2000) — Anne Carson

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mixed book of short poems, epitaphs, scripts, and essays that puts ancient figures on modern time.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2000 matches the Knopf edition and the Canadian Encyclopedia. A Vintage paperback is dated 13 February 2001. The Griffin Poetry Prize came in 2001. Keep 2000 as the first year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Virginia Woolf and Thucydides (A modern novelist and an ancient historian, set side by side on war and time); The TV Men (A sequence that films mythic and literary figures as if for television)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book breaks her habit of one long poem.
It opens with Virginia Woolf and Thucydides thinking about war.
Epitaphs (short tomb texts) mark many cultures and stories.
The TV Men pieces put Sappho, Lazarus, Tolstoy, and others on a screen.
Father's Old Blue Cardigan faces her father's illness.
The closing piece is an epitaph for her mother, using Virginia Woolf's crossed out words.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Lahore novel about a fired banker, drugs, desire, and class after the nuclear tests.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2000 is correct. Hamid began a draft in a Princeton class taught by Toni Morrison, then finished the book while working at McKinsey. The first publication year is 2000.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Darashikoh Shezad (Daru) (A fired banker who becomes the accused man); Mumtaz (Ozi's wife, who begins an affair with Daru); Aurangzeb (Ozi) (Daru's rich friend and Mumtaz's husband)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Darashikoh Shezad, called Daru, loses his bank job in Lahore.
His rich friend Aurangzeb, called Ozi, returns from abroad.
Daru falls for Ozi's wife, Mumtaz.
He slides into drugs, debt, and crime.
The names recall the Mughal trial of Dara Shikoh by Aurangzeb.
The story sits in the summer of the 1998 nuclear tests.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A student hunts the life of a biographer and finds only scraps about three real men.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2000 is correct for the Chatto and Windus book. A scholarly chronology also says 2000. A separate Wikipedia page says 1 November 2001. Use 2000 in the exam.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Phineas G. Nanson (A postgraduate who wants a biography and finds only pieces); Scholes Destry-Scholes (The obscure biographer whose own life will not come clear)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Phineas G. Nanson leaves literary theory for facts he can touch.
He tries to write the life of the biographer Scholes Destry-Scholes.
The man himself stays almost unknown.
Phineas finds fragments on Linnaeus, Francis Galton, and Henrik Ibsen.
The novel mixes those real lives with invented papers.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An old woman tells family secrets around her sister's death and a hidden novel.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2000 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published it on 2 September 2000. It won the Booker Prize that year. This is Atwood's first Booker win, not the shared prize of 2019.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Iris Chase Griffen (The elderly narrator who controls the family story); Laura Chase (Iris's sister, whose death opens the book); Richard Griffen (Iris's rich and cruel husband); Alex Thomas (A radical young man tied to both sisters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Iris Chase writes a memoir in old age.
Her sister Laura drove a car off a bridge.
A novel said to be Laura's sits inside Iris's story.
That inner novel holds a science fiction tale of a blind assassin.
Newspapers, letters, and memory keep changing who wrote what.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An orphan's rise follows the Burmese royal family from the fall of Mandalay into war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2000 is correct. Ravi Dayal and Penguin India published it. Ghosh later withdrew it from the Commonwealth Writers Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Rajkumar (An Indian orphan who becomes a teak trader in Burma); Dolly (An attendant of the Burmese princesses, later Rajkumar's wife); King Thebaw (The last king of Burma, exiled by the British to Ratnagiri); Uma (The Collector's wife, who befriends Dolly and later travels the world)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1885 the British take Mandalay, and the royal family is sent to Ratnagiri in India.
Rajkumar, an Indian orphan, sees Dolly, a girl in the palace service, and loves her.
He grows rich in teak and later finds Dolly in exile.
Their families spread into rubber, soldiering, and the Second World War.
The novel asks how empire uses Indian soldiers and traders against other Asian peoples.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays on jet lag, airports, and what the word home means in a mixed up world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2000 is correct. Knopf, New York, February 2000. Bloomsbury issued a British edition the same year. The translation flag in the database is wrong. The book was written in English.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Pico Iyer (The essayist, using his own travels as the thread)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Knopf published the book in February 2000.
The subtitle is Jet Lag, Shopping Malls, and the Search for Home.
Iyer begins at Los Angeles airport, a town of shops with no real town.
He moves through Hong Kong hotels, the Atlanta Olympics, and Japan.
A global soul may be a person of many cultures, or a person always in transit.
The question of the book is where such a person can say home.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two wartime friends and their London families live with migration, faith, and science.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2000 is correct. Wikipedia dates the Hamish Hamilton book to 27 January 2000. A television adaptation followed in 2002.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Archie Jones (An indecisive Englishman who often chooses by flipping a coin); Samad Iqbal (Archie's Bangladeshi friend, a waiter torn between faith and London life); Irie Jones (The daughter of Archie and Clara, unsure of her place); Magid and Millat Iqbal (Twin brothers who take opposite paths, one scientific and one militant)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel focuses on the later lives of two wartime friends - The Bangladeshi Samad Iqbal and The Englishman Archie Jones and their families in London.
It depicts the picture of Dickens' A Tale of Two Cities.
On New Year's Day 1975, Archie Jones steps back from ending his life.
He marries Clara Bowden, a younger Jamaican woman, and they have a daughter, Irie.
His friend Samad Iqbal, a Bangladeshi waiter, has twin sons, Magid and Millat.
Samad sends Magid to Bangladesh, but the boy returns devoted to science.
Millat joins a strict Muslim group, while the Chalfen family pushes a FutureMouse experiment.
At the show, Archie is shot in the thigh, and the mouse escapes.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A British woman obsessed with Kabul disappears, and her husband and daughter go looking for her.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Kushner wrote it before 11 September 2001. Kika Markham read a version of the first scene in London in July 1999. That reading is not the premiere. Performances at New York Theatre Workshop began on 5 December 2001. Opening night was 19 December 2001, directed by Declan Donnellan. The database year 2001 is correct. The database genre Fiction is not.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The Homebody (A London woman whose monologue opens the play and who then disappears in Kabul); Milton Ceiling (Her husband, who comes to Kabul without her curiosity or her language); Priscilla Ceiling (Their daughter, who refuses the easy story of her mother's death)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The Homebody speaks a long monologue from an old guidebook to Kabul.
She describes an Afghan shopkeeper whose fingers were cut off.
She travels to Afghanistan and vanishes.
Her husband Milton and her daughter Priscilla search Kabul under Taliban rule.
One report says a mob killed her.
Another says she is alive and married.
The play does not settle it.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Conflicting papers reconstruct the killing of an American woman in a 1989 riot.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2001 is correct, but the nonfiction label is wrong. Wikipedia lists Riot under fiction, 2001. Tharoor's site calls it a novel and dates it 10 September 2001. He says he began it in December 1996 and finished near the end of 2000. The story is set in 1989.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Priscilla Hart (An American woman killed during the riot in Zalilgarh); The town speakers (Officials, friends, and witnesses whose accounts clash)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The fictional town is Zalilgarh, in Uttar Pradesh.
During a communal riot in 1989, Priscilla Hart is stabbed to death.
She is an American who has been living and loving in that town.
Diaries, letters, and reports give many versions of her death.
No single voice owns the truth.
Tharoor began the novel in 1996 and finished it near the end of 2000.

items.title: "The Algebra of Infinite Justice" (2001) — Arundhati Roy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays attack nuclear pride, big dams, and the war that followed the 2001 attacks.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2001 matches the first Indian book. A British Flamingo edition followed in 2002. The title essay appeared in periodicals in 2001. This is a book of essays, not a play. The database genre Drama is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Arundhati Roy (The essayist speaking in her own voice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
3. War is Peace (2001)
The End of Imagination answers India's nuclear tests of 1998.
The Greater Common Good attacks the Sardar Sarovar dam on the Narmada.
Power Politics says ordinary people, not only experts, must judge such projects.
The title essay answers the American war after the attacks of September 2001.
Later essays in the book look at violence in Gujarat and at empire.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Lambert family struggles through illness, money, and one last Christmas.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2001 is correct. Wikipedia dates the Farrar, Straus and Giroux edition 1 September 2001. Britannica places it weeks before 11 September 2001 and records the 2001 National Book Award.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Alfred Lambert (The strict father, a retired railroad man, now ill); Enid Lambert (The mother who wants one last family Christmas); Gary Lambert (The eldest son, a banker in Philadelphia); Chip Lambert (The middle son, a failed teacher living in New York); Denise Lambert (The daughter, a chef whose affairs cost her a job)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Alfred and Enid Lambert raised their children in the Midwestern town of St. Jude.
The adult children are Gary, Chip, and Denise.
Alfred has Parkinson's disease, and his mind begins to fail.
Enid pushes the children toward one last Christmas at home.
The Christmas fails, and Alfred is moved into a nursing home.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An old Parsi widower with Parkinson's disease is moved between his stepchildren and his daughter's crowded flat.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2002 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published it in 2002, and it was a Booker shortlist that year. One Wikipedia infobox prints 31 December 2001. Use 2002 for exam order.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nariman Vakeel (An elderly Parsi widower whose illness forces the family to rearrange itself); Roxana (Nariman's daughter, who takes him into her small flat); Yezad (Roxana's husband, strained by money and by the new duty); Mr Kapur (A man who hopes the city can be free of political terror)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nariman Vakeel is a retired professor of 79, living in Bombay.
He has Parkinson's disease (an illness of shaking and stiff movement) and then breaks an ankle.
His stepchildren can no longer manage him.
He moves in with his daughter Roxana, her husband Yezad, and their sons.
The small flat and Yezad's money worries turn care into a crisis.
A parallel strand follows Mr Kapur and the political fear in the city.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Nazneen leaves a Bangladeshi village for an arranged marriage in Tower Hamlets.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2003 is correct. The Booker Prize page and Ali's bibliography name Doubleday as the publisher, on 2 June 2003. One novel page names Scribner instead. Use Doubleday for the British first edition. The film is 2007.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nazneen (A young wife who grows from obedience toward choice); Chanu (Her older husband, full of plans that fail); Karim (A younger activist who brings sewing and becomes her lover); Hasina (Nazneen's sister, whose letters come from Dhaka)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Her debut novel "Brick Lane" was named after Brick Lane, a street at the heart of London's Bangladeshi Community.
The novel follows the life of Nazneen, a Bangladeshi woman who moves to London at the age of 18 to marry an older man Chanu, who has a face like a frog.
They live in Tower Hamlets. At first Nazneen's English consists only of 'Sorry' and 'Thank you'.
The novel explores her life and adaptations in the community as well as character of Chanu and their larger ethnic community.
An additional narrative strand covers the experiences of Nazneen's sister Hasina through the device of her correspondence.
The novel provoked controversy within the Bangladeshi community as they thought Ali has negatively portrayed people from the Sylhet region.
Greer criticized Monica Ali's "Brick Lane" as lack of authenticity as she had never spent much time in Brick Lane community.
Her other important books are: 1- Brick Lane (2003) 2- Alentejo Blue 3- In the Kitchen (2009) 4- Untold Story (2011): It is about princess Diana.
Nazneen comes to London at eighteen to marry Chanu.
At first her English is only sorry and thank you.
Letters from her sister Hasina show a harder life in Dhaka.
Chanu fails at work, and Nazneen sews at home for money.
She meets Karim and begins an affair.
She learns to choose, and she does not simply follow fate.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An aging novelist gives lectures on animals, evil, and belief, then faces a gate.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2003 is correct. Secker and Warburg published it on 30 September 2003. It was longlisted for the Booker Prize. Do not date the whole book 1999.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Elizabeth Costello (An aging novelist who lectures and doubts her fame); John (Her son, who travels with her and is embarrassed by her)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Elizabeth Costello is a famous Australian writer, weary of her early fame.
Her novel The House on Eccles Street retells Joyce from Molly Bloom's side.
She travels with her son John and lectures on realism and on animals.
Many of the lectures reuse pieces Coetzee had already given.
The Lives of Animals (1999) is absorbed into this book.
At the end she must explain her beliefs before a gate that may be the afterlife.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A quiet Delhi history teacher is attacked for a lesson on Basava and must choose a side.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2003 is correct. The story is set in 2000. That setting year is not the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Shiv Murthy (A middle aged history professor in New Delhi); Meena (A young woman with a broken knee who stays in his house); Basava (The twelfth century reformer and poet whose life Shiv teaches)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In the year 2000, Shiv Murthy teaches history at an open university in New Delhi.
He writes a lesson on Basava, a medieval reformer who opposed caste.
Hindu zealots attack the lesson and threaten his work.
Meena, a young woman with a broken knee, comes to stay while his wife is away.
He also faces the memory of his father, a freedom fighter who disappeared.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Kambili grows up under a violent Catholic father in Enugu, then tastes freedom in Nsukka.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2003 is correct for the first edition. Algonquin published it in the United States on 30 October 2003. Fourth Estate published it in Britain in 2004.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kambili Achike (The narrator, a shy girl of fifteen who learns to speak); Eugene Achike (Her rich Catholic father, generous in public and violent at home); Jaja (Her brother, who takes the blame for their father's death); Aunty Ifeoma (A lecturer in Nsukka whose freer house changes the children)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Algonquin Books published the novel in the United States in 2003.
Fourth Estate published the British edition in 2004.
Kambili tells how her brother Jaja refuses communion and the house breaks open.
Their father Eugene is a public hero and a private tyrant.
Their mother Beatrice poisons him, and Jaja goes to prison in her place.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Bengali American son struggles with the odd name his father gave him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2003 is correct. Houghton Mifflin published the novel in September 2003. Mira Nair later filmed it.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gogol Ganguli (The son, later legally Nikhil, caught between two names); Ashoke Ganguli (The father, saved in a train wreck by a page of Gogol); Ashima Ganguli (The mother, lonely in America and keeper of Bengali custom); Moushumi (Gogol's wife, whose affair ends the marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ashoke and Ashima Ganguli leave Kolkata and settle near Boston.
Ashoke once survived a train crash while holding a page of Gogol.
They name their son Gogol.
The boy grows up hating that name.
He becomes Nikhil, studies architecture, and drifts from his parents.
After Ashoke dies, Gogol returns to the book and the family story.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic fantasy about a public hero, a secret young man, and a returning demon.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The catalog year 2003 matches the author's account of the first Penguin India edition. Wikipedia and WorldCat list a 2004 Penguin India edition. A current Penguin India page says December 2005, which is a later listing. These are not three different novels.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Asvin (A prince of Avranti who is shaped into the public hero); Kirin (Maya's friend, a ravian who must act in secret); Maya (A spellbinder, a worker of magic, who tries to understand Kirin's past); Danh Gem (The rakshas whose promised return drives the plot)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Old prophecies say the rakshas (a demon) Danh Gem will return, and a hero will rise.
Prince Asvin is sent on a quest and is trained to be that hero.
Maya, a magic worker, learns that her friend Kirin belongs to a hidden people.
Kirin is pushed to work in secret with the people who want Danh Gem back.
On the day of the return he faces a hard choice and takes the dark lord's place.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems of a man who leaves 1990s Bombay and watches New York on 11 September 2001.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2004 is correct. Penguin in India and Rattapallax Press in New York both date the book 2004. The database calls it fiction. It is poetry.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The speaker leaves the violent street politics of 1990s Bombay.
He looks for a calmer life in New York.
He then sees the attacks of 11 September 2001.
English is his language and also his only country.
Water, addiction, and forgiveness run through the poems.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eight stories of women leaving, or failing to leave, a hard life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2004 is correct for the book. McClelland and Stewart published Runaway in Toronto in 2004. It won the Giller Prize that year. The title story had appeared in The New Yorker in 2003. The database file calls this book poetry. That label is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Carla (A young wife who wants to escape Clark and their failing life); Clark (Carla's husband, angry, controlling, and full of schemes); Juliet (The woman whose life is told in Chance, Soon, and Silence); Sylvia Jamieson (The neighbour who comes back from Greece and offers help)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In the title story, Carla lives with Clark and keeps a goat named Flora.
A neighbour, Sylvia Jamieson, offers Carla a way out of the marriage.
Clark talks of money and threats, and Carla tries to refuse the scheme.
Three linked stories, Chance, Soon, and Silence, follow a woman named Juliet.
Juliet later loses touch with her daughter Penelope.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Kathy H recalls Hailsham, where clones are raised to give their organs.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2005 is correct. Faber and Faber published it. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize and lost to John Banville's The Sea.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kathy H (The narrator, a clone who works as a carer); Tommy (Kathy's friend, a donor with little gift for art); Ruth (Kathy's school friend, who later regrets keeping her from Tommy); Miss Emily (The head of Hailsham)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Kathy H, aged 31, is a carer for organ donors.
She remembers Hailsham, a boarding school with almost no outside contact.
Her friends are Ruth and Tommy.
Miss Lucy tells them they are clones, made to donate organs.
They hope love might delay the donations.
That hope is false.
Donors complete, which means they die.
Time magazine named it the best novel of 2005.

items.title: "No Country for Old Men" (2005) — Cormac McCarthy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Llewelyn Moss takes drug money in Texas, and the killer Anton Chigurh hunts him.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Knopf published the novel on 19 July 2005. McCarthy had first shaped the story as a screenplay. The Coen brothers' film opened in 2007 and won the Academy Award for Best Picture. Database year 2005 is the book, not the film.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Llewelyn Moss (A welder and Vietnam veteran who takes the drug money); Anton Chigurh (A killer who recovers the money and decides fates by a coin); Ed Tom Bell (An aging sheriff who feels overmatched by the new violence); Carla Jean Moss (Llewelyn's wife, killed by Chigurh after she calls the coin)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1980, Moss finds a case of drug money in the Texas desert.
He goes back with water for a dying man, and that choice starts the hunt.
Anton Chigurh tracks the cash, while Sheriff Ed Tom Bell tries to help.
Moss is killed in El Paso.
Chigurh then kills Carla Jean after a coin toss.
Bell retires and dreams of his father riding ahead with fire in a horn.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two unlike families clash over art, race, and campus politics near Boston.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2005 is correct. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 2005 and won the Orange Prize in 2006. Do not use 2006 as the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Howard Belsey (A Rembrandt scholar whose liberal ideas fail in his own home); Kiki Belsey (Howard's African American wife); Monty Kipps (A conservative rival who challenges the campus on race and faith); Carlene Kipps (Monty's wife, who leaves a painting to Kiki)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Howard Belsey, a white English professor, lives in Wellington with his wife Kiki.
His rival is Monty Kipps, a conservative Trinidadian scholar who moves to the same campus.
The wives, Kiki and Carlene, become friends over a Haitian painting.
Carlene dies and means the painting for Kiki, but Monty keeps it.
Howard's affairs and a failed lecture leave the marriage badly shaken.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A Mumbai waiter explains his life so a lawyer can show he did not cheat.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2005 is correct. His site dates the book 1 April 2005. A 2022 profile says he wrote it in two months while posted in London (2000-2003). The film is 2008.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ram Mohammad Thomas (An orphan waiter whose name holds Hindu, Muslim, and Christian parts); Smita Shah (The lawyer who hears his story, and who is really the girl Gudiya); Salim (Ram's friend, who dreams of becoming a film star); Prem Kumar (The quiz host, whom Ram blames for harming people he loves); Nita (The young woman Ram loves and marries)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ram Mohammad Thomas wins the show Who Will Win a Billion? and is jailed.
Police say a poor orphan could not know every answer.
His lawyer, Smita Shah, hears one life story for each question.
The stories cross Delhi, Agra, and the slums of Mumbai.
Smita is really Gudiya, a girl he once tried to save.
He is freed, and he marries Nita.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A theory book that defends adaptation as a normal way of retelling stories.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2006 is correct for the first edition. The revised edition is 2013. Her own site also mentions a 2012 reprint. The catalog genre Poetry is wrong. This is theory.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hutcheon asks what happens when a story moves into a new medium.
She looks at film, opera, songs, games, and theme parks.
She says an adaptation is both a finished product and a process.
Audiences often know the earlier version and compare the two.
She rejects the habit of calling every adaptation a lesser copy.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A vast novel from the 1893 Chicago fair to the years after World War I.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2006 is correct. Penguin Press published it on 21 November 2006. Let the reader beware is from Pynchon's own synopsis of the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Webb Traverse (An anarchist who uses dynamite against mine and railroad bosses); Scarsdale Vibe (A rich man behind the killing of Webb Traverse); The Chums of Chance (A boyish airship crew, including Randolph St. Cosmo)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Penguin Press published the novel on 21 November 2006.
The story runs from the Chicago World's Fair of 1893 to just after World War I.
It moves through America, Europe, Mexico, and Central Asia.
Webb Traverse, a dynamiter, is killed, and his sons seek revenge.
The Chums of Chance, a crew on an airship, weave through the many plots.

items.title: "Half of a Yellow Sun" (2006) — Adichie, Chimamanda Ngozi

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Olanna, Odenigbo, and the houseboy Ugwu live through the Biafran war.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2006 is correct. The British edition is from Fourth Estate. The American edition is also 2006, from Knopf. It won the Women's Prize for Fiction in 2007.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ugwu (A village boy who becomes Odenigbo's houseboy and a witness to war); Odenigbo (A radical mathematics professor at Nsukka); Olanna (Odenigbo's partner, from a rich Igbo family); Kainene (Olanna's twin, who runs a refugee camp and does not return); Richard (An English writer who loves Kainene and studies Igbo art)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel was published in 2006.
The title names the sun on the Biafran flag.
Ugwu comes from a village to work for the professor Odenigbo in Nsukka.
Olanna leaves a rich Lagos life to join Odenigbo, and her twin is Kainene.
The war of 1967 to 1970 scatters them into hunger, flight, and loss.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Game coders whose surnames start with J survive a chaotic Vancouver office.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2006 is correct. The first Canadian edition is from Random House Canada, and the United States edition is from Bloomsbury. It is a novel, not a second copy of Microserfs.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ethan Jarlewski (The narrator, a game coder in the JPod office); Kaitlin (A coworker Ethan grows close to)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Random House Canada and Bloomsbury published JPod in 2006.
Ethan Jarlewski narrates from a video game company.
His pod is named JPod because the surnames start with J.
The pages mix the story with spam, numbers, and office junk.
Readers often call it a later take on Microserfs.
It is a novel of 2006, not a poem and not Generation X.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A huge Mumbai crime novel about a policeman and a gangster who dies as the case starts.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Penguin India and Faber published it in 2006. HarperCollins published the United States edition in January 2007. The catalog year 2006 is right for the first publication. A Netflix series followed in 2018. Do not use 2018 as the novel's date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sartaj Singh (A Sikh police inspector in Mumbai, first seen in the 1997 stories); Ganesh Gaitonde (A powerful gangster who tells his life and then dies)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Inspector Sartaj Singh gets a tip about the gangster Ganesh Gaitonde.
Gaitonde speaks to Sartaj, then kills himself in a concrete hideout.
One track tells Gaitonde's rise through the Bombay underworld.
The other track follows Sartaj as he hunts the meaning of those last words.
The case grows past one gang and takes in the whole city.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Tambu enters a mostly white convent school while the liberation war scars her family.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2006 is correct. Ayebia Clarke Publishing in Britain issued the first edition. Later Graywolf reprints are not the first publication.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tambudzai (The same narrator, now a student in a mostly white convent school.); Nyasha (Tambu's questioning cousin, still part of the family story.); Babamukuru (The uncle whose authority and war injuries still shape Tambu's chances.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ayebia Clarke in Britain published this sequel in 2006.
Tambu begins secondary school at the Young Ladies College of the Sacred Heart.
A mine blast in the war injures her uncle and her sister.
At the white school she meets unfair treatment and lost credit for her work.
After school she takes an advertising job and still feels cut off from herself.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A retired judge, his granddaughter Sai, and the cook's son Biju face loss in India and America.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2006 is correct. Hamish Hamilton and Atlantic Monthly Press published it in 2006. It won the Booker Prize that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sai (An orphan girl living with her grandfather in Kalimpong); Jemubhai Patel (Sai's grandfather, a retired judge shaped by England); Biju (The cook's son, living as an illegal worker in the United States); The cook (Biju's father, who serves the judge and waits for news of his son)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The story is centered on two main characters Biju and Sai.
Biju is an illegal Indian Immigrant living in the U.S, the son of the cook who works for Sai's grandfather.
Sai, is a girl living in the mountainous 'Kalimpong' with her maternal grandfather Jemubhai.
The action of the novel takes place in 1986.
The Novel follows the journey of Biju and Sai, an Anglicized Indian girl living with her grandfather in India.
The Gorkhaland Movement is used as a historic backdrop in the novel.
The retired judge Jemubhai Patel is a man disgusted at Indian ways and customs, so much so, that he eats chapatis with a knife and fork, hates all Indians including his father, whom he break ties with and wife who he abandons at his father's place after torturing her but he never accepted by the British in spite of his education and adopted mannerism.
The story is set in 1986, in Kalimpong and in the United States.
Sai, an orphan, lives with her grandfather, the retired judge Jemubhai Patel.
The judge was trained in England and now scorns Indian ways.
Biju, the cook's son, works illegally in America and moves from one hard job to another.
The Gorkhaland movement (a demand for a Nepali speaking region) disturbs the hill town.
The novel links colonial shame, migration, and violence across two generations.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A father and son walk south through a dead America and try to stay good.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Knopf published it on 26 September 2006. It won the 2007 Pulitzer Prize for Fiction. A film followed in 2009. One database label calls it drama, but it is a novel. Database year 2006 is correct for the book.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The man (The father, who is already ill as they travel); The boy (His son, who keeps asking whether other people are good guys); The mother (The boy's mother, already dead by suicide before the journey)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An unnamed disaster has killed almost all life and covered the roads in ash.
A father and his boy push a cart south, hoping to reach the sea.
They hide from people who eat human flesh, and once find a hidden store of food.
The father says they are the good guys and that they are carrying the fire.
The father dies, and another family takes the boy on.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A survivor walks out of the 2001 attacks and cannot return to ordinary time.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2007 is correct. The New Yorker excerpt is April 2007, and the Scribner book is May 2007. The attacks in the story are 2001, not the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Keith (A survivor who walks away from the towers through ash and rubble); Falling Man (A performance artist who restages the fall in public places)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
An excerpt called Still Life appeared in The New Yorker in April 2007.
Scribner published the novel in May 2007.
Keith walks north through ash, smoke, and falling paper.
The book follows how that morning changes the life after it.
A performance artist called Falling Man repeats the image of a fall.
The novel studies news pictures of terror and the work of starting again.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Changez tells an American stranger in Lahore how he left a New York career after 2001.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2007 is correct. Hamish Hamilton published the British book on 1 March 2007. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize that year. It did not win.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Changez (A Pakistani lecturer who narrates his American years); The American (A silent, nervous listener in the Lahore cafe); Erica (An American writer Changez loves); Jim (The man at Underwood Samson who recruits Changez)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In a Lahore cafe, Changez stops an unnamed American.
He tells of Princeton, then a job at Underwood Samson.
He loves Erica, who still grieves for a dead boyfriend.
After the attacks of 11 September 2001, his feeling about America changes.
He grows a beard, leaves the firm, and returns to Lahore.
The book ends before we know what the American reaches for.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A mother lies awake before she tells her twins a secret about their father.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2007 is correct. Picador published the novel in 2007. It did not win the Booker Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Paula Hook (The mother whose thoughts make the whole novel.); Mike Hook (Her husband, who is part of the morning confession.); Nick and Kate (The sixteen-year-old twins who are still asleep.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Paula Hook is awake in the night while her family sleeps.
In the morning she and Mike will speak to the twins.
The twins are Nick and Kate, and they are sixteen.
The secret is about who their father is.
An unnamed donor, not Mike, is the birth father.
The whole book stays inside Paula's thoughts on that one night.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In the late 1600s, Florens is given away, and a small farm holds many kinds of bondage.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2008 is correct. Knopf published the novel on 11 November 2008. It is a later slavery novel, not the third book of the Beloved trilogy. That third book is Paradise, 1997.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Florens (A young enslaved girl whose telling frames the novel); Jacob Vaark (A European farmer who takes Florens to pay a debt); Rebekka (Jacob's wife, sent from England to marry a man she has not seen); Lina (A Native woman on the farm, survivor of a smallpox outbreak)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel is set in colonial America in the late seventeenth century.
Jacob Vaark, a farmer, accepts a girl as payment of a debt.
That girl is Florens, who narrates much of the book.
The household also holds Lina, Sorrow, and Jacob's wife Rebekka.
They are Native, Black, and European, and none is simply free.
When Rebekka falls ill, Florens is sent on a dangerous journey.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Linked stories of class and faith in the fictional coastal town of Kittur.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Picador published it in India on 1 November 2008. Britain and the United States published it in 2009. The database year 2008 is the Indian first edition. Much of it was written before The White Tiger, though the Indian book came later.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The people of Kittur (Separate speakers in linked stories, not one continuing hero)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
This novel counts for the period between the assassination of India Gandhi and Rajiv Gandhi.
The title means the years between two killings of Indian prime ministers.
Indira Gandhi was killed in 1984, and Rajiv Gandhi was killed in 1991.
Each story enters a different street, caste, or job in Kittur.
Kittur is based on Mangalore, then changed to hold more kinds of lives.
Places and names return, but there is no single hero.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Farmers, sailors, and a ruined landlord meet on the ship Ibis in the opium trade.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2008 is correct. The Indian edition appeared on 14 October 2008. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize. It did not win.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Deeti (A village woman who escapes her husband's funeral pyre); Kalua (An ox driver of a lower caste who flees with Deeti); Zachary Reid (An American sailor who becomes an officer on the Ibis); Neel Rattan Halder (A raja convicted and transported after an opium debt); Paulette Lambert (A French orphan in Calcutta who boards the Ibis in disguise)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In the 1830s, Deeti's husband works in an opium factory on the Ganges.
She flees a forced death on his pyre with Kalua, a man of a lower caste.
Zachary Reid, a mixed race American sailor, rises on the ship Ibis.
The raja Neel Rattan Halder is jailed and put on the same ship.
The Ibis sails for Mauritius with indentured workers (people bound by contract to labour far away).

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Meera tells of a hard marriage and a fierce love for her son in independent India.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2008 is right. W. W. Norton lists 12 February 2008. This is the second novel in the India trilogy, after The Death of Vishnu (2001).

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Meera (The narrator, a young woman whose marriage and motherhood shape the novel); Dev (The singer Meera marries, from a strict family); Roopa (Meera's elder and more beautiful sister); Arya (Dev's brother, drawn to Meera and to right-wing politics); Ashwin (Meera's son, and the centre of her consuming love)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Meera is seventeen when she first sees the singer Dev.
She takes him from her elder sister Roopa, then the marriage turns harsh.
Dev's family is strict.
His brother Arya wants Meera and backs harsh nationalist politics.
A brief kindness with her sister-in-law Sandhya does not last.
After her son Ashwin is born, her love for him takes over the story.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A village driver writes how he murdered his employer and became a businessman.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Atlantic published it in Britain and HarperCollins in India in 2008. It won the Man Booker Prize in 2008. The database year 2008 is correct. The film came later, in 2021.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Balram Halwai (The narrator, a driver who becomes a Bangalore businessman); Ashok (The landlord's son whom Balram drives and later kills); Pinky Madam (Ashok's wife, who hits someone on the road and leaves); Wen Jiabao (The Chinese premier who never answers Balram's letters)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel provides a darkly humorous perspective of India's class struggle in a globalized world as told through a retrospective narration from Balram Halwai, a village boy. He is praised one day as a rare "white tiger" by a visiting School inspector".
The novel depicts Balram's killing his master in Delhi and flees to Bangalore. Ultimately he transcends his sweet maker caste and becomes a successful entrepreneur, establishing his own Taxi Service.
In this novel Balram believes that there are two Indians - "The Impoverished Darkness of the Rural inner continent" and the "Light of urban coastal India".
Balram Halwai writes seven night letters to the Chinese premier.
He leaves a poor village, works in a tea shop, and learns to drive.
He drives Ashok, a landlord's son, in Dhanbad and then in Delhi.
He calls the trap of the poor the Rooster Coop.
He kills Ashok, takes a bribe, and starts a taxi firm in Bangalore.

items.title: "The Woman Who Thought She Was a Planet and Other Stories" (2008) — Vandana Singh

fields.label: Work Title
fields.value: The Woman Who Thought She Was a Planet and Other Stories

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 2008 collection of stories and one essay that set strange science inside Indian lives.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2008 is the first book edition, from Zubaan and Penguin India. Separate stories came earlier: The Room on the Roof in 2002, the title story in 2003, and Delhi in 2004. A later Zubaan note says 2009, but that is not the first edition year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The woman in the title story (She tells her husband that small alien creatures live inside her.); Her husband (He must face her claim and the crack in their ordinary home.); The Delhi watcher (A man who meets people from other times in the same city.); The mathematics teacher (In Infinities, he wants to understand what infinity means.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Zubaan and Penguin India published the first edition in 2008.
In the title story, a woman tells her husband that tiny alien beings live in her body.
In Delhi, a man meets figures from the city's past and its future.
Infinities follows a mathematics teacher who longs to grasp infinity.
The Tetrahedron follows a girl in Delhi who finds a tetrahedron (a solid with four faces).
The book also includes an essay, A Speculative Manifesto.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Poems of grief after the death of his wife, Shakti Bhatt, in 2007.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2008 is correct for the book. The Sahitya Akademi Award is 2012. The database calls the book fiction. It is poetry.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book is dedicated to his wife, who died in 2007.
Private grief opens into a wider sense of loss.
He uses old forms, including the sonnet, the ghazal, and the sestina.
A ghazal repeats an end phrase.
A sestina repeats six end words.
The Sahitya Akademi Award for English came in 2012, four years after the book.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Eight stories on Bengali American children, parents, loss, and new ground.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2008 is correct. Alfred A. Knopf published the book in April 2008. It won the Frank O'Connor International Short Story Award that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ruma (A daughter in Seattle, unsure how to live with her father); Ruma's father (A retired widower who wants a freer old age); Hema (A scholar who meets Kaushik again in Rome); Kaushik (A photographer whose life is cut short by the 2004 tsunami)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book holds eight stories in two parts.
In the title story, a widowed father visits his daughter Ruma.
Ruma has left her law job and feels she should house her father.
The last three stories follow Hema and Kaushik over many years.
The title comes from a preface by Nathaniel Hawthorne.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Chef Gabriel Lightfoot's London hotel life breaks after a porter is found dead.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2009 is correct. It is her third novel, after Brick Lane in 2003 and Alentejo Blue in 2006. Do not call it the immediate next book after Brick Lane.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Gabriel Lightfoot (An ambitious chef from a northern mill town); Lena (A young migrant connected with the dead porter); Charlie (Gabriel's girlfriend, who leaves when she learns of Lena)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Gabriel Lightfoot is executive chef at the Imperial Hotel.
His kitchen staff come from many countries.
A night porter is found dead in the basement.
Gabriel shelters Lena, a young migrant tied to that death.
His restaurant plan, his girlfriend, and his family story all crack.
The hotel becomes a picture of a Britain unsure of itself.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays ask how Indian democracy can live beside mass violence and unfreedom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2009 matches the Penguin India book. Some lists print 2010. The American title is often Field Notes on Democracy. These are essays, and many appeared in papers first.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Arundhati Roy (The essayist reporting on Indian politics in her own voice)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title essay links democracy with the danger of genocide (the mass killing of a people).
Roy writes about the 2002 violence in Gujarat.
Other pieces turn to Kashmir, Maoist regions, and the power of the state.
She treats the essays as field notes, reports from events she has watched.
Many chapters began as talks or as pieces in newspapers and magazines.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Berglund marriage cracks under love, politics, and a wish to be free.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2010 is correct. Wikipedia dates the American edition 31 August 2010. Britannica confirms the year 2010.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Patty Berglund (Walter's wife, whose private confession drives much of the plot); Walter Berglund (A lawyer who turns to environmental work); Richard Katz (Walter's college friend, a rock musician and Patty's lover); Joey Berglund (The son whose choices shake the marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Patty and Walter Berglund seem like a model couple in St. Paul.
Their son Joey moves toward the family next door.
Patty has an affair with Walter's old friend, the musician Richard Katz.
Walter works to save a small songbird and a piece of wild land.
The family comes apart, then the bonds pull them back.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: His last collection weighs illness, memory, and the links between people.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2010 is correct. Faber published it on 2 September 2010. It won the Forward Prize that October.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The poet (An aging speaker who remembers help, loss, and recovery)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the twelfth and the final poetry collection of Heaney.
It won him Forward Poetry Prize 2010 and Irish Times Poetry Prize 2011.
The first poem of collection is Had I Not been Awake. Famous Quote: "There is risk and truth to yourselves and the world before you".
Faber published Human Chain in 2010.
It was his first collection after a stroke in 2006.
Poems recall being lifted, helped, and returned to life.
Memory reaches back to childhood and to the dead.
The book won the Forward Prize for Best Collection in 2010.
It was his last new book of poems.
He died in 2013.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A boxed elegy for her brother Michael, folded like an accordion and built on Catullus 101.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2010 matches the Canadian Encyclopedia and a Harvard Crimson review of April 2010. The New Directions web page lists 1 April 2009. Use 2010 as the publication year. Her brother died in 2000. That is not the book year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anne Carson (The sister who tries to translate both a Latin poem and a lost brother); Michael (Her brother, who disappeared in 1978 and died in 2000); Catullus (The Roman poet whose poem 101 mourns his own brother)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Michael left Canada in 1978 and lived under other names.
He died in Copenhagen in 2000, before they could meet again.
Carson mourns him through Catullus 101, a Latin elegy for a brother.
Each Latin word gets a dictionary page, like a slow translation.
Photos, letters, and scraps sit with the words.
The pages fold out in one long strip, inside a box.

items.title: "Attack of the Difficult Poems" (2011) — Charles Bernstein

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Later essays that defend hard poems and joke about how to read them.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2011 is correct. The book is in English. The catalogue translation flag does not fit this essay collection.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Charles Bernstein (The critic and comic guide to difficult poems)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The University of Chicago Press published the book in 2011.
The subtitle calls the pieces essays and inventions.
The opening mimics an advice guide to the difficult poem.
Bernstein says a hard poem may be trying to catch your attention.
Other pieces discuss readings, sound archives, and poetry month.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Ibis story moves to Canton, where a Parsi merchant races a Chinese ban on opium.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2011 is correct. It was published on 18 June 2011. This is a novel, the second Ibis book. The database genre label Poetry is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Bahram Modi (A Parsi opium merchant from Bombay, father of Ah Fatt); Neel Rattan Halder (The former raja, now a fugitive working as Bahram's clerk); Ah Fatt (Bahram's son by a Chinese woman, escaped from the Ibis); Paulette Lambert (The French botanist's daughter, hunting a rare plant in China); Lin Zexu (The Chinese official sent to stop the opium trade)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
After a storm, some people from the Ibis reach Canton, while others go on to Mauritius.
Bahram Modi, a Parsi trader from Bombay, brings a huge opium cargo to China.
China is moving to stop the trade, led by Commissioner Lin Zexu.
Neel becomes Bahram's munshi (clerk and translator) in the foreign quarter.
The book ends just before the First Opium War breaks open.

items.title: "The Sense of an Ending" (2011) — Julian Barnes

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: An old man learns that his tidy memory of youth left out the harm.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Jonathan Cape published it on 4 August 2011. It won the Booker Prize in October 2011. The database year 2011 is correct. A film of the novel appeared in 2017.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Tony Webster (The retired narrator, whose memory is incomplete); Veronica Ford (Tony's former girlfriend, who keeps the missing diary); Adrian Finn (The brilliant school friend who later dies by suicide); Sarah Ford (Veronica's mother, whose will reopens the past)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The title is borrowed from a book of the same name by Frank Kermode first published in 1967 subtitled "Studies in the Theory of Fiction".
It is divided into two parts "one" and "two" both are narrated by Tony Webster.
In October 2011, it was awarded Man Booker's Prize and the following year nominated in the novels category at Costa Book Awards.
Tony Webster recalls school friends and the clever Adrian Finn.
At university he dates Veronica, and the romance ends in anger.
Adrian later goes out with Veronica and then takes his own life.
Decades later a lawyer's letter brings Tony a small bequest.
Veronica's mother has left him money and two documents.
He rereads a cruel letter he had forgotten writing.
He thinks he understands the past, but Veronica says he still does not.
The young man he meets is the son of Veronica's mother, Sarah.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Her last story book, closing with four pieces close to her own life.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2012 is correct. McClelland and Stewart published Dear Life in 2012. It was her last collection. The Canadian Encyclopedia notes the Trillium Book Award for it in 2013. The database file calls this book poetry. That label is wrong.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The mother in To Reach Japan (A woman traveling by train with her young daughter toward Toronto)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Most of the stories return to southwestern Ontario, with Toronto nearby.
To Reach Japan follows a mother and her child on a long train ride.
The last four pieces are grouped under the heading Finale.
Munro called those four pieces autobiographical in feeling, though only in part.
She said they were the closest things she had to say about her own life.

items.title: "From the Ruins of Empire" (2012) — Pankaj Mishra

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A history of Asian thinkers who answered Western empire and remade political ideas.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Allen Lane published the UK book in London in 2012. The US edition is also 2012. The database calls it poetry and places it in Unit 2. That label is wrong. It is nonfiction. It won the Crossword Award for nonfiction in 2013.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani (A Muslim intellectual and traveller who framed Islam against Western power); Liang Qichao (A Chinese reform writer who rethought the state after defeat); Rabindranath Tagore (The Indian poet who appears as a voice for Asia's separate future)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book asks how Asia could recover dignity after Western conquest in the late 1800s.
It follows Jamal al-Din al-Afghani, a Muslim thinker who travelled across Asia and Europe.
It follows Liang Qichao, a Chinese reformer who studied Japan, America, and revolution.
It follows Rabindranath Tagore, the Indian writer who argued for Asia's own path.
Mishra ties their hopes to later nations, parties, and religious movements.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Four people from one London estate struggle with class, friendship, and adult choice.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2012 is correct. Wikipedia dates the Hamish Hamilton book to 27 August 2012. A BBC film of the novel was shown in 2016.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Leah Hanwell (A social worker who stays near her old estate and hides a wish not to have children); Natalie Blake (Born Keisha, she is a barrister who feels trapped by her success); Felix Cooper (A man leaving addiction, murdered on his way home); Nathan Bogle (A once promising boy who now lives by crime)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Leah Hanwell still lives near the Caldwell estate in north west London.
Her friend Keisha Blake has become Natalie, a successful lawyer.
Felix Cooper tries to leave drugs behind and is killed after a train quarrel.
Natalie breaks down at Carnival and walks the streets with Nathan Bogle.
The women tell the police that Nathan knows about the killing.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A comic history of how Canada and the United States have treated Native people, especially over land.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Doubleday Canada published it on 13 November 2012. It won the RBC Taylor Prize in 2014 and the British Columbia National Award for Canadian Non-Fiction. A film version premiered in 2020. The database year 2012 is correct. The database genre Fiction is not. When the book appeared, King still said he was part Cherokee. In 2025 he rejected that claim.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Thomas King (The essayist, speaking in a comic, personal voice rather than as a novel character)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
King tells Native history in North America as a conversation, not as a neutral textbook.
He separates romantic images, living people, and people defined by law.
Films and stories keep a dead, costume version of Indians in public view.
Governments in Canada and the United States move, define, and reduce Native nations.
The argument returns to land.
As long as Native people hold land, the conflict continues.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: During the Emergency, a young journalist in fictional Mangobaag goes underground and later becomes a statue.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2012 matches Wikipedia and The Hindu, which call it the debut already in stores. HarperCollins India is the publisher. One later academic page says 2011. Do not use 2011 as the publication year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Raj Iyer (A young journalist who vanishes and later becomes a town statue); Teacher Bhatt (A retired schoolmaster who longs to be known as a writer); Rabia Sheik (A resident of the same small world, chasing an ordinary life); Shankar Iyer (Another Mangobaag neighbour living through the Emergency)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
India is under the Emergency (the 1975 to 1977 suspension of civil rights).
Raj Iyer, a young journalist, lives by the Vicks mango tree in Mangobaag.
He publishes a mocking piece and then goes underground.
Years later he reappears as a bronze statue in a park.
Nobody is sure why the town now calls him a hero.
Teacher Bhatt, Rabia Sheik, and Shankar Iyer chase smaller dreams beside that story.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Passengers on a London to Delhi flight gain powers, and one of them wants to rule the world.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Catalog year 2012 is correct for the first edition. Titan Books published it in the UK on 6 July 2012 and in the US on 9 July 2013. The author has said he began writing it in 2009. That start year rests on one interview, so it is not entered as a fixed composition date.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Aman Sen (A young man who can control communications and tries to steer the others); Vir (An Indian Air Force pilot who can now fly on his own); Uzma (A British Pakistani actress whose power is extreme charm); Jai (An almost unkillable man who wants military rule of the world)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Aman Sen leaves a plane from London to Delhi and finds he can master networks.
Everyone on that flight gains a power that matches a deep wish.
Vir, a fighter pilot, can fly.
Uzma gains overwhelming charm.
Jai is nearly impossible to hurt, and he wants to rule the world.
Aman tries to use the powers to help people, but every help also harms someone.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 2013 poetry book on the mind, time, and consciousness from birth toward dementia.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2013 is correct. Graywolf Press published the book, and Oberlin College notes September 2013. The Pulitzer Prize came in 2014. That prize year is not the publication year.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Graywolf Press published 3 Sections in 2013.
The book mixes rhymed lyrics, long meditations, and a prose essay.
The poems look at human consciousness from birth toward dementia, a loss of memory.
The poem This Morning opens with three visions of disaster.
The Pulitzer Prize for Poetry went to this book in 2014.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Ifemelu and Obinze love, migrate, and meet again across Nigeria, America, and Britain.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2013 is correct. Knopf published it on 14 May 2013. It won the National Book Critics Circle Award for Fiction. The database calls it poetry. It is a novel.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Ifemelu (A Nigerian woman whose blog records race in America); Obinze (Her first love, who migrates to London and later grows rich in Lagos)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Alfred A. Knopf published the novel on 14 May 2013.
Ifemelu leaves Nigeria to study in the United States.
There she learns what it means to be called Black, and she writes a blog on race.
Obinze cannot get an American visa and spends hard years in London.
Years later both return to a richer Nigeria and ask if love can start again.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A childless couple is broken by village taunts and a temple festival custom.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The catalog year 2013 is the English translation. The Tamil novel Madhorubhagan was published by Kalachuvadu in 2010. Aniruddhan Vasudevan's English version, One Part Woman, came from Penguin India in 2013. A United States edition from Grove Atlantic came in 2018.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kali (A farmer who loves Ponna but cannot bear the festival plan); Ponna (Kali's wife, blamed for their childlessness and sent to the festival)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Kali and Ponna have been married for twelve years and have no child.
The village taunts them, and some people tell Kali to take a second wife.
The families point to the chariot festival of Ardhanarishvara (a form of Shiva who is half woman) at Tiruchengode.
On one day of that festival, the usual ban on sex outside marriage is set aside.
Ponna is taken to the festival without a clear yes from Kali, and the marriage cracks.

items.title: "Tales from a Vending Machine" (2013) — Anees Salim

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Hasina Mansoor, a young woman at an airport vending machine, tells her longings and troubles.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2013 is correct. Wikipedia, The Hindu, and Literaturforum Indien all place this HarperCollins novel in 2013, after The Vicks Mango Tree.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Hasina Mansoor (A young woman who tends an airport vending machine and watches the world)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Hasina Mansoor is a young Muslim woman.
She works at a vending machine in an airport.
Travelers and the changing aviation business pass in front of her.
The voice is lively, but the troubles are real.
The book helped publishers look again at his earlier manuscripts.
It is a novel of one working life, not a book of folk tales.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In a threatened Mumbai, Sarita and Jaz both search for the missing Karun.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2013 is right. W. W. Norton published it. It closes the trilogy. He had planned a Brahma novel, then based this book on Devi instead.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Sarita (Karun's wife, who crosses the city to find him); Karun (A missing physicist, loved by both Sarita and Jaz); Jaz (Karun's former male lover, searching for him in the chaos); Devi (The mother goddess whom the city hopes will save it)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Mumbai is nearly empty under the threat of nuclear war.
Sarita searches for her husband Karun, a physicist.
She carries a last pomegranate, hoping it will help her find him.
Jaz, Karun's former lover, joins the search for his own reasons.
Hindu and Muslim gangs fill the streets, and both seekers move toward Devi.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A fierce novel about the 1968 burning of 44 Dalit labourers in Kilvenmani.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2014 is correct. UK edition: Atlantic Books, April 2014. Indian edition: HarperCollins, April 2014. The massacre itself was on 25 December 1968, not in 2014.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A sharp voice that steps into the story and argues with the reader); The Kilvenmani labourers (Landless Dalit men, women, and children who strike for wages); The landlords (Upper caste owners who answer the strike with fire)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Atlantic Books in Britain and HarperCollins in India published it in April 2014.
Landlords in Tanjore district rule landless Dalit workers in the rice fields.
Communist organisers help the workers demand better wages.
On 25 December 1968, landlords and their men attack Kilvenmani.
They lock 44 people, including women and children, in a hut and burn it.
The narrator keeps breaking the story to say how hard it is to write this truth.

items.title: "When God Is a Traveller" (2014) — Arundhathi Subramaniam

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A 2014 poetry book about sacred journeys, city life, gender, and being human.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Bloodaxe in Britain and HarperCollins in India both published it in 2014. The catalog year 2014 is correct. The Sahitya Akademi Award for this book came in 2020, not in 2014.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The speaker (A traveller who looks for the divine in myth and in city life)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems follow a speaker who seeks the divine in ordinary places.
They mix Hindu myth with life in a huge Indian city.
They face doubt, the body, love, and the limits of a human life.
The book asks how a person steps into a story and also steps out of it.
It was a Poetry Book Society Choice and was shortlisted for the Eliot Prize.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: The Ibis story ends in the First Opium War, among soldiers, traders, and a widow.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2015 is correct. John Murray published it on 28 May 2015. It is the last Ibis novel. It won the Crossword Book Jury Award in fiction that year.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kesri Singh (Deeti's brother, an Indian sepoy in British service); Zachary Reid (The American sailor who enters the China trade); Shireen Modi (Bahram Modi's Parsi widow, travelling to China); Neel Rattan Halder (The former raja, still running from a false conviction)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1839 Kesri Singh, Deeti's brother, serves the British as a sepoy (an Indian soldier).
Zachary Reid pushes into the opium business and hides his mixed birth.
Shireen Modi, Bahram's widow, sails toward China to face her husband's secret child.
Neel stays a fugitive after the false case that ruined him.
The First Opium War of 1839 to 1841 pulls them into the fighting.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A young inter-caste couple returns to a village that will not accept the bride.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The catalog year 2016 is the English translation. The Tamil novel Pookkuzhi came out in 2013. Aniruddhan Vasudevan's English Pyre was published by Hamish Hamilton in 2016. A Pushkin Press paperback in 2022 was longlisted for the International Booker Prize in 2023.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Kumaresan (A young man who brings his new wife home and hopes the village will calm down); Saroja (His wife, marked as an outsider by her looks and her unknown caste); Marayi (Kumaresan's mother, who leads the hostility to the marriage)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Kumaresan and Saroja marry in secret because they come from different castes.
They go to his rocky village, and his mother Marayi curses the match.
Neighbours doubt Saroja's caste, and a village council cuts the couple off from common life.
Saroja learns of a plan to kill her while Kumaresan is away.
The villagers set the bushes alight around her as his cycle is heard returning.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Two girls who love dance grow into very different lives in London and West Africa.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2016 is correct. Wikipedia dates the Hamish Hamilton book to November 2016. It was longlisted for the Booker Prize in 2017.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A mixed race woman whose name is never given, daughter of a Jamaican mother); Tracey (The narrator's gifted childhood friend, who stays in the old flat); Aimee (A global pop star who employs the narrator and starts a school abroad)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
In 1982 the unnamed narrator meets Tracey at a tap class in north London.
Tracey can dance.
The narrator has flat feet and turns toward books.
As an adult the narrator works for a pop star named Aimee.
Aimee builds a girls' school in a West African village, and the project turns sour.
The narrator is fired, her mother is dying, and she goes back to Tracey's flat.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Essays argue that the modern novel has failed to face climate change.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2016 is correct. It is nonfiction, not a novel. The database genre label Fiction is wrong. It grew from lectures at the University of Chicago in 2015.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Ghosh gave lectures on climate and fiction at the University of Chicago in 2015.
Part one, Stories, asks why serious novels avoid huge climate events.
Part two, History, ties the crisis to colonialism and cities built near dangerous coasts.
Part three, Politics, says empire, not only capitalism, drives the carbon economy.
He sets the Paris climate deal beside a 2015 church letter on the earth.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Archie Ferguson is born once in 1947 and then lives four different American lives.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2017 is correct. UK: Faber and Faber, 31 January 2017. It was shortlisted for the Man Booker Prize in 2017. The winner was Lincoln in the Bardo by George Saunders.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Archie Ferguson (One boy who becomes four parallel lives); Rose Ferguson (His mother, present in the family story); Stanley Ferguson (His father, whose business luck shifts between the versions)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Faber published the British edition on 31 January 2017. Henry Holt published it in the United States the same year.
Archibald Isaac Ferguson is born on 3 March 1947.
From that one birth, four separate lives run side by side.
Small accidents send each Ferguson toward a different family, love, and fate.
The four stories cross the storms of American life in the later twentieth century.
The novel was shortlisted for the Man Booker Prize in 2017 and did not win.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A history of how modern life feeds the anger behind today's strongman politics.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Published in 2017 by Allen Lane in the UK and by Farrar, Straus and Giroux in the United States. The database unit, non-fictional prose, matches the book. The full title is Age of Anger: A History of the Present.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Voltaire (The Enlightenment writer Mishra uses as a voice of rational progress); Jean-Jacques Rousseau (The thinker Mishra credits with seeing the hurts of modern life early)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book asks why nationalist anger and strongman politics (rule by force and grievance) spread in the 2010s.
Mishra says this shock began with modern industry and new ideas, not only with today's headlines.
He retells the quarrel of Voltaire and Jean-Jacques Rousseau in the Enlightenment (the 1700s push for reason).
He argues that Rousseau foresaw rootlessness, rivalry, and the hunger for goods.
He rejects the claim that liberal democracy (rights plus elections) has ended history.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Nadia and Saeed escape a war city through magic doors that open onto other countries.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
