fields.value: Database year 2017 is correct. Hamish Hamilton published the British edition on 2 March 2017. Riverhead published the American edition in the same year. It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize and did not win.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nadia (An independent woman who leaves her family and later leaves Saeed); Saeed (A more traditional young man who travels with Nadia); Saeed's father (He stays behind so he will not burden the couple)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Nadia and Saeed meet in a city that is sliding into civil war.
Saeed's mother is killed, and Nadia moves into the family home.
They pay to pass through a black door.
The door takes them to a refugee camp on Mykonos, then to London.
They later reach Marin, in California, and grow apart.
Years later Nadia returns and meets Saeed again.

items.title: "The Ministry of Utmost Happiness" (2017) — Arundhati Roy

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A hijra in a Delhi graveyard and a woman tied to Kashmir share a broken India.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2017 is correct. Hamish Hamilton published it on 6 June 2017. It was placed on the Booker long list. It did not win the prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Anjum (A hijra who founds a guest house in a Delhi graveyard); Tilo (An architect drawn into Kashmir and into a network of friends); Musa (Tilo's Kashmiri love, who becomes a militant); Saddam Hussain (A graveyard guest who wants justice for his father)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Anjum is born intersex and lives as a hijra (a transgender woman in South Asian society).
She leaves the hijra house and builds the Jannat Guest House in a Delhi graveyard.
The story also follows Tilo, an architect linked to three men and to Kashmir.
Violence in Gujarat, the Bhopal disaster, and the Kashmir war enter their lives.
The separate lives meet among mourners, militants, and people the city pushes aside.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A writer tells how marriage to a professor becomes beating, control, and escape.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2017 is correct. Full title: When I Hit You: Or, A Portrait of the Writer as a Young Wife. It was shortlisted for the Women's Prize for Fiction in 2018.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: The narrator (A young writer whose marriage is the story); The husband (A university professor who isolates her and beats her)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The novel appeared in 2017. Its subtitle echoes Joyce: a portrait of the writer as a young wife.
The unnamed narrator, a writer, falls in love with a university professor.
She moves with him to a small town and loses her email, her friends, and her work.
He beats her and forces sex on her, calling this a husband's right.
She writes the story in her head and finally leaves.
In 2018 it was shortlisted for the Women's Prize for Fiction and did not win.

items.title: "The Widows of Malabar Hill" (2018) — Sujata Massey

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Perveen Mistry, a woman lawyer in 1920s Bombay, uncovers a plot against three widows.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: The database year 2018 is correct. Wikipedia and Soho Press date the Soho Crime edition to January 2018. In India the same novel is called Murder on Malabar Hill. The story is set in the 1920s, not in 2018.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Perveen Mistry (A young Parsi woman lawyer who defends women's rights); Omar Farid (A wealthy Muslim mill owner whose will starts the case); The three widows (Farid's wives, living in seclusion and at risk of losing their inheritance)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Perveen Mistry joins her father's law firm in Bombay.
She is a Parsi, educated at Oxford, and one of India's first woman lawyers.
Three widows of the dead mill owner Omar Farid live in purdah on Malabar Hill.
Purdah means strict seclusion.
They do not speak with men.
All three seem to sign away their inheritance, and one signs with an X.
Perveen investigates, and the case becomes a murder.

fields.value: An older Tambu struggles in independent Zimbabwe, and the novel speaks to her as you.

fields.value: Tambudzai (The heroine again, now middle aged and addressed as you.)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Graywolf Press in the United States published it on 7 August 2018.
Tambu is now a tired woman in Harare, still chasing the success school promised.
The story says you, so the reader stands inside her shame and anger.
Jobs, housing, and violent men fail her, and she turns back toward her village.
The novel shows how old colonial harm and hard markets still wound a free country.
It was shortlisted for the Booker Prize, a major British novel prize, in 2020.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: In 1945 London, Nathaniel and his sister are left with a guardian called the Moth.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2018 is correct. Jonathan Cape published it on 8 May 2018. It was longlisted for the Man Booker Prize in 2018 and was not the winner.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Nathaniel (The narrator, a boy of fourteen in 1945 who later retells the past); Rachel (Nathaniel's sister, left behind with him); The Moth (The strange guardian who may be a criminal); The Darter (A friend of the Moth who draws the children into his work); Rose (Their mother, whose secret war work explains the abandonment)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jonathan Cape published the novel on 8 May 2018. It was longlisted for the Booker Prize.
It is 1945. London is still damaged by the Blitz (the wartime bombing).
Fourteen year old Nathaniel and his sister Rachel are left by their parents.
Their guardian is a shadowy man they call the Moth.
His friend the Darter pulls the children into secret, half criminal work.
Years later Nathaniel learns his mother Rose had hidden wartime duties.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A modern Don Quixote, dazed by television, travels America with an imagined son.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note
fields.value: Database year 2019 is correct. Quichotte was published in 2019 and shortlisted for the Booker Prize.

fields.label: Key Characters / Speakers
fields.value: Quichotte (A travelling salesman who models himself on Don Quixote); Sancho (The son Quichotte imagines as his companion); Sam DuChamp (The crime writer who invents Quichotte)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
A writer of spy novels creates a character named Quichotte.
Quichotte is a salesman lost in television and love.
He travels the roads of America, as Quixote once rode out.
His companion is Sancho, a son he imagines into being.
The writer's own family troubles echo the invented quest.
The novel was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 2019.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: Three women tell what happens in Gilead fifteen years later.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.value: Aunt Lydia (A powerful Aunt who records her own secret history); Agnes Jemima (A young woman raised inside Gilead); Daisy (A young woman raised in Canada)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book returns to the world of The Handmaid's Tale.
It is set about fifteen years after Offred's story.
Aunt Lydia writes a secret account from inside Gilead.
Agnes grows up in Gilead, and Daisy grows up in Canada.
Their papers together threaten the rulers of Gilead.

fields.value: A poetry book about love, friendship, and what remains when a story ends.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The poems speak of passion, friendship, and talk between people.
They also speak of myth and of moments when the human meets the divine.
A set of poems imagines Avvaiyar, a wise woman poet of Tamil literature.
The title names a love that is deeper than plot or nostalgia.
Westland published the Indian edition in 2019, and Bloodaxe published the British edition in 2020.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
It is the first novel of a planned trilogy, A Key to All Mythologies.
The story opens on 23 December 1971, in a suburb near Chicago.
Russ Hildebrandt, a pastor, wants to leave a cold marriage.
His wife Marion and their children Clem, Becky, and Perry each hide a crisis.
Each person wants a freedom that the others may wreck.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Klara is an AF, an Artificial Friend, waiting in a shop.
She is solar-powered and treats the Sun as a living kindness.
Josie, a sick lifted child (genetically enhanced), chooses her.
Josie's mother wants Klara to continue Josie if the girl dies.
Klara begs the Sun to heal Josie.
Josie recovers and leaves for college.
Faber published the novel on 2 March 2021. It was longlisted for the Booker Prize.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A historical novel about Rani Jindan, the last queen of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.

fields.label: NTA Publication Trap / Edition Note

fields.value: Jindan Kaur (Last queen of Ranjit Singh and mother of the child king Dalip); Ranjit Singh (Founder of the Sikh Empire and Jindan's husband); Dalip Singh (Jindan's son, who inherits the throne as a child)

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
Jindan, a kennel keeper's daughter, becomes Ranjit Singh's youngest queen.
After the king dies, she rules for her small son Dalip as regent (a stand-in ruler).
She leaves the zenana (women's quarters) and speaks to the Khalsa (Sikh) troops.
She resists the British in the wars for Punjab, but the kingdom is taken.
The British imprison her, exile her, and separate her from her son.

fields.label: One-Line Hook & Simple Summary
fields.value: A woman breathes a south Indian empire into life and lives to see it fall.

fields.label: Storyline / Argument Breakdown
fields.value:
The book pretends to retell an old epic by Pampa Kampana.
As a girl she receives a goddess's gift of long life and speech.
She whispers a city, Bisnaga, out of a bag of seeds.
Bisnaga stands for the historical empire of Vijayanagara.
She lives for more than two centuries and watches the city rise and fall.
The novel was published in February 2023, after the 2022 attack.

fields.value: Sonia and Sunny, two young Indians, meet across India and America after their families once tried to match them.

Sonia and Sunny first notice each other on an overnight train.
Their grandparents had already tried to arrange a match, and that plan drove them apart.

Sunny is a journalist in New York, trying to leave his mother and a violent family feud.

The book mixes a love story, a family saga, and a magical tale.

Sillitoe's story The Loneliness of the Long Distance Runner, which concerns a teenager, Smith from Nottingham is convicted for robbing a bakery and sent to Borstal (a prison for a convict set up in Britain) where he finds solace (comfort in a time of distress) in long distance running. He intentionally looses the race.

(1872-1970)
Bertrand Arthur William Russell, 3rd Earl of Russell was a British philosopher, logician Mathematician, Historian, Social critic and Political activist.
In the early 20th century, Russell let the British revolt against idealism. He is also considered one of the founders of Analytic Philosophy.
He was born in Monmouthshire (Britain) in 1872.
His Philosophical essay On Denoting has been considered the paradigm of Philosophy.
His work has had a considerable influence on specially the philosophy of language, epistemology and metaphysics.
Russell was a prominent anti-war activist, championed anti-imperialism.
He campaigned against Adolf Hitler, then criticized Stalinist's Totalitarianism.
In 1950 Russell was awarded the The Nobel Prize in Literature in recognition of his varied and significant ideals and freedom of thought.
At the age of 11 his brother Frank introduced him to work of Euclid which transformed Russell's life.
He was a member of Co-efficients Dining Club of social reforms set up in 1902 by the Fabicin campaigners Sidney and Beatrice Webb.
Russell was elected as Fellow of the Royal Society in 1908.
In 1941 G. H. Hardy wrote 61 page pamphlets titled Bertrand Russell ad Trinity.
A History of Western Philosophy (1945), became a best seller and provided Russell with a steady income for the remainder of his life.
In the King's Birthday Honours of 9 June 1949, Russell was awarded with the Order of Merit.
George VI said about him: "You have sometimes behaved in a manner that you would not do if generally adopted".
Russell made a cameo appearance, playing himself in the anti-war Hindi film Aman which was released in India in 1967.
He died of influenza on 02 February 1970 at his home.
He belongs to analytic school of Philosophy and was influenced by P. B. Shelley and J. S. Mill.

Christopher Fry was an English poet and a playwright.
He is well known for his verse drama The Lady's Not for Burning which made him a major force in theaters in 1940's and 1950's.
He was born as Arthur Hammond Harris; in Bristol.
He was the son of Charles John Harris and Emma Marguerite Fry Hammond Harris.
In 1920,he met the writer Robert Gritting who became his lifetime friend.
His play about Dr. Thomas John Bernardo, the founder of Children's Homes toured in fund raising amateur production in 1935.
Although Fry lived till 2005, his poetic style of drama began to fall out of fashion with the advent of Angry Young Man Movement of British theater in 1950's.
His last play was The Ringing of Bells (2001).
His wife Phyllis whom he married in 1936 died in 1987.
The later life of Fry lived in village of East Dean in the West Sussex and died of natural causes in 2005.
He has often been compared to T. S. Eliot in his taste for poetic drama.
His early works included a comedy A Phoenix Too Frequent (1996) based on the Latin writer Petronius (identified with a novelist Gaius Petronius who was in Emperor Nero's court.)
He also adapted Jean Anvuilh's Ring Round the Moon (1950).
The Lady's Not for Burning (1949) became famous west end play starring Gielgud and Richard Burton.
In 1986, he wrote One Thing More, a play about the 7th century Northumbrian monk named Caedmon.
He translated Henry Ibsen's Peer Gynt.

It is a comic novel that labels the story of 6 months academic exchange program between fictional universities located in Rummidge (modeled on Birmingham in England) and Plotinus (modeled on Berkeley in California), in the state of Euphoria .
The two academics taking part in the exchange are both aged 40, and have different academic systems of their native countries.
The English participant is Philip Swallow while the American is Morris Zapp.
The novel ends with these two couples convened in a New York hotel room to decide their fates.
The novel ends without clear cut decision through the sequel Small World: An Academic Romance in which it reveals that Swallow and Zapp return to their own country. (1955- )
Geraldine Brooks is an Australian-American journalist and author whose 2005 Novel "March" won the Pulitzer Prize for fiction in 2006.
While retaining her Australian passport, she became a United States citizen in 2002.
As a foreign correspondent for The Wall Street Journal, she covered crisis in Africa, the Balkans and the Middle East with the stories from Persian Gulf.
Brooks' first book, Nine Parts of Desire (1994) based on her experiences among Muslim women in the Middle east, was an International best seller.
Foreign Correspondence (1997) was a memoir and travel adventure about a child enriched by penal from around the world and her adult quest to find them.
Her first novel Year of Wonders published in 2001, set in 1666, the story depicts a young woman's battle to save fellow villagers as well as her own soul when the Bubonic Plague suddenly strikes her small Derbyshire village of Eyam. The protagonist is Anna Frith.
Her next novel March (2005) was inspired by her fondness for Louisa May Alcott's Little Woman, which her mother had given her.
In her next novel "People of the Book" (2008), Brooks explored a fictionalized history of the Sarajevo Haggadah. This novel was inspired by her reporting (For the New Yorker) of human interest stories emerging in the aftermath of the 1991-1995 breakup of Yugoslavia.
This novel won the both Australian Book of the Year Award and the Australian Literary Fiction Award 2008.
Her 2011 novel "Caleb's Crossing" is inspired by the life of Caleb Cheishahteamauk, a wampanoacf converting to Christianity who was the first Native American to graduate from Harvard College, an achievement of 17th century. Important Works of Geraldine Brooks: Novels 1. Year of Wonders: A Novel of the Plague (2001): It is a historical fiction. 2. March (2005): Historical Novel, retells Louisa May Alcott's novel Little Women from the point of view of Alcott's protagonist's absent father. Brooks has inserted the novel into the classic tale, revealing the events surrounding March's absence during the American Civil War in 1862. 3. People of the Book (2008): It is a historical novel. The story focuses on imagined events surrounding protagonist and real historical part of still extant Sarajevo Haggadah, one of the oldest surviving Jewish illuminated texts.
It tells the fictional story of Hanna Heath, an Australian Book, and Consorter who is restoring the Haggadah. 4. The Secret Chord (2015): A historical based on the life of the Biblical King David in the period of the Second Iron age. The title is taken from Leonard Cohen's Song-Hallelujah"

Dame Margaret Drabble Lady Holroyd is an English novelist, biographer and critic.
She was born in Sheffield, England to novelist John F. Drabble and teacher Kathleen Marie.
She joined the Royal Shakespeare Company at Strafford -upon-Avon in 1960.
Drabble published 18 novels through 2013.
Her first novel A Summer Bird Cage was published in 1963.
Het third novel The Millston (1965) brought her The John Llewelly Rhys Memorial Prize in 1966 and Jeruselam the Golden in 1965.
She also won the James Tait Black Memorial Prize in 1967, for Jerusalem the Golden (an autobiographical novel).
She also wrote The Needle Eye in 1972.
A theme of her novel is the co-relation between contemporary English society and its members.
Drabble also edited two edition of The Oxford Companion to English Literature in 1958 and 2000.
In 2011, A Day in the Life of A Smiling Woman, is a collection of Drabble's short stories.
Drabble chaired the National Book League (now Book Trust) from 1980-1982.
She was awarded the Golden PEN Award by English PEN, for "A Lifetime Distinguished Service to Literature".
She was married to actor Clive Swift (1960-1975).
In 1982 she married writer and biographer Sir Michael Holroyd.
Three of Drabble's first six novels have biblical titles. The Milestone was the first, Jerusalem the Golden is second and The Needle's Eye is third.
AC Byatt (older sister of Margaret) was not happy with the representation of their mother by Drabble.

He was originally born as Avidger Rousseau Emanuel in 1879, in England but died in New York in 1960.
He was primarily a writer of pulp fiction. Pulp Fiction: The term was originated from 20th century magazines which were printed on cheap 'pulp' paper and published fantastic fiction for the general entertainment of mass audience.
He was an active writer in Great Britain as well as in United States during first half of 20th century.
During first two decades of his career he wrote pre-dominantly under the following pen names:.
Victor Rousseau.
H. M. Egbert.
V. R .Emanuel But in 1930, he officially abandoned these numerous pseudonyms and established himself as Victor Rousseau in the field of pulp fiction.
In London he wrote his first novel, Derwent's Horse which is a fictional humorous account of two recruits within the spoofed Bethune's mounted infantry.
In 1902, he wrote his second novel Spartacus. It was written along the lines of Gustav Flaubert's novel, Salammbo.
Rousseau assisted with the Jewish encyclopedia published by Funk and Wagnalls in 1905-1906.
In early 1906-1907 he wrote Florida regional articles for the Baltimore articles.
He took an editorial post with Will Carleton's Everywhere Magazine.
The first professional magazine of Rousseau was The Last Cartridge.
In 1909 he wrote his landmark series The Surgeon of Souls which featured Dr. Evan Brodsky, a man who believed in faith and hypnotism as a cure towards laying ghosts etc. As it was received very poorly so the surviving tales were reprinted as original fiction with Weird Tales Magazine under the pseudonym Victor Rousseau.
The first Science fiction was the ill fated series The Devil Chair. John Haynes, an English man stripped of inherited land in America, is paralyzed by a bullet to the spine and rail-roaded into prison and left there to rot.
While in workshops Haynes fashions a gyroscopic device that whilst adhered initially to a boot, propels him a couple hundred miles/hour and whilst affixed to any object, can't be removed until he himself deactivates it.
In 1913 through 1919, he moved from New York to Canada and there he was influenced to write best fictions of his literary career, with Jacqueline of Golden River, and Wooden Spoil.
In 1914, his magnum opus The Messiah of Cylinder was published. It was an answering cry against H. G. Wells' When the Sleeper Wakes.
